papers.selection_reason: VLA model with learned foveation actions replacing wrist cameras for manipulation.
papers.title: FoveaVLA: Foveation Actions Replace the Wrist Camera in VLAs
papers.tldr: FoveaVLA replaces a wrist camera with learned image foveation, enabling external-camera VLAs to recover fine manipulation details and improve real-world performance.

papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of large vision language models (LVLMs) has made geolocation inference from images highly accurate and accessible. This poses serious privacy risks: a passive adversary with black-box LVLM access can infer a user's location from a single photo with no metadata. Existing protection methods rely almost exclusively on adversarial perturbation, which introduces perceptible visual artifacts and utility degradation. We identify the visual-geolocation asymmetry: geolocation-decisive clues, such as street signs, tend to be visually peripheral but dominate location inference. Exploiting this asymmetry, we propose GeoCloak, an agentic framework for semantics-preserving geolocation privacy protection. It acts as a clue-aware planner that analyzes each image to identify geolocation-relevant clues, dispatches targeted semantic edits to directly suppress peripheral clues, and autonomously configures adversarial perturbation to further suppress residual geolocation features, all under iterative utility-aware feedback. We evaluate GeoCloak on four diverse datasets spanning 108 countries and 576 cities against five LVLMs and three inference methods. GeoCloak reduces overall city-level accuracy from 41.2% to 9.9%, approximately half of the best-performing baseline, while achieving substantially superior utility preservation both qualitatively and quantitatively. We hope this work takes a meaningful step toward practical, semantics-preserving geolocation privacy protection, giving users greater control over the location information inadvertently embedded in their shared images.
authors: Yixin Wu, Mingjie Li, Yun Shen, Michael Backes, Yang Zhang
bullets: Targets the risk that black-box vision-language models can infer locations from ordinary photos without metadata.
Exploits the asymmetry that geolocation-critical clues, such as street signs, are often visually peripheral.
Uses an agentic planner for clue detection, targeted semantic edits, adaptive perturbation, and utility-aware iteration.
Evaluated across four datasets covering 108 countries and 576 cities, with five LVLMs and three inference methods.
Reduced city-level geolocation accuracy from 41.2% to 9.9% while preserving utility better than the evaluated baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic manipulation of geolocation clues in LVLMs, relevant to spatial/geolocation understanding and multimodal model robustness.
papers.title: GeoCloak: An Agentic Framework for Semantics-Preserving Geolocation Privacy via Peripheral Clue Manipulation
papers.tldr: GeoCloak protects image geolocation privacy by identifying and editing peripheral location clues while preserving overall image semantics.

papers.abstract: In recent years, with advances in multimodal interaction technologies and the growing demand for intelligent emotional support, Multimodal Emotional Support Conversation (MESC) has emerged as an important task. However, existing systems still suffer from shallow responses and inappropriate support strategies due to weak semantic feedback, cross-dimension reward compensation, and coarse reasoning supervision. To address these challenges, we propose FACES, a fine-grained gated semantic alignment framework for MESC. Specifically, FACES integrates multi-source rewards to construct multidimensional semantic and functional alignment signals, employs a non-compensatory gated fusion mechanism to reduce cross-dimension reward offset, and leverages structured Chain-of-Thought (CoT) anchors to perform token-level credit assignment. Under a controlled response-length protocol, FACES improves the average MLLM-based evaluation score from 3.61 to 4.04 and achieves an 80.22% pairwise win rate over SOTA. Human evaluation under the same protocol yields a 75.3% preference rate. Results on three external datasets further support transferability. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/OCT-ARR/arr.
authors: Hang Ren, Peidong Wang, Yichen Gao, Wen Zhang, Jiayang Yu, Xiaocui Yang, Shi Feng
bullets: Targets shallow responses and inappropriate support strategies caused by weak semantic feedback, reward compensation, and coarse reasoning supervision.
Combines multi-source rewards into multidimensional semantic and functional alignment signals.
Uses non-compensatory gated fusion to reduce cross-dimension reward offset and structured CoT anchors for token-level credit assignment.
Under controlled response length, improves the average MLLM evaluation score from 3.61 to 4.04, with an 80.22% pairwise win rate and 75.3% human preference rate.
Results on three external datasets support transferability; code and dataset are publicly available.
papers.selection_reason: Multimodal emotional support conversation framework with gated semantic alignment and CoT supervision.
papers.title: FACES: Fine-grained Gated Semantic Alignment for Multimodal Emotional Support Conversation
papers.tldr: FACES improves multimodal emotional-support responses through fine-grained reward alignment, gated fusion, and structured reasoning supervision.

papers.abstract: Progress toward general intelligence in the physical world requires scaling robot learning across diverse environments and interactions. However, existing robot policies use shared parameters that remain fixed across interaction contexts. When different operations favor competing parameter adjustments, fitting their mixture can leave individual operations insufficiently adapted. Our atomic-task diagnostics reveal competing update directions in both vision-language and action parameters, with source-improving updates increasing loss on other tasks. This motivates MorphAct, a contextual parameterization framework that dynamically adjusts robot policy parameters as interaction contexts change. Two coupled generators produce context-dependent low-rank updates for the vision-language and action modules. Their coupling follows the policy's computational dependency: vision-language updates shape the representations that condition action-side parameter generation. Both generators are trained jointly through the native action objective, without operation labels or expert-adapter targets. MorphAct improves performance across three VLA backbones on LIBERO and Meta-World, with gains of up to 16.30%. In real-world evaluation, it achieves gains of up to 14% over $\pi_{0.5}$. Ablations support the benefits of contextual parameter generation and representation coupling.
authors: Ziyan Liu, Jiting Liu, Weihong Zhong, Wenda Yu, Yeqiu Chen, Jason Li, Xiaojiang Peng, Shuyuan Hu, Kai Wang, Bo Zhao
bullets: Fixed shared parameters can struggle when different robot operations require competing updates.
MorphAct generates context-dependent low-rank updates for both vision-language and action modules.
Coupled generators follow the policy’s dependency structure, letting vision-language updates influence action-side parameter generation.
The framework is trained with the native action objective, without operation labels or expert-adapter targets.
It reports gains of up to 16.30% on LIBERO and Meta-World and up to 14% over π₀.₅ in real-world evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Contextual parameter generation for VLA robot policies, improving adaptation across interaction contexts.
papers.title: MorphAct: Robot Policies Morphing with the Worlds They Act In
papers.tldr: MorphAct dynamically morphs robot-policy parameters to fit changing interaction contexts, improving manipulation performance across simulated and real-world evaluations.

papers.abstract: Chemistry evaluation has moved past multiple-choice probes toward open-ended expert problems, yet the benchmarks that define the current frontier still score answer endpoints alone. Such scoring conflates memorized facts with stepwise derivation, treats visual and textual inputs as interchangeable, and confounds long-horizon planning with stepwise execution. These blind spots prevent any diagnosis of where the reasoning chain breaks in a model. We present ChemArgus, a competition-level chemistry benchmark drawn from chemistry competition material, textbooks, and research papers, whose scoring replaces the answer endpoint with three measurement properties. Fine-grained scoring grades every subquestion point by point with partial credit, so a score lands at the level of the step rather than the outcome. Multimodal capability is priced on every problem containing a real image, paired with a controlled text description, so visual understanding is measured against text on identical tasks. Diagnostic attribution reads paired metrics that share one scoring unit and differ only in context construction, so a gap between two scores isolates a single cause, namely integration, propagation, or local reasoning. GPT-5.6-Sol scores 23.2% on unassisted whole-problem solving against 28.8% and 30.4% under the two sequential metrics, a gap measuring the integration burden. Through rubric partial credit and these cause-isolating score gaps, ChemArgus shows not only whether a model answers chemistry correctly but where its reasoning chain fails, so that every score it reports doubles as a diagnosis, a readout of the chain rather than a verdict, aiming to guide language models step by step on their path toward chemistry expertise, one corrected step at a time, each step priced by the rubric, point by point.
authors: Hanyao Guo, Mo Cui, Zihan Tan, Leixin Sun, Yichun Wang, Yinan Shen, Guojun Zhu, Jia Jiang, Erhao Chen, Zui Chen, Wenzhe Gao, Zhihao Yu, Qijun Wang, Yetian Zhu, Jiande Chen, Chuhang Pei, Yao Jiang, Yichen Fan, Pinhan Wang, Xiaorui Pan, Qianyi Zhu, Yang Liu, Mang Ye, Guancheng Wan
bullets: Targets blind spots in endpoint-only evaluation, including memorization versus derivation, visual versus textual understanding, and planning versus execution.
Uses point-by-point rubric scoring with partial credit to evaluate intermediate subquestion steps.
Pairs real-image problems with controlled text descriptions to measure multimodal understanding on equivalent tasks.
Compares sequentially constructed metrics to attribute score gaps to integration, propagation, or local reasoning.
For GPT-5.6-Sol, reports 23.2% on unassisted whole-problem solving versus 28.8% and 30.4% on the two sequential metrics, illustrating an integration gap.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and diagnostic methodology for multimodal LLM reasoning, separating visual and textual understanding.
papers.title: ChemArgus: Automated Scientific Diagnostics for Lab-Grade Multimodal Chemistry Reasoning: A Frontier Benchmark
papers.tldr: ChemArgus is a diagnostic multimodal chemistry benchmark that identifies which reasoning steps and capabilities cause models to fail, rather than scoring only final answers.

papers.abstract: Scaling self-supervised contrastive reinforcement learning (CRL) to 1000-layer Euclidean neural networks has enabled state-of-the-art goal-reaching performance, yet wall-clock time scales linearly with depth. We find that changing the geometry achieves stronger performance with far shallower networks. This matters in complex navigation environments, where walls can make route distance deviate substantially from Euclidean distance. In a U-shaped maze, we show that the longer the route, the more it deviates from Euclidean distance. Hyperbolic CRL addresses this mismatch by replacing Euclidean distances in CRL's contrastive objective with geodesic distances in hyperbolic space. On hard navigation tasks, inductive bias beats scale: depth 64 hyperbolic agents outperform 1024-layer-deep Euclidean networks while training more than $12 \times$ faster and using about $13 \times$ fewer parameters. We observe that hyperbolic agents behave qualitatively better in hard humanoid mazes, where they follow corridors to reach goals, whereas Euclidean agents try straight-line shortcuts over walls. Our results show that matching the representation geometry to the task can substitute for substantial network depth. Code is at https://github.com/Probabilistic-and-Interactive-ML/HypGCRL .
authors: Timo Klein, Thomas Lang, Andrii Shkabrii, Lukas Miklautz, Yllka Velaj, Sebastian Tschiatschek
bullets: Euclidean distance poorly reflects route distance in environments with obstacles and walls.
Hyperbolic CRL replaces Euclidean distances in the contrastive objective with hyperbolic geodesic distances.
Depth-64 hyperbolic agents outperform depth-1024 Euclidean agents on hard navigation tasks.
Hyperbolic agents train over 12× faster and use about 13× fewer parameters.
In hard humanoid mazes, hyperbolic agents follow corridors instead of attempting straight-line paths through walls.
papers.selection_reason: Goal-conditioned RL with hyperbolic representations for navigation in maze and humanoid environments.
papers.title: Outperforming 1000 Euclidean Layers With Hyperbolic Goal-Conditioned RL
papers.tldr: Hyperbolic goal-conditioned contrastive RL matches maze geometry, enabling much shallower agents to outperform far deeper Euclidean networks while training faster and using fewer parameters.

papers.abstract: Transformers can perform in-context reinforcement learning without parameter updates. However, existing theoretical constructions often require context sizes that grow with the number of sampled transitions, leading to increasing memory costs in large-scale problems. This raises a fundamental scalability question: how much context is intrinsically necessary to carry out such learning? We answer this question for fixed-policy TD evaluation. We show that, with a shared linear decoder, the minimum context dimension required to exactly reproduce the first $L$ TD iterates is the Krylov dimension induced by the sampled transitions. When the available context dimension $m$ falls below this threshold, exact reproduction is no longer possible. In this regime, we characterize the optimal approximation error and show that it decays as $\Theta(\gamma^m\max\{1,1/(m(1-\gamma))\})$ where $\gamma$ is the discounting factor. Moving from representation complexity to actual memory cost, we characterize the optimal retained memory for exact continuous representations as $\Theta(nk_L)$ and show experimentally that on a sampled task whose exact rank is full but whose numerical rank is small, a context accurate to $10^{-2}$ is $88.7\%$ smaller than the sparse sufficient statistics of TD. Finally, we establish the learnability of the shared executor through pretraining by proving global convergence of an auxiliary objective over effective attention parameters under suitable task diversity. Experiments across diverse TD evaluation problems validate parameter recovery and the predicted context--accuracy tradeoff.
authors: Yajie Zhao, Yingjun Mo, Zhiyong Wang, Bo Tang, Chao Xu, Fang Kong
bullets: For fixed-policy TD evaluation with a shared linear decoder, exact reproduction of the first L TD iterates requires context dimension equal to the transitions’ induced Krylov dimension.
Below this threshold, exact reproduction is impossible; the optimal approximation error decays as Θ(γ^m max{1, 1/[m(1−γ)]}).
The optimal retained memory for exact continuous representations scales as Θ(nk_L).
On a sampled task with full exact rank but low numerical rank, context accurate to 10⁻² used 88.7% less memory than TD’s sparse sufficient statistics.
The paper also proves global convergence for pretraining the shared executor under suitable task diversity, with experiments validating parameter recovery and the context–accuracy tradeoff.
papers.selection_reason: Provable transformer context compression and memory-accuracy tradeoffs directly relate to efficient token/context handling.
papers.title: Provable Transformer Context Compression for In-Context Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: The paper characterizes the minimum context and memory needed for transformers to reproduce or approximate TD-learning iterates in-context, and shows substantial compression is possible when sampled transitions have low numerical rank.

papers.abstract: Reconstruction of 3D structures using under-ice AUV video footage has been inaccurate, although it is not certain whether this is due to shortcomings in the methods or an inherent deficiency of the capture system. We test four different models for reconstruction on the same Antarctic under-ice AUV video (Icefin, Kamb Ice Stream): classical feature matching SfM, differentiable photometric splatting, volumetric depth fusion, and a pose-free feed-forward foundation model. All four fail, each in a distinct way: near-total registration yielding almost no structure, geometrically broken output despite healthy photometric metrics, a persistent coverage artifact, and unstable cross-chunk scale. We show that all four are consistent with the same capture regime, a small camera-baseline-to-scene-depth ratio. Following our analysis, we propose a detection system that flags this type of failure in minutes, rather than hours of wasted compute.
authors: Ana-\c{S}tefania Kog\u{a}lniceanu, Kl\'ara Orb\'an, Ashwin Nedungadi, Stefan L\"udtke, Kuderna-Iulian Ben\c{t}a
bullets: Evaluates four reconstruction approaches on the same Antarctic under-ice AUV video.
All methods fail differently: insufficient registration, geometric distortion, coverage artifacts, or unstable scale.
The failures share a common cause: a low camera-baseline-to-scene-depth ratio.
Proposes a detector that flags likely reconstruction failure within minutes instead of after extensive computation.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes and predicts failure regimes of 3D reconstruction from underwater AUV video, relevant to robust 3D vision.
papers.title: Why 3D Reconstruction Breaks Down on Under-Ice AUV Video, and How to Predict It
papers.tldr: Under-ice AUV video can make 3D reconstruction fail across very different methods because the camera baseline is too small relative to scene depth, but this failure can be detected quickly.

papers.abstract: Looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models combine parameter reuse with sparse computation to improve performance under matched budgets. Prior work demonstrates that different loop visits can play different roles even when they share parameters. To probe the contributions of different loop visits, we learn separate residual coefficients in a model that applies a shared block twice, observing a smaller scale in the first visit. Fixed coefficient experiments show that reducing the first visit's scale preserves or improves performance, whereas the same reductions to the second hurt it. This asymmetry motivates us to explore asymmetric compute allocation. We propose \textbf{LatentLoop}, which compresses the first visit's sequence, retains full resolution in the second, and reallocates saved computation to increase the hidden size. We further learn how strongly the first visit updates the full sequence, and share MoE weights across visits while using separate attention parameters to accommodate their different sequence resolutions. Across 15 configurations spanning 1.3B--7B parameters, with the largest budget exceeding $10^{21}$ FLOPs, LatentLoop consistently lowers validation NLL. At a fitted NLL of 1.988, predicted compute savings are 19.0\% and 7.9\% relative to vanilla MoE and the looped baseline. It also improves average scores on nine benchmarks at all sizes in 0-shot and 5-shot settings. These results suggest asymmetric compute allocation is a promising direction for looped MoE models.
authors: Zefeng He, Yunkai Chai, Xiaoyang Chen, Tong Zhu, Zongliang Wu, Yun Luo, Yafu Li, Yu Cheng
bullets: Different loop visits contribute asymmetrically: reducing computation in the first visit is less harmful than reducing it in the second.
The method compresses the first visit’s sequence, keeps the second at full resolution, and increases hidden size with the saved compute.
It learns the first visit’s update strength, shares MoE weights across visits, and uses separate attention parameters for differing resolutions.
Across 15 configurations from 1.3B to 7B parameters, it consistently lowers validation NLL and improves average scores on nine benchmarks in 0-shot and 5-shot settings.
At fitted NLL 1.988, it predicts 19.0% and 7.9% compute savings versus vanilla MoE and the looped baseline, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: Looped MoE language model architecture with asymmetric compute allocation and sequence compression for efficiency.
papers.title: LatentLoop: Scaling Looped MoE Models with Asymmetric Compute Allocation
papers.tldr: LatentLoop improves looped MoE efficiency by compressing the first loop visit and reallocating its saved computation to model capacity.

papers.abstract: Federated fine-tuning enables large language models (LLMs) to learn collaboratively from distributed client data, but malicious client updates can compromise global model safety. As federated tasks evolve, changing malicious update patterns challenge the ability of existing defenses to maintain reliable risk detection over time. To address this challenge, we propose Safe-FCL, a framework integrating continual risk awareness with fine-grained safety aggregation for federated continual learning of LLMs. Specifically, the Continual Risk Awareness (CRA) mechanism learns emerging risk patterns across sequential tasks and constrains detector updates using a protective subspace derived from historical features, mitigating forgetting of previously learned malicious patterns while adapting to new risks. To translate risk awareness into aggregation-level safety control, the Fine-Grained Safety Aggregation (FGSA) mechanism combines client-level risk assessments from CRA with module-level deviations from historical update behavior to adaptively regulate aggregation contributions, suppressing potentially malicious updates while minimizing unnecessary restrictions on benign updates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Safe-FCL outperforms current SOTA methods, improving global-model Rule and MD-Judge scores in federated continual learning by 0.41% and 0.64%, respectively, while increasing average risk recognition accuracy by 2.01%.
authors: Shuaijie Ma, Yongkang Hu, Yu Cheng, Jiuan Zhou, Yi Xie, Yushuo Zhang, Zhaoxia Yin
bullets: Addresses changing malicious-update patterns that can undermine global LLM safety over sequential federated tasks.
Continual Risk Awareness preserves historical risk knowledge while adapting to emerging threats.
Fine-Grained Safety Aggregation combines client-level risk and module-level update deviations to regulate contributions.
Experiments report gains of 0.41% in Rule, 0.64% in MD-Judge, and 2.01% in average risk-recognition accuracy.],
problem that?
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses continual learning of LLMs under evolving federated tasks, fitting the continual/online learning subtopic.
papers.title: Safe-FCL: Continual Risk Awareness and Fine-Grained Safety Aggregation for Federated Continual Learning of LLMs
papers.tldr: Safe-FCL improves safety in federated continual learning of LLMs by continually detecting evolving malicious updates and selectively limiting their aggregation impact.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) jointly predict future visual states and robot actions, but processing dense future-frame tokens incurs substantial inference latency. We propose CF-Prune, a training-free framework for pruning future-frame tokens in pretrained WAMs. Our key insight is that future visual predictions support action generation and therefore need not preserve every visual detail required for high-fidelity video synthesis. CF-Prune combines instruction and action attention to identify task-relevant tokens during the initial denoising forward pass, even when future-frame and action representations remain highly noisy. An entropy-based phase identification mechanism further retains dense computation during precision phases to mitigate pruning-induced performance degradation. Experiments on RoboLab, RoboCasa, and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate consistent inference speedups. At a 35% pruning ratio, CF-Prune achieves average speedups of 1.19-1.27x while improving task success rates. At a 50% pruning ratio, it achieves 1.29-1.33x average speedups on both simulation benchmarks, with overall success rates within 1.0 percentage point of the baseline.
authors: Baekseung Kim, Junhoo Lee, Sohyeon Hong, Suhyun Jeon, Minkyu Kim, Seungyeon Kim, Donghoon Han, Nojun Kwak
bullets: Addresses high inference latency from dense future-frame token processing in world action models.
Uses instruction and action attention to identify task-relevant tokens during early denoising, without training.
An entropy-based phase mechanism keeps dense computation during precision-sensitive phases.
At 35% pruning, it delivers 1.19–1.27× speedups while improving task success rates.
At 50% pruning, it reaches 1.29–1.33× speedups on simulation benchmarks with success within 1.0 percentage point of baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free future-frame token pruning for world action models, improving inference efficiency on manipulation tasks.
papers.title: Complementary Future Token Pruning for World Action Models
papers.tldr: CF-Prune accelerates pretrained world action models by pruning less task-relevant future-visual tokens while preserving robot-action performance.

papers.abstract: Weight pruning can degrade the accuracy of large reasoning models (LRMs), yet it remains unclear whether it damages reasoning itself. We find that much of this degradation stems from a failure to stop rather than to reason. As sparsity increases, pruned LRMs increasingly fail to terminate within the token budget, often after the correct answer has appeared in their reasoning, instead falling into repetitive loops, even though they still recognize where the dense model would stop. We further find that the hidden-state difference between terminating and looping continuations is consistent across pruned checkpoints, suggesting a shared direction associated with committing to an answer. Building on this, we propose Termination-Guided Activation Steering (TGAS), a training-free method that adds this direction to the residual stream at inference time. Across six LRMs, three pruning pipelines, and math and code benchmarks, TGAS improves termination and overall accuracy while reducing repetitive reasoning and generation length, showing that this failure is actionable.
authors: Minh-Anh Nguyen, Nguyen T. Ha Lan, Xiyan Fu, Dung D. Le, Wei Lu
bullets: Pruned models frequently continue reasoning past a correct answer and exceed the token budget through repetitive loops.
This degradation reflects impaired termination more than impaired reasoning: models often recognize where the dense model would stop.
Terminating and looping continuations show a consistent hidden-state difference across pruned checkpoints.
Termination-Guided Activation Steering (TGAS) adds this shared direction to the residual stream during inference.
Across six models, three pruning pipelines, and math/code benchmarks, TGAS improves termination and accuracy while reducing repetition and generation length.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes and recovers pruned large reasoning models via termination-guided activation steering.
papers.title: To Reason but Not to Stop: Understanding and Recovering Pruned Large Reasoning Models
papers.tldr: Pruning often makes large reasoning models loop instead of stop, and a training-free activation-steering method can recover termination and accuracy.

papers.abstract: This work presents a compact and reproducible pipeline for synthesizing and curating image-based instruction-response pairs for DCVLR. We draw from the Cauldron collection and use Magpie-style instruction and response synthesis with Qwen2.5-VL-7B Instruct to create concise, image-conditioned instruction pairs. The pipeline consists of instruction synthesis, conditioned on input images and controlled via a system prompt, sanitization, tagging, and filtering of the instructions based on the score obtained by a reward model (DeBERTa-v3). We retain samples with positive scores to maximize the quality of the generated instructions. We observe that score distributions have a median and mean reward score of ~ 1.53 and ~ 1.75 respectively, indicating that most generated instructions are of good quality. The resulting dataset contains diverse instructions in the math, spatial, and social reasoning domains.
authors: Eleni E. Kasoura, Dimitrios Damianos, Georgios Paraskevopoulos, Vassilios Katsouros
bullets: Starts from the Cauldron image collection and generates concise instruction-response pairs with Qwen2.5-VL-7B Instruct using Magpie-style synthesis.
Sanitizes and tags generated instructions before filtering them with a DeBERTa-v3 reward model.
Retains samples with positive reward scores; the abstract reports mean and median scores of approximately 1.75 and 1.53.
The resulting dataset covers math, spatial, and social reasoning domains.
The work is presented as a DCVLR competition submission with an emphasis on compact, reproducible data construction.
papers.selection_reason: Synthetic instruction-data pipeline for image-conditioned multimodal instruction tuning, relevant to multimodal LLM training.
papers.title: Instruction Mining From Images: Constructing a Synthetic Dataset for Multimodal Learning ILSP DCVLR Competition Submission
papers.tldr: A compact pipeline uses vision-language generation and reward-based filtering to build a synthetic dataset of diverse image-conditioned instructions for multimodal learning.

papers.abstract: Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3) is a foundation model for image and video segmentation that sets the state of the art in visual object tracking. Its tracker, inherited from SAM 2, stores information from past frames in a memory bank, managed by a simple First-In-First-Out rule, allowing temporal consistency in complex videos. Several recent methods improve SAM 2 with hand-crafted memory update rules, each targeting a specific failure mode, such as distractors, occlusions, or object motion. However, their gains transfer only partially to the stronger SAM 3 backbone. We instead present a more general, data-driven approach that frames memory control as a sequential decision-making task. SAM3RL is an extension of the SAM 3 tracker with a lightweight memory controller, trained by reinforcement learning, that decides which frames enter the memory bank in order to maximize tracking performance. SAM3RL sets a new state of the art on 10 of 12 tracking and video object segmentation benchmarks, outperforming all hand-crafted rules without any runtime overhead. The same approach applied to SAM 2 gives SAM2RL, which outperforms hand-crafted rules on 9 of the 12 benchmarks, showing the generality of our method across model generations.
authors: Tom\'a\v{s} \v{C}\'i\v{z}ek, Matej Straka, Illia Volkov, Mat\v{e}j Kripner, Ervin Maci\'c, Jiri Matas, Klara Janouskova, Martin Schmid
bullets: Addresses the limitations of FIFO and hand-crafted memory-update rules for handling distractors, occlusions, and object motion.
Adds a lightweight memory controller that treats memory selection as a sequential decision-making problem.
The controller is trained with reinforcement learning to maximize tracking performance.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on 10 of 12 tracking and video object segmentation benchmarks.
Applying the same approach to SAM 2 also outperforms hand-crafted rules on 9 of 12 benchmarks, indicating cross-generation generality.
papers.selection_reason: RL-based memory control for visual object tracking in SAM 3; fits video understanding and tracking.
papers.title: SAM3RL: Memory Control via Reinforcement Learning for Visual Object Tracking
papers.tldr: SAM3RL uses reinforcement learning to control which frames enter SAM 3’s memory bank, improving visual object tracking without runtime overhead.

papers.abstract: Reasoning over infinitely long documents is becoming a reality with recurrent memory agents. However, increasing context length exacerbates the trade-off between reasoning performance and inference efficiency. Inspired by Kahneman's account of fast and slow thinking, we propose MemDuet, a dual-process memory framework that learns to coordinate a small language model for fast, parallel evidence selection from raw context chunks (System 1) with a large language model for memory-update verification and memory updates in document order (System 2). We train MemDuet in three stages: supervised fine-tuning of System 1 for evidence selection, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) of System 2 for verification and memory rewriting, and joint optimization of both policies to coordinate selection and updating for long-context reasoning. Experiments on diverse long-context reasoning benchmarks (RULER-HQA, LongBench v2, and 2WikiMultiHopQA) demonstrate a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off as context length grows. Averaged across evaluation settings on the three datasets, MemDuet achieves an end-to-end inference speedup of 9.74x and an output-token reduction of 73.91% relative to RL-MemAgent.
authors: Jiangcheng Song, Haodong Jing, Yulin Mu, Lesong Tao, Jixin Wang, Jin Cui, Tianjing Ren, Runxuan Xie, Yongqiang Ma, Nanning Zheng
bullets: Addresses the accuracy–inference-efficiency trade-off in reasoning over very long documents.
Uses a small language model for parallel evidence selection and a large language model for ordered memory verification and updates.
Trains the two systems through supervised evidence-selection tuning, GRPO-based memory optimization, and joint coordination.
Evaluated on RULER-HQA, LongBench v2, and 2WikiMultiHopQA, achieving a 9.74× end-to-end speedup and 73.91% fewer output tokens than RL-MemAgent.
The abstract scopes results to the reported long-context benchmarks and evaluation settings.
papers.selection_reason: Dual-process memory framework for long-context reasoning with improved accuracy-efficiency trade-off.
papers.title: MemDuet: Learning Dual-Process Memory for Long-Context Reasoning
papers.tldr: MemDuet coordinates fast evidence selection with slower memory verification to improve long-context reasoning efficiency while preserving accuracy as contexts grow.

papers.abstract: Learning and executing long-horizon robot manipulation as complete task trajectories raises data-collection costs, lim?its capability reuse, and causes local failures to cascade into later task stages. We introduce manipulation units (MUs) as reusable operations, each defined by a local goal, an initi?ation condition, and observable success and failure criteria. MUs are learned and verified individually. During execution, consecutive MUs remain coupled through shared environ?ment dynamics. We formulate MU-Structured Manipulation (MUSM) and realize it through MU-Centric Orchestration (MUCO). Given language and vision, MUCO constructs an MU sequence, matches each MU to compatible policy models in a frozen capability registry, and dispatches the model with the highest calibrated success rate. Visual verification checks MU outcomes against success and failure criteria and governs transitions, enabling retry or fallback to another model from the current state without re-executing verified MUs. Canonical keys enable checkpoint reuse for equivalent MUs across tasks without new demonstrations or updates. We evaluate MUCO on RLBench, RoboTwin 2.0, and five real-world tasks. MUCO achieves higher complete-task success and verified progress, stronger failure containment, and lower error propagation than baselines. Results demonstrate cross-task MU reuse and het?erogeneous policy composition without joint training, shared backbones, or common action representations.
authors: Xiangyi Wei, Hanzhe Yao, Jingwen Shang, Zhenhong Wu, Yang Li, Changbo Wang
bullets: Targets costly data collection, limited capability reuse, and cascading failures in complete-trajectory learning.
Represents each manipulation unit with a local goal, initiation condition, and observable success/failure criteria.
Uses language and vision to sequence units, select policies from a frozen capability registry, and verify outcomes before proceeding.
Supports checkpoint reuse for equivalent units and composes heterogeneous policies without joint training, shared backbones, or common action representations.
Evaluations on RLBench, RoboTwin 2.0, and five real-world tasks report higher complete-task success and verified progress, with better failure containment and lower error propagation than baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Compositional long-horizon manipulation framework using language, vision, and reusable policy units.
papers.title: MUCO: A Mani-Unit-Structured Manipulation Framework for Compositional Long-Horizon Robot Tasks
papers.tldr: MUCO decomposes long-horizon robot tasks into reusable, verifiable manipulation units and orchestrates compatible policies with retries and fallback to contain failures.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents increasingly improve by distilling experience into reusable skills, but errors in that experience can persist in learned rules and affect later tasks. Existing evaluations largely examine clean learning or perturbations encountered after skills are frozen, leaving robustness during self-evolution insufficiently understood. We introduce RSE-Bench, to our knowledge the first benchmark for evaluating skill self-evolution under ordinary, non-adversarial noise. It spans four domains and six benchmarks, with controlled perturbations to instructions, environmental evidence, execution records, and outcome--record pairings that preserve the underlying tasks and native scoring rules. The protocol separates noise during learning from input-side noise at evaluation, testing frozen skill stores on held-out tasks. We also introduce \textsc{RSEClaw}, a method-agnostic framework supporting consistent noise injection and process diagnostics of actual exposure and skill updates. Across three methods and two backbones, noisy learning retains only $25.5\%$--$42.1\%$ of the aggregate gain achieved by clean self-evolution, depending on the noise type. Perturbations confined to execution records and outcome--record pairings cause average losses comparable to input-side noise, despite leaving the original executions and evaluations intact. Diagnostics further identify differences in candidate skill text that coexist with small changes in mean held-out performance.
authors: Tao Yu, Zhongtian Luo, Yuchen Long, Yiheng Lu, Yuxuan Zhou, Yanpei Gong, Siyi Cao, Yuqing Wu, Haopeng Jin, Zhenghao Zhang, Yujia Yang, Jingmin Zhu, Yunyun Hou, Xinming Wang, Hongzhu Yi, Jiachen Liu, Sirui Wang, Nan Duan, Yan Huang, Liang Wang, Tianjin Huang, Yanyan Zou
bullets: Introduces RSE-Bench, a benchmark spanning four domains and six benchmarks for evaluating robustness to non-adversarial noise during skill learning.
Tests perturbations to instructions, environmental evidence, execution records, and outcome–record pairings while preserving underlying tasks and native scoring.
Separates noise during learning from input-side evaluation noise using frozen skill stores on held-out tasks.
Across three methods and two backbones, noisy learning preserves only 25.5%–42.1% of the aggregate gain from clean self-evolution, depending on noise type.
RSEClaw provides method-agnostic noise injection and diagnostics, revealing that execution- and outcome-record noise can hurt comparably to input noise.
papers.selection_reason: Studies skill self-evolution in agents under noise, relating to continual learning from experience and adaptation during deployment.
papers.title: When Non-Adversarial Noise Hurts Learning: Benchmarking Skill Self-Evolution in Agents
papers.tldr: RSE-Bench shows that ordinary noise during agents’ skill self-evolution can sharply reduce later learning gains, even when tasks and evaluations remain unchanged.

papers.abstract: Adapting a single vision-language model to medical image parsing requires training choices that reflect the demands of each task. We study task-specific adaptation with Qwen3.5-9B for FLARE 2026 Task 3, covering six task families and seven imaging modalities. Our system couples a shared, frozen 4-bit backbone with LoRA adapters selected from the input question. We customize adapter ranks and prompts, rebalance rare classification targets, and supplement regression training with dermatology classification examples. On the fixed internal holdout, the task-specific adapters achieve a dataset-macro balanced accuracy of 0.7791 for classification, a dataset-macro micro-F1 of 0.6286 for multi-label classification, a counting mean absolute error (MAE) of 11.73, a dataset-macro detection F1 of 0.8914, a dataset-macro regression MAE of 9.78, and a report-generation CRIMSON score of 0.8204. On the organizer's 1,703-example hidden-validation set, the submitted system achieves 0.8496 classification balanced accuracy, 0.5338 sample-averaged multi-label F1, and 14.5950 regression MAE. The final 30.1 GB container averages 3.1 seconds per case, including model loading, and produces identical outputs across repeated verification runs. The benefits vary across tasks, supporting the use of task-specific adapter configurations and image budgets within a shared medical vision-language model. Code is available at https://github.com/TahaSabir0/FLARE26-Hexapus.
authors: Taha Sabir, Alberto Montero Molina, Thinh Quang Ly, Veronika Dmitrenko, Mohammad Yaqub, Tausifa Jan Saleem
bullets: Uses a shared 4-bit backbone with adapters selected from the input question, plus task-specific ranks, prompts, and image budgets.
Addresses class imbalance and augments regression training with dermatology classification examples.
On an internal holdout, reports classification balanced accuracy of 0.7791, detection F1 of 0.8914, regression MAE of 9.78, and report-generation CRIMSON of 0.8204, among other task metrics.
On 1,703 hidden-validation examples, achieves 0.8496 classification balanced accuracy, 0.5338 sample-averaged multi-label F1, and 14.5950 regression MAE.
The final 30.1 GB container averages 3.1 seconds per case; results indicate that task-specific adapter configurations benefit some tasks differently.
papers.selection_reason: Task-specific LoRA adaptation of a multimodal LLM for medical image parsing; fits multimodal LLM adaptation.
papers.title: Multimodal Medical Image Parsing with Task-Specific Low-Rank Adapters
papers.tldr: A shared frozen Qwen3.5-9B vision-language model with question-selected, task-specific LoRA adapters supports diverse medical image parsing tasks across six task families and seven modalities.

papers.abstract: The reintegration of people in the workplace after an upper-limb injury is often a long process. Collaborative robots and humanoids operating in shared workspaces must adapt their behavior to the physical capabilities of their human partners. Achieving this requires robots to autonomously estimate task-relevant human mobility during interaction, without relying on external clinical assessments. In this work, we formulate the estimation of upper-limb functional mobility as an active perception problem. We model task-available upper-limb functional ranges of motion through impairment coefficients that parameterize reductions of healthy joint limits, and integrate this representation into a human model used by the robot during interaction. Based on this formulation, we propose an online active perception pipeline in which the robot actively probes the user through repeated handover requests while progressively updating a Bayesian belief over the impairment coefficients. This enables the robot to continuously refine its internal model of the user's joint-level capabilities through interaction rather than passive observation. The proposed framework was evaluated through simulation studies and a proof-of-concept physical validation with a robotic platform and enacted human impairments, demonstrating that the pipeline can accurately recover the impairment coefficients during real human-robot handovers.
authors: Francesco Semeraro, Marta Lagomarsino, Alberto Ranavolo, Arash Ajoudani
bullets: Addresses the need for robots to adapt to human physical capabilities after upper-limb injury without external clinical assessments.
Represents functional mobility as reductions of healthy joint limits using impairment coefficients.
Uses an online active-perception pipeline with repeated handover requests and Bayesian belief updates.
Validated in simulation and a physical proof-of-concept with enacted impairments, accurately recovering impairment coefficients during handovers.
papers.selection_reason: Active perception of human mobility during physical handovers; embodied interaction though not core learning-based manipulation.
papers.title: Active Perception of Upper-Limb Functional Mobility through Human-Robot Handovers
papers.tldr: A robot learns a person’s upper-limb mobility during repeated handovers by actively probing them and updating a Bayesian impairment model.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models suffer significant accuracy drops under common corruptions. While test-time adaptation (TTA) successfully mitigates these shifts in CLIP-like contrastive models, its application to generative multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remains underexplored and uniquely challenging due to their sequential token generation. In this work, we demonstrate that representation-based TTA fails to recover performance in MLLMs. Our experiments reveal that even when violating standard TTA assumptions by leveraging target data offline, sample-blind feature alignment recovers only marginal accuracy. We attribute this failure to the nature of corruption shifts: unlike CLIP-like architectures, which benefit from a shared domain-shift direction within a single pooled classification embedding, MLLM visual token sequence shifts are nearly orthogonal and span the full embedding space.These findings bound what any sample-blind, position-shared correction at a single encoder site can achieve, establishing that representation-space interventions alone might be insufficient to ensure corruption robustness in MLLMs.
authors: Miko{\l}aj Pi\'orczy\'nski, Wojciech Masarczyk, Damian S\'ojka, Sebastian Cygert, Bart{\l}omiej Twardowski
bullets: MLLMs experience substantial accuracy drops under common corruptions, and standard TTA strategies do not transfer reliably from CLIP-like models.
Even with offline access to target data, sample-blind feature alignment provides only marginal recovery.
MLLM corruption shifts are nearly orthogonal across visual tokens and span the embedding space, unlike the shared shift direction in pooled CLIP representations.
These results limit the effectiveness of position-shared, single-layer representation corrections for MLLM robustness.
The findings suggest that representation-space interventions alone may be insufficient for corruption robustness in generative MLLMs.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes test-time adaptation limits for multimodal LLMs, directly relevant to test-time learning and multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: On the Limits of Representation-Based Test-Time Adaptation for Multimodal LLMs
papers.tldr: Representation-based test-time adaptation is fundamentally limited for improving corruption robustness in multimodal LLMs because their visual-token shifts are diverse rather than aligned.

papers.abstract: Majority Voting (MV) is a simple and widely used strategy which improves the reasoning accuracy of Large Language Models (LLMs) by allocating additional inference-time computation. Specifically, in MV multiple Chain-of-Thoughts (CoTs) are independently sampled and the most frequent final answer is selected. In this work, we propose Length-Conditioned Majority Voting (LCMV), a Test-Time Training approach which improves MV leveraging an empirical observation that has recently been established in several studies: longer CoTs tend to be associated with a lower probability of correctness. We formulate this inductive bias as a length-conditioned prior probability, which is modeled by a simple logistic function. Moreover, we adapt this prior at test time using only unlabeled testing data and without fine-tuning the LLM. Finally, the adapted prior is used to weight the vote of each sampled answer. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs and reasoning benchmarks show that LCMV consistently improves over both standard MV and existing length-based and confidence-based aggregation strategies, while retaining the simplicity and model-agnostic nature of MV. Our code is available at: https://github.com/aimagelab/LCMV.
authors: Fiorenzo Parascandolo, Enver Sangineto, Xiaoyi Yu, Wenhui Tan, Jipei He, Ruihua Song, Rita Cucchiara
bullets: Targets the tendency for longer chain-of-thoughts to be less likely correct.
Models this length-dependent correctness prior with a simple logistic function.
Adapts the prior using unlabeled test data, without fine-tuning the LLM.
Uses the adapted prior to weight votes from independently sampled answers.
Experiments across multiple LLMs and reasoning benchmarks show consistent gains over standard MV and other aggregation methods.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time adaptation of majority voting using a length-conditioned prior for LLM reasoning.
papers.title: Frustratingly Easy Majority Voting Using Length Conditioning
papers.tldr: LCMV improves majority voting for LLM reasoning by weighting answers according to a test-time learned prior based on chain-of-thought length.

papers.abstract: Unsupervised temporal action localization (UTAL) aims to identify action categories and localize their temporal boundaries without annotation supervision. Existing methods typically derive supervision for both tasks solely from RGB and optical-flow representations, often resulting in noisy category assignments and inaccurate temporal boundaries. In this work, we reveal an overlooked property of video codecs: group-of-pictures quantization patterns preserve category-discriminative dynamics, while motion-vector and residual variations exhibit pronounced responses around action transitions. Based on this insight, we propose CoDy, a codec dynamics-guided framework that exploits the codec as complementary information to the visual view for UTAL. CoDy integrates a codec-enhanced view with RGB and flow through confidence-aware consensus clustering, producing reliable soft pseudo-labels. It further converts codec dynamics into a class-agnostic boundary prior, which supervises visual boundary learning and guides proposal initialization and iterative refinement. The codec branches are only used during the training stage and introduce no extra codec-side computation at inference. Extensive experiments on THUMOS14 and ActivityNet v1.3 demonstrate that CoDy consistently outperforms existing UTAL methods and achieves state-of-the-art localization performance. These results establish codec signals as effective annotation-free priors for jointly inferring which actions occur and when they occur.
authors: Tianyu Yan, Qingyi Yang, Qin Yang, Xufei Guo, Yuan Tang, Rui Wang, Yixue Hao, Long Hu
bullets: Addresses noisy pseudo-labels and inaccurate boundaries in unsupervised temporal action localization.
Combines RGB, optical flow, and codec-enhanced features with confidence-aware consensus clustering to generate soft pseudo-labels.
Uses motion-vector and residual changes as a class-agnostic boundary prior for proposal initialization and iterative refinement.
Codec branches are used only during training, adding no codec computation at inference.
Achieves state-of-the-art localization performance on THUMOS14 and ActivityNet v1.3.
papers.selection_reason: Unsupervised temporal action localization using codec dynamics as priors; fits video understanding.
papers.title: CoDy: Codec Dynamics as Complementary Priors for Unsupervised Temporal Action Localization
papers.tldr: CoDy uses video codec dynamics as complementary, annotation-free priors to improve unsupervised action recognition and temporal boundary localization.

papers.abstract: Continual learning aims to acquire new knowledge while retaining previously learned knowledge. However, updating shared parameters when learning new tasks often overwrites existing knowledge, causing catastrophic forgetting. Memory replay methods mitigate catastrophic forgetting but rely on previous samples, raising privacy, memory, and scalability concerns. On the other hand, parameter isolation-based methods preserve learned knowledge but may limit knowledge transfer, whereas regularization promotes adaptability but remains susceptible to interference between old and new tasks. To maintain the stability-plasticity trade-off, this paper proposes Stability-Plasticity-Aware Region Selection (SPARS), a replay-free hybrid framework combining global parameter isolation with localized parameter regularization. SPARS estimates parameter importance using either the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) or a novel Confidence Score (CS) estimator that leverages logit sensitivity and achieves comparable performance to FIM without requiring labelled data. Based on parameter importance, SPARS partitions parameters into three importance-aware regions namely, winning, neighboring, and non-important parameter regions. Each region receives a different adaptation strategy: selective freezing, soft regularization, or unrestricted learning based on its role in the stability-plasticity trade-off. To mitigate classifier bias in class-incremental learning, we employ Quadratic Discriminant Analysis to improve performance on previously learned classes .Experiments on CIFAR-10 and TinyImageNet demonstrate consistent improvement in average incremental accuracy over existing isolation- and regularization-based methods across task- and class-incremental learning. On TinyImageNet, SPARS achieves the best performance with 6% improvement for class-incremental learning while retaining over 60% of parameters for future tasks.
authors: Teif Aldaajani, Huda Hakami, Maha A. Thafar
bullets: Addresses catastrophic forgetting without storing previous samples, avoiding replay-related privacy, memory, and scalability concerns.
Combines global parameter isolation with localized regularization to balance stability and plasticity.
Uses FIM or a label-free Confidence Score estimator to divide parameters into winning, neighboring, and non-important regions.
Applies selective freezing, soft regularization, or unrestricted learning according to each region’s importance.
Improves average incremental accuracy on CIFAR-10 and TinyImageNet; on TinyImageNet, it reports a 6% gain in class-incremental learning while retaining over 60% of parameters for future tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a continual learning framework balancing stability and plasticity, directly matching continual and online learning.
papers.title: SPARS: A Stability-Plasticity-Aware Region Selection Framework for Continual Learning
papers.tldr: SPARS is a replay-free continual-learning framework that preserves important knowledge while retaining substantial parameter capacity for future tasks.

papers.abstract: We introduce SEA-HELM Audio, a Southeast Asian (SEA) multilingual evaluation framework that extends the text-based SEA-HELM benchmark to assess performance degradation in cascaded automatic speech recognition and large language model (ASR-LLM) pipelines. Using synthesized speech, we compare speech-input and text-input performance across five languages (Chinese, English, Malay, Indonesian, and Tamil) on multiple-choice reasoning and instruction-following tasks. We evaluate open-weight and commercial ASR-LLM systems using identical verifiers and quantify the speech gap as the difference between text and speech accuracy. Results show substantial degradation, with accuracy drops of 9.00 to 18.50 percentage points for multiple-choice reasoning and 20.00 to 42.86 points for instruction following. Tamil exhibits the largest degradation, exceeding 40 percentage points. Our findings highlight the limitations of text-only benchmarks in predicting voice-agent reliability and demonstrate the value of SEA-HELM Audio for evaluating multilingual voice-agent systems.
authors: Yixian Tan, Aulia Adila, Jonathan Heng, Kunat Pipatanakul, Donghang Wu, Anocha Sutaveephamochanon
bullets: Extends the text-based SEA-HELM benchmark to evaluate cascaded ASR–LLM pipelines.
Compares synthesized speech and text inputs across Chinese, English, Malay, Indonesian, and Tamil.
Assesses multiple-choice reasoning and instruction-following using identical verifiers across open-weight and commercial systems.
Speech causes 9.00–18.50 percentage-point drops on reasoning and 20.00–42.86-point drops on instruction following.
Tamil shows the largest degradation, exceeding 40 percentage points, challenging text-only estimates of voice-agent reliability.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates multilingual ASR-LLM voice-agent pipelines, relevant to multimodal LLM systems.
papers.title: SEA-HELM Audio: Evaluating Multilingual ASR-LLM Pipeline Performance Across SEA-HELM Subsets
papers.tldr: SEA-HELM Audio measures how much multilingual ASR–LLM systems lose when processing speech instead of text, revealing substantial performance degradation across Southeast Asian languages and tasks.

papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to scale, their energy consumption during inference has become a critical concern. While Autoregressive (AR) models are the industry standard, Diffusion Language Models (DLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative capable of parallel token generation. In this paper, we perform a comparative energy benchmark of diffusion models (LLaDA-8B, Dream-7B) against AR counterparts (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B). We analyze the trade-offs between model architecture, KV-cache optimization, and Joules-per-token efficiency. Our results show that at longer sequences (200--600 tokens), diffusion models achieve 2.5--2.7 J/token, approximately 2$\times$ more efficient than AR models with KV-cache (5.3--5.7 J/token). KV-cache provides substantial benefits for AR models at longer sequences (50--70\% energy reduction).
authors: Boris Ruf, Marcin Detyniecki
bullets: Compares energy use during inference for diffusion models LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B with AR models Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B.
Analyzes architecture, KV-cache optimization, and joules-per-token efficiency.
For 200–600-token sequences, diffusion models use 2.5–2.7 J/token versus 5.3–5.7 J/token for AR models with KV-cache.
KV-cache reduces AR energy consumption by 50–70% at longer sequence lengths.
Scope is limited to the evaluated models and sequence lengths.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks energy consumption and KV-cache efficiency of diffusion versus autoregressive language models, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: Energy Consumption Analysis of Discrete Diffusion and Autoregressive Language Models
papers.tldr: Diffusion language models can use roughly half the inference energy per token of autoregressive models on longer sequences, while KV-cache substantially improves AR efficiency.

papers.abstract: We propose DeltaStreamer, a novel agentic framework for streaming video understanding inspired by how humans observe, remember, and investigate. Streaming video understanding requires a system to retain evidence before knowing which details future queries will need. Existing approaches often obscure event transitions and omit relevant details when compressing video history, and cannot recover missing visual evidence. DeltaStreamer addresses these limitations by combining change-aware memory with query-driven planning and targeted evidence gathering with replay. Before a query arrives, it continuously observes the stream and explicitly records visual changes in structured memory, preserving how events unfold rather than only what is present. When a query arrives, a query-driven planner identifies the required evidence and guides memory retrieval and targeted replay. By revisiting historical frames, the agent can recover visual details omitted during observation and ground its answer in evidence beyond the retained descriptions. This connects continuous observation with active investigation tailored to each question. Experiments on OVO-Bench and StreamingBench demonstrate improvements over representative streaming video understanding methods, with overall scores of 66.07% and 59.53%, respectively. Project page: https://bbbbchan.github.io/DeltaStreamer/
authors: Boyuan Sun, Deshui Miao, Wenzhao Gao, Shaoyong Jia, Shaohui Jiao, Chi Liu, Yan Shu, Derek Li, Bryan Dai, Shengsheng Qian, Qibin Hou
bullets: Continuously records visual changes in structured memory, preserving event transitions and temporal evolution.
Uses query-driven planning to identify needed evidence and guide memory retrieval.
Replays targeted historical frames to recover details omitted during initial observation.
Reports overall scores of 66.07% on OVO-Bench and 59.53% on StreamingBench.
Addresses limitations of compressed video histories that lose details and cannot recover missing evidence.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic streaming video understanding with change-aware memory and query-driven replay; fits video understanding.
papers.title: DeltaStreamer: Towards Human-Like Agentic Streaming Video Understanding
papers.tldr: DeltaStreamer improves streaming video understanding by combining change-aware memory with query-driven replay to preserve and recover evidence for future questions.

papers.abstract: Memory-efficient subspace optimization has emerged as a practical approach to reducing the memory cost of LLM training while preserving optimization performance. Previous algorithms typically rely on the leading singular subspace of stochastic gradients, yet the gradient noise may dominate the subspace in later training stages and can prevent convergence. To overcome this limitation, we adopt a residual correction framework, which maintains the optimizer states in the subspace and adds the orthogonal residual gradient to the parameter update. We first integrate this scheme into momentum SGD to develop SMRC, which attains an $O(T^{-1/4})$ convergence rate for a fixed orthonormal basis, matching that of full-space momentum SGD. Our analysis introduces a subspace virtual iterate to resolve the coupling between the momentum and the residual correction. Furthermore, we extend SMRC to a multi-stage variant which periodically recomputes bases to track the evolving dominant subspace and retains the same rate. Since each basis refresh breaks the consistency of the virtual iterates, we devise a boundary correction approach that aligns them across stages. Beyond momentum SGD, we incorporate our framework into Muon and propose PMRC, which applies the matrix sign to the projected momentum. Through a weighted momentum tracking analysis that accounts for the residual gradient, we establish an $O(T^{-1/4})$ convergence rate for PMRC, which matches the rate of full-space Muon. We also design a multi-stage PMRC with periodically refreshed bases, which maintains a convergence rate of the same order. Extensive experimental results confirm the effectiveness and efficiency of our algorithms.
authors: Sifan Yang, Hongyi Tao, Dingzhi Yu, Haomin Bai, Wei Jiang, Silin Gao, Pi Bu, Lijun Zhang
bullets: Addresses convergence degradation when gradient noise overwhelms the leading singular subspace late in training.
Introduces SMRC, which keeps optimizer states in the subspace and adds the orthogonal residual gradient to updates.
Extends SMRC to multi-stage basis refreshes using boundary correction to maintain consistency across stages.
Introduces PMRC for Muon by applying the matrix sign to projected momentum, with weighted momentum tracking analysis.
Theory gives O(T^{-1/4}) convergence for both SMRC and PMRC, matching their full-space counterparts; experiments support effectiveness and efficiency.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes memory-efficient subspace optimization for LLM training, directly relevant to reducing memory requirements in AI systems.
papers.title: Memory-Efficient Subspace Optimization with Residual Correction: From Momentum SGD to Muon
papers.tldr: Residual correction makes subspace-based momentum SGD and Muon memory-efficient while preserving full-space convergence rates under fixed or refreshed subspaces.

papers.abstract: Robot-free collection with handheld interfaces enables scalable acquisition of human demonstrations for policy learning. However, existing handheld interfaces often provide limited intuitive force feedback, making contact-rich demonstration collection challenging for human operators. To address this, we present FOMI, a force-feedback manipulation interface with a scissor-shaped mechanism, which transmits object interaction forces directly to the operator's hands through actuation links without force sensors. This intuitive force feedback supports real-time action adjustment during robot-free collection of contact-rich demonstrations. Around FOMI, we build a demonstration collection system that integrates sensor calibration, data acquisition, and synchronization for robot-free collection. By further mapping pose changes and gripper opening of FOMI to robot end-effector poses and gripper commands, the system also supports teleoperation. Across four contact-rich tasks, FOMI improves collection efficiency by approximately 29% and 18% over the best baselines in robot-free collection and teleoperation, respectively. Demonstrations collected with FOMI in both modes enable policies to perform challenging contact-rich manipulation tasks with high success rates.
authors: Yishu Shen, Yiming Luo, Ruilin Wang, Bowen Yang, Shuai Yang, Fangyi Xu, Yujun Shen, Fu Zhang, Boyu Zhou, Yinghao Xu
bullets: Addresses limited intuitive force feedback in existing handheld interfaces for contact-rich tasks.
Uses a scissor-shaped, sensor-free mechanism to transmit interaction forces directly to the operator’s hands.
Includes calibration, data acquisition, synchronization, and mappings to robot poses and gripper commands.
Improves collection efficiency by approximately 29% for robot-free collection and 18% for teleoperation across four tasks.
Collected demonstrations support policies that achieve high success rates on challenging contact-rich manipulation tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Force-feedback interface for collecting contact-rich human demonstrations to train manipulation policies.
papers.title: FOMI: A Force-Feedback Manipulation Interface for Teaching Contact-Rich Manipulation
papers.tldr: FOMI is a force-feedback handheld interface that improves the collection and teleoperation of contact-rich manipulation demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Enterprise group chats record project progress, decisions, task ownership, and other organizational information valuable to enterprise agents. Reliable retrieval is challenging because evidence spans interleaved threads, channels, and time, with meaning and authority conditioned on the speaker. Neither RAG's independent chunk retrieval nor memory systems' summary-based consolidation can reliably recover such distributed evidence. We present EGCForest, a novel multi-view hierarchical memory framework for enterprise group chats. EGCForest organizes an immutable message log into three complementary forests: a Channel forest for temporal workflows, an Actor forest for speaker-conditioned context, and an Artifact forest for deliverable lifecycles. Cross-view connections are enabled by a Placement Map and sparse structural bridges. Built on this memory backbone, EGCForest retrieves and assembles evidence by jointly leveraging message-level relevance, hierarchical context from forest summaries, and cross-view links, recovering distributed evidence. Experiments on three enterprise-chat benchmarks show that EGCForest consistently outperforms RAG and memory-system baselines, improving answer accuracy by up to 20.85 points over MemOS while supporting efficient online retrieval.
authors: Lingxi Cui, Jinhao Ruan, Wenqing Wei, Guo Yi, Li Rao, Ke Chen, Lidan Shou
bullets: Addresses retrieval challenges caused by interleaved threads, channels, time, and speaker-dependent authority.
Builds three complementary forests: Channel for workflows, Actor for speaker context, and Artifact for deliverable lifecycles.
Uses a Placement Map and sparse structural bridges to connect information across views.
Combines message relevance, hierarchical summaries, and cross-view links to assemble evidence.
Outperforms RAG and memory-system baselines on three enterprise-chat benchmarks, with up to 20.85-point accuracy gains over MemOS.
papers.selection_reason: Hierarchical agent memory for retrieval; fits the LLM memory subtopic.
papers.title: EGCForest: Structured Agent Memory Organization for Enterprise Group Chats
papers.tldr: EGCForest organizes enterprise group-chat memory across multiple hierarchical views to retrieve distributed evidence more reliably and efficiently.

papers.abstract: LLMs absorb vast knowledge from training data, yet their inherently probabilistic nature offers no guarantee that this knowledge will surface in their outputs. To bridge this gap, Knowledge Extraction Enhancement (KEE) techniques such as activation steering, decoding adjustments, and prompting modify inference, potentially reinforcing existing predictions or surfacing less accessible answers. Yet their evaluations centered on aggregate accuracy, which obscures diverse effects by collapsing recovered failures and disrupted successes into a single score. We introduce MAPLE, a unified framework for characterizing how KEE techniques affect parametric knowledge extraction. Its diagnostic metrics disentangle these effects at the surface, probability, and beyond-sampling levels by measuring answer recovery and disruption, gold-token rank shifts on unrecovered failures, and recovery of answers missed by fixed-budget sampling. We evaluate six KEE techniques spanning decoding, activation steering, and prompting across three model families: OLMo2, Qwen2.5, and Llama3. Our analysis reveals distinct effects and trade-offs across techniques, highlighting the value of MAPLE for understanding and comparing KEE beyond aggregate accuracy.
authors: Minsuh Joo, Youna Kim, Choonghyun Park, Soo Kyung Kim, Hyunsoo Cho
bullets: Aggregate accuracy can hide whether a technique recovers failures, disrupts successes, or reveals answers missed by sampling.
MAPLE measures effects at surface, probability, and beyond-sampling levels.
Its metrics track answer recovery/disruption, gold-token rank shifts, and recovery beyond fixed-budget sampling.
The study evaluates six decoding, activation-steering, and prompting techniques across OLMo2, Qwen2.5, and Llama3.
Results show distinct trade-offs between techniques, supporting more informative KEE comparisons.
papers.selection_reason: Diagnostic framework for LLM parametric knowledge extraction techniques; fits LLM foundation model evaluation.
papers.title: MAPLE: A Multi-Axis Parametric Knowledge Extraction Lens for LLM Evaluation
papers.tldr: MAPLE provides a multi-axis framework for evaluating how knowledge-extraction enhancements recover, disrupt, or uncover LLM answers beyond aggregate accuracy.

papers.abstract: Integrating world models into Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) has emerged as a promising direction, enabling policies to anticipate future dynamics beyond reactive observation-to-action mapping. However, existing approaches vary simultaneously in their world representations, integration paradigms, and policy backbones, making it difficult to determine what truly matters for effective world model integration. To disentangle these factors, we categorize existing efforts into four representative paradigms, namely Implicit Future Alignment, Explicit Future Query, MoT Future Expert, and External World Predictor. We instantiate each within a unified framework and systematically evaluate these paradigms with diverse world representations and policy backbones across in-domain, out-of-domain, long-horizon, dynamic, few-shot, and real-world settings. Our study yields four main findings: 1) world representation effectiveness is paradigm-dependent, whereas 2D semantic representations offer robust, cross-paradigm gains; 2) no single paradigm is universally optimal, yet the decoupled MoT Future Expert offers competitive overall performance, particularly in OOD robustness; 3) world modeling consistently benefits policies built on standard VLMs, while decoupled designs exhibit greater compatibility with pretrained VLAs; and 4) world modeling improves performance over action-only baselines across multiple settings, with notable gains on long-horizon and dynamic tasks. Project page and video demonstrations are available at https://dylanmqs.github.io/WM-in-VLAs/.
authors: Qisen Ma, Yixiang Chen, Yuan Xu, Peiyan Li, Jiabing Yang, Kai Wang, Jianhua Yang, Jianlou Si, Jun Huang, Jing Liu, Nianfeng Liu, Yan Huang, Liang Wang
bullets: The study compares four integration paradigms: Implicit Future Alignment, Explicit Future Query, MoT Future Expert, and External World Predictor.
World-representation effectiveness is paradigm-dependent, while 2D semantic representations provide robust gains across paradigms.
No paradigm is universally best; the decoupled MoT Future Expert performs competitively overall and is particularly robust out of distribution.
World modeling consistently helps standard VLM-based policies and improves action-only baselines, especially on long-horizon and dynamic tasks.
Decoupled designs are more compatible with pretrained VLAs, with evaluation spanning in-domain, OOD, few-shot, long-horizon, dynamic, and real-world settings.
papers.selection_reason: Systematically studies world model integration in Vision-Language-Action models, directly relevant to embodied AI and interactive world models.
papers.title: What Matters for World Modeling in Vision-Language-Action Models?
papers.tldr: A systematic study finds that world modeling improves vision-language-action policies, but its effectiveness depends on the representation, integration paradigm, and policy backbone.

papers.abstract: Text-to-video (T2V) generation models can produce visually realistic videos that nevertheless violate the physical consequences implied by the prompt and scene. Existing benchmarks largely rely on holistic plausibility scores or broad quality dimensions, leaving it unclear which physical behavior is being tested and why a model fails. We introduce PhyMetric, a scene-level diagnostic benchmark that recasts physical plausibility evaluation as verifiable, scene-grounded question answering. PhyMetric contains 1{,}115 scenes spanning 50 physical categories across six domains, paired with 8{,}920 answer-balanced binary questions over 12 evaluation dimensions. Each scene is associated with eight targeted yes/no questions and a structured physical prior specifying the governing law, expected temporal sequence, observable signatures, and common failure modes. At evaluation time, a vision-language model (VLM) judge answers each question from question-aware sampled frames conditioned on the prior, and correctness is hierarchically aggregated into scene, dimension, physical category, and model scores. Experiments on four open-source T2V models and three VLM judges show that scene-specific binary QA is a critical component of the protocol: when each targeted question is replaced by a single generic plausibility query, evaluator accuracy drops to the chance level. Structured physical priors offer a complementary signal that improves human alignment of the resulting scores, with effects that vary across VLM judges of different capacity. These findings establish PhyMetric as a benchmark that turns physical plausibility evaluation from opaque holistic scoring into interpretable, scene-level inspection. Our project page is available at: https://mengsiwei.github.io/PhyMetric/.
authors: Siwei Meng, Xuerou Cai, Rui Hu, Ping Liu
bullets: Benchmarks 1,115 scenes across 50 physical categories and six domains with 8,920 balanced binary questions.
Each scene includes eight targeted questions and a structured prior covering governing laws, temporal sequences, observable signs, and failure modes.
A VLM judge answers questions from sampled frames, with scores aggregated from scene level to model level.
Across four open-source T2V models and three VLM judges, targeted QA is essential; generic plausibility questions perform at chance.
Structured physical priors improve alignment with human judgments, with effects varying by VLM judge capacity.
papers.selection_reason: Scene-level diagnostic benchmark for physical plausibility in text-to-video generation via VLM-based QA; fits video understanding and evaluation.
papers.title: PhyMetric: Diagnosing Physical Plausibility in Text-to-Video Generation via Scene-Level QA
papers.tldr: PhyMetric evaluates whether text-to-video outputs obey scene-specific physical laws using targeted, interpretable visual question answering.

papers.abstract: LLM agents are evolving from a single model calling tools to planners that orchestrate multiple expert models whose capabilities live in distinct weights. This shift breaks a hidden assumption of today's serving systems: that the working set of models fits in GPU memory. On the memory-constrained GPUs typical of private and edge deployments, naive whole-model swapping serializes weight transfer with computation and, without host-backed KV restoration, discards session state at a switch. We present JointServe, a serving system that treats weight shards and KV blocks as residency objects competing for one unified memory budget. JointServe exploits three structural properties of agent workloads (directed calls, gapped execution, and dual-state residency) to prepare models before they are called: an intent signal parsed from the caller's own output stream triggers prefetch during generation, partial k* residency reduces switching to incremental layers, and a preemptive transfer scheduler protects live-session KV with a guaranteed bandwidth share. A carve-out control step adjusts the weight/KV allocation as workload demands change. Evaluations show that JointServe reduces session completion time by 21.7% over the strongest whole-model swap baseline and stays usable in a crash regime where every whole-model swap baseline fails to finish (a 46-fold gap). On replayed SWE-bench, tau-bench, and OSWorld traces, it cuts session completion time by up to 49% and lifts SLO attainment from 2.8-24.5% to 76.8-100%.
authors: Daijin Hu
bullets: Targets agent workloads whose multiple expert models cannot simultaneously fit in GPU memory.
Uses caller-output intent signals to prefetch models, partial k* residency for incremental switching, and bandwidth-aware transfer scheduling to protect live-session KV state.
Dynamically reallocates the unified memory budget between weights and KV blocks as workload demands change.
Reduces session completion time by 21.7% versus the strongest whole-model-swapping baseline and remains usable in crash scenarios where those baselines fail.
