On SWE-bench, tau-bench, and OSWorld traces, improves completion time by up to 49% and raises SLO attainment to 76.8–100%.
papers.selection_reason: Serving system optimizing weight/KV memory on constrained GPUs; directly relevant to KV cache and memory efficiency.
papers.title: JointServe: Serving Multi-Model Agents on Memory-Constrained GPUs
papers.tldr: JointServe accelerates multi-model LLM-agent serving on memory-constrained GPUs by jointly managing model weights and KV cache residency.

papers.abstract: Dynamical system (DS)-based learning from demonstration generates flexible robot motions, but existing guarantees rely on certificate generation to obtain formal guarantees of safety and goal convergence. We propose a symbolic supervisory control architecture that automatically generates a fail-safe backup plan, certifying safety, reachability, and actuator feasibility directly from the robot's dynamics, independent of the learned DS. A nominal controller tracks the learned DS, while the supervisory controller monitors safety and target convergence, providing non-conservative intervention when the nominal controller violates necessary constraints. Experimental results include simulations and real robot deployment with various 2D and 3D datasets, including handwriting datasets, validating the effectiveness of our approach in providing formal guarantees with learned motion even in complex, dynamic environments.
authors: Ashok Kumar, Mahathi Anand, Angela Schoellig, Abdalla Swikir
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of formally certifying flexible motions generated by dynamical-system learning from demonstration.
Uses a nominal controller to track the learned motion and a symbolic supervisory controller to monitor safety and convergence.
Automatically generates a fail-safe backup plan directly from the robot’s dynamics, independently of the learned dynamical system.
Intervenes non-conservatively when necessary constraints are violated.
Validated in simulations and on a real robot across 2D and 3D datasets, including handwriting, and in complex dynamic environments.
papers.selection_reason: Learned robot motion with formal safety certification via supervisory control; fits robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Learning from Demonstrations meets Symbolic Control - A Supervisory Control Architecture for Formal Certification of Learned Motion
papers.tldr: A symbolic supervisor adds formal safety, reachability, and actuator-feasibility guarantees to robot motions learned from demonstrations.

papers.abstract: An agent that drives an LLM sends the model the same conversation again and again, and each turn adds only a little text at the end. Inference engines reuse the KV cache of the shared prefix, so only the new tokens pass through the model. However, tokenization has no such shortcut. The CPU front end of the serving engine converts every request back into token IDs from its first character, which lengthens the time to first token (TTFT) and consumes CPU on every turn. We present Delta Tokenizer, a CPU tokenization front end that tokenizes only the delta between a request and the previous request of the same session. It retains the earlier token sequence, encodes again only the appended text and the short tail whose tokens the append could affect, and joins the two only at a position the tokenizer's splitting rules themselves cannot move, which keeps the result exact. For long requests with no state to reuse, it cuts the text where practical tokenizers already keep neighboring pieces independent, encodes the pieces on several cores at once, and concatenates the outputs into the reference encoding, exactly. A shared CPU pool schedules these chunks together with the short incremental updates, so an update runs between two chunks rather than behind an entire long job. The incremental path shortens the tokenization of a session turn by roughly 40x relative to the Hugging Face reference tokenizer, and on 16 cores the chunk-parallel path encodes a four-million-character request 8.2x faster than a serial encode and 1.6-2.1x faster than LoPT. Inside SGLang, Delta Tokenizer reduces the median TTFT through the chat interface by 59% at 100K tokens and brings the P99 TTFT of agent sessions down 9.5x under load and 23x when long requests tie up the front end. Every output we checked matches the reference, among them 41.8 billion documents encoded by its fast encoder.
authors: Zhenyu Zhang, Zhichao Cao
bullets: Targets agent sessions where each request repeats a long prefix and appends only a small delta, avoiding full re-tokenization.
Re-tokenizes only the appended text plus a short affected tail, then joins it at a tokenizer-safe boundary for exactness.
Splits stateless long requests into independently encodable segments and processes them in parallel across CPU cores.
A shared scheduler interleaves incremental updates with long-request chunks to reduce queueing delays.
Reports roughly 40× faster incremental tokenization, up to 8.2× faster long-request encoding on 16 cores, and lower TTFT in SGLang.
papers.selection_reason: Efficient incremental and parallel tokenization for long prompts; directly reduces LLM serving latency.
papers.title: Delta Tokenizer: Reference-Identical Tokenization of Session Deltas and Segment-Parallelism for Long Prompts on Multicore CPUs
papers.tldr: Delta Tokenizer accelerates repeated and long-prompt tokenization on multicore CPUs while preserving exact reference-tokenizer outputs.

papers.abstract: Recent work lets LLM agents evolve their own harness, up to the team itself. Yet in human groups, the same abilities achieve different outcomes under different social conditions. Borrowing the notion of scaffolding from developmental psychology, we investigate whether the social scaffolding of a self-evolving multi-agent system (MAS), namely its team composition and structure of interdependence (e.g., collaboration, conformity, or competition), shapes how the team evolves. We present AGORA (Agents Growing through Organization and Relational Arrangements), a framework that varies the two axes independently across three evolution mechanisms. Across web search, codebase understanding, and document QA, we find that (1) evolution alone rarely helps, while the right scaffolding surpasses a strong agent evolved alone by up to 25 points; (2) it does so by moving authority to the most capable member while the others step back; and (3) this member, having grown within the team, outperforms the same model alone. Designing a self-evolving MAS thus requires designing its social scaffolding, which shapes not only how its agents learn, but who gets to lead.
authors: Seojin Hwang, Youngmin Choi, Hwanhee Lee
bullets: Studies how collaboration, conformity, and competition shape self-evolving multi-agent systems.
Introduces AGORA, which independently varies team composition and interdependence across three evolution mechanisms.
Evaluates the framework on web search, codebase understanding, and document QA.
Finds that evolution alone rarely helps, while suitable scaffolding improves performance by up to 25 points over a strong agent evolved alone.
The strongest member can outperform the same model working alone after developing within the team.
papers.selection_reason: Self-evolving LLM multi-agent systems; social scaffolding and evolution mechanisms relevant to online adaptation.
papers.title: Evolve Together, Fall into Place: How Social Scaffolding Shapes Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems
papers.tldr: Social scaffolding—team composition and interdependence—determines whether self-evolving multi-agent systems improve, often by enabling the strongest member to emerge and lead.

papers.abstract: Video world models aim to simulate complex environments with realistic appearance and dynamics. Maintaining consistency over long interactions requires tracking past actions and understanding how those actions affect the environment. Video world models can only generate partial observations of the entire world at a time. Remembering past observations alone may not be sufficient in every scenario, as they may no longer reflect the world after a sequence of actions. We introduce a paradigm that decouples a persistent, updatable abstract state from the visual state. The abstract state keeps track of the entities' changes as the world evolves, and is used to condition the visual state, which represents the current view. We propose StateCraft, a novel architecture that pairs a language model with a video diffusion model to evolve the dynamic world. We evaluate our approach on generative interfaces, which pose a substantial challenge because a single action may change parts of the state that are not currently visible. To support training and evaluation, we develop a data collection pipeline that produces informative, densely annotated trajectories at scale without human or agent supervision, together with a benchmark measuring generation quality, memory, and controllability. On this benchmark, our approach improves surpasses the state-of-the-art baselines. We demonstrate that StateCraft maintains high self-consistency and strong generation quality over long trajectories. Because the abstract state is explicit, it can be edited directly, and generation follows edits to states never observed in the data. Finally, a proof-of-concept 3D experiment, in which actions change the illumination of an unobserved room, shows that the paradigm can also be applied to spatial environments. Project page: https://insait-institute.github.io/StateCraft/.
authors: Lorenzo Venturoli, Nedko Savov, Xi Wang, Marc Pollefeys, Luc Van Gool
bullets: Addresses the limits of visual memory when actions affect currently unseen parts of an environment.
Pairs a language model for abstract-state evolution with a video diffusion model for visual generation.
Introduces a scalable, automatically generated trajectory pipeline and a benchmark for quality, memory, and controllability.
Outperforms stated baselines on the benchmark and maintains self-consistency and generation quality over long trajectories.
Abstract states can be directly edited, enabling generation from states not observed during training; a proof-of-concept extends the approach to 3D environments.
papers.selection_reason: Augments video world models with persistent abstract-state reasoning for long-horizon interactive simulation.
papers.title: StateCraft: Augmenting Video World Models with Abstract-State Reasoning
papers.tldr: StateCraft improves long-horizon video world modeling by maintaining an editable abstract state alongside visual observations to track hidden world changes.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding's effectiveness is governed by two quantities: the acceptance rate of drafted tokens and the cost of producing them. We show the two objectives can be co-optimized with algorithm-system co-design, and present JetSpec++, which retains a strong learned draft model while hiding its cost almost entirely. JetSpec++ combines three components: intra-block self refinement, which trains the draft model to iteratively correct its own parallel predictions within a block of tokens; inter-block foresight drafting, which begins the next block before the current one is verified; and pipelined drafting and verification, which overlaps the two stages so drafting's marginal wall-clock cost approaches zero. In comparison with state-of-the-art speculative decoding methods, JetSpec++ attains a wall-clock speedup of up to $7.45\times$ over autoregressive (AR) decoding and $1.54\times$ over DSpark, with up to 1,361 tokens per second for a single request on GB200, and an average acceptance length of 8.94 across seven benchmarks, while preserving the target model's output distribution. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/hao-ai-lab/JetSpec.
authors: Zhaoxiang Feng (UC San Diego), Lanxiang Hu (UC San Diego), Haoran Yuan (UIUC), Yu-Yang Qian (Nanjing University), Jihui Yang (Meta), Peng Zhao (Nanjing University), Yibo Zhu (StepFun), Tajana Rosing (UC San Diego), Hao Zhang (UC San Diego)
bullets: Uses intra-block self-refinement to iteratively correct parallel draft predictions.
Starts drafting the next token block before verifying the current one via inter-block foresight.
Pipelines drafting and verification to nearly hide drafting’s wall-clock cost.
Reports up to 7.45× speedup over autoregressive decoding and 1.54× over DSpark, while preserving the target model’s output distribution.
Achieves an average acceptance length of 8.94 across seven benchmarks and up to 1,361 tokens/s for a single request on GB200.
papers.selection_reason: Speculative decoding with pipelined drafting and verification; directly reduces LLM inference latency.
papers.title: JetSpec++: Foresight Parallel Drafting with Self Refinements
papers.tldr: JetSpec++ accelerates speculative decoding by co-optimizing token acceptance and drafting cost through self-refinement, foresight, and pipelined execution.

papers.abstract: Crash Moment Localization aims to localize the major physical impact that interrupts controlled flight in an onboard first-person-view (FPV) video recorded by a drone, thereby providing a temporal reference for retrospective crash analysis in aerial robotics. However, existing crash-video datasets predominantly target surveillance or dash-camera footage, and their annotation schemes and task formulations are not designed for temporal localization of the major physical impact in UAV onboard FPV videos. To address this gap, we present FPV-CRASH, a dataset and fixed-protocol reference evaluation for offline Crash Moment Localization in drone FPV videos. FPV-CRASH contains 1,052 drone FPV clips (526 Crash and 526 Normal); each Crash clip has a single-frame reference annotation for the Crash Moment, and every clip is paired with four English captions automatically generated from sampled frames and the known Crash/Normal label. Normal clips carry no timestamp target and provide training-time background supervision. The captions support an auxiliary Text-to-Video Retrieval task, whereas localization inference remains video-only. We further provide a heatmap-based reference model that estimates a continuous Crash Moment timestamp from sparsely sampled frames. Under the fixed, non-source-disjoint clip-level protocol, the reference model reduces MAE from 1.12 s for the strongest fixed timing-prior baseline to 0.56 s (a 50% relative reduction) and achieves a median absolute error (MedAE) of 0.33 s; the fraction of clips localized within 0.5 s rises from 37.14% to 65.71%. The release includes annotations, available source video identifiers and URLs, clipping metadata, fixed split lists, and preprocessing code so that the reportable portion can be reconstructed without redistributing source footage. At submission time, all source-compilation URLs remained accessible.
authors: Jifan Zhang, Tingyu Wang, Qian Liu, Zhedong Zheng
bullets: Targets offline temporal localization of major physical impacts in UAV onboard FPV footage, a gap in existing crash datasets.
Contains 1,052 clips: 526 Crash and 526 Normal; Crash clips have single-frame crash annotations, while Normal clips provide background supervision.
Includes four automatically generated English captions per clip for auxiliary text-to-video retrieval, though localization is video-only.
A heatmap-based model improves MAE from 1.12 s to 0.56 s and raises localization within 0.5 s from 37.14% to 65.71%.
Provides reproducible metadata, split lists, annotations, and preprocessing code without redistributing source videos.
papers.selection_reason: Dataset and reference model for temporal crash moment localization in drone FPV videos.
papers.title: FPV-CRASH: A Dataset for Offline Crash Moment Localization in Drone First-Person-View Videos
papers.tldr: FPV-CRASH introduces a dataset and benchmark for locating the major crash moment in drone FPV videos, with a reference model achieving 0.56 s MAE.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) holds the promise of learning a policy that can outperform what is shown in the data. However, in practice, such systems suffer from instability and hyperparameter sensitivity. In contrast, supervised learning provides a stable and scalable training objective, but is fundamentally limited by the quality of the demonstrated behavior. In this paper, we ask whether we can perform policy optimization with something as simple and stable as supervised learning but as performant as RL. Unfortunately, naively training the policy with supervised learning and conditioning on future rewards or advantages typically underperform dedicated RL methods. We introduce a new policy extraction method, Advantage Guidance, that retains the simple supervised learning structure with advantage conditioning while outperforming prior RL methods through effective conditional training and contrastive diffusion guidance during sampling. We show that Advantage Guidance can significantly improve a model's ability to respond to conditional advantage signals, and the contrastive guidance during sampling can use the learned advantage-conditioned policy to target the KL-regularized optimal policy. Empirically, we find that Advantage Guidance significantly outperforms prior state-of-the-art RL methods on 26 long-horizon, sparse reward tasks across datasets with varying degrees of optimality.
authors: Zhiyuan Zhou, Sergey Levine
bullets: Targets RL instability and hyperparameter sensitivity while retaining supervised learning’s simplicity.
Uses effective conditional training to improve policy responsiveness to advantage signals.
Applies contrastive diffusion guidance during sampling to target the KL-regularized optimal policy.
Outperforms prior state-of-the-art RL methods across 26 long-horizon, sparse-reward tasks with varying data quality.
papers.selection_reason: General RL policy extraction method with advantage conditioning and contrastive diffusion guidance; transferable to robot policy learning.
papers.title: Reinforcement Learning via Advantage Guidance
papers.tldr: Advantage Guidance combines supervised learning with advantage conditioning and contrastive diffusion guidance to achieve strong policy optimization on challenging sparse-reward tasks.

papers.abstract: Computationally lightweight manipulation policies predict executable actions with low inference latency, but prediction errors can limit task success. Iterative generative policies can achieve higher task success rates, but repeated network evaluations increase inference latency. Refining action proposals from computationally lightweight policies can combine these strengths, but the amount of refinement needed varies across states. We introduce RAIN (Refine Actions If Needed), a framework that predicts action errors at different refinement levels to decide whether and how much to refine each executable proposal, before performing any refinement. We train an ensemble to predict these errors by comparing action proposals and their refined versions with expert actions from offline demonstrations, without requiring explicit labels of refinement needs. Calibration balances uncertainty, computation, and temporal consistency. We evaluate RAIN on eight ManiSkill tasks and four real-robot tasks. In simulation, our policy achieves 66.6% success, approaching the best evaluated diffusion-policy success rate with 5.71 times lower policy latency. On the real robot, success increases from 55.0% with Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) to 72.5%, with comparable average successful completion time. Matched controls show that dynamic routing maintains the strongest observed fixed-refinement success level with 26.6% fewer refiner evaluations. Project page: https://rain-policy.github.io/.
authors: Hanlin Liu, Zichen Zhou, Jiacheng Zhang, Liuyuan Na, Jin Jin, Guangyan Chen, Yufeng Yue, Gen Li, Fangqiang Ding
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between lightweight, low-latency policies and slower iterative generative refinement.
Predicts action errors at multiple refinement levels to select whether and how much to refine each proposal.
Uses an ensemble trained from offline demonstrations without explicit labels for refinement needs, with calibration for uncertainty, computation, and temporal consistency.
Evaluated on eight simulated ManiSkill tasks and four real-robot tasks.
Achieves 66.6% simulation success with 5.71× lower policy latency than the best evaluated diffusion policy; real-robot success rises from 55.0% to 72.5% over ACT.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive action-chunk refinement that predicts refinement need to balance task success and inference latency in manipulation.
papers.title: Refine Actions If Needed: Adaptive Action Chunk Refinement for Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: RAIN adaptively refines robot action proposals only when needed, improving task success while reducing the latency and computation of repeated refinement.

papers.abstract: Medical prescribing errors for multimorbid patients, who require complex drug regimens, are a major patient safety concern. These errors often stem from fragmented decision-making across medical specialties, a critical coordination failure that leads to adverse drug events and rehospitalizations. To address this coordination challenge, we introduce PRISMATIC, a multi-agent architecture where specialized agents, each representing a workflow role, collaboratively generate and refine treatment plans. Operating on a blackboard architecture, the system first structures patient information from clinical notes, then iteratively develops safe, rational, and interpretable drug regimens. The agents' collaboration is governed by two novel adaptive coordination mechanisms: (1) Dynamic Self-Updating Weight Adjustment (DSWA), a long-term mechanism that adjusts the influence weights of agents based on historical case outcomes, enabling the system to adapt and trust more reliable specialists over time. (2) Discrepancy Feedback Precise Calibration (DFPC), a short-term mechanism where agents provide iterative feedback to resolve disagreements and eliminate prescription conflicts for the current patient. Experiments on patient records from the MIMIC-IV database show that PRISMATIC significantly reduces drug conflicts, improves prescription coverage, and enhances treatment consistency compared to strong LLM baselines. Our work demonstrates that structuring clinical co-treatment as a multi-agent coordination problem offers a promising path toward safer and more coherent multidisease management.
authors: Ziyang Ling, Shuyu Lu, Ziyi Chen
bullets: Targets prescribing errors caused by fragmented coordination across medical specialties.
Uses a blackboard architecture to structure clinical notes and iteratively refine interpretable drug regimens.
Introduces DSWA for long-term agent trust adjustment based on historical outcomes.
Introduces DFPC for short-term feedback that resolves agent disagreements and prescription conflicts.
On MIMIC-IV records, it reduces drug conflicts and improves prescription coverage and treatment consistency versus LLM baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive multi-agent coordination with online weight adjustment; transferable to continual/online adaptation in agent systems.
papers.title: PRISMATIC : Prescription Risk Inspection System for Multi-Agent Treatment Interaction in Clinical Decision-Making
papers.tldr: PRISMATIC uses adaptive multi-agent collaboration to detect and resolve medication conflicts in complex multimorbid treatment planning.

papers.abstract: Soft spectral clipping (SSC) reduces gradient singular values, but its effect depends on the gradient scale and clipping threshold. We introduce CAST (Clipping with Adaptive Scales and Thresholds), a history-adaptive extension of SSC. AdamW's previous second moment sets row and column scales. An exponential moving average of the clipped output's estimated spectral norm sets each matrix's threshold. CAST restores the original coordinates before the AdamW update. We train a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with 19.08B total parameters for 83.89B tokens. CAST achieves lower training and mean validation losses than nine gradient-processing baselines, with the fewest relative gradient spikes. It reaches the best baseline's final smoothed training loss in 7.2\% fewer steps.
authors: Jiacheng Li, Jianchao Tan, Kefeng Zhang, Yuchen Xie, Xunliang Cai
bullets: Addresses SSC’s sensitivity to gradient scale and clipping thresholds.
Uses AdamW’s previous second moment for row/column scaling and an EMA of clipped spectral norms for per-matrix thresholds.
Restores original coordinates before applying the AdamW update.
On a 19.08B-parameter MoE trained for 83.89B tokens, CAST had lower training and mean validation losses than nine baselines.
Produced the fewest relative gradient spikes and matched the best baseline’s final smoothed training loss in 7.2% fewer steps.
papers.selection_reason: History-adaptive spectral clipping for LLM pretraining; directly relevant to large language model training.
papers.title: CAST: History-Adaptive Spectral Clipping for LLM Pretraining
papers.tldr: CAST adaptively scales and thresholds soft spectral clipping to stabilize LLM pretraining and accelerate optimization.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong potential for general-purpose robotic manipulation, but extending them to bimanual dexterous manipulation introduces a high-dimensional and structured action space. Existing bimanual VLA policies commonly concatenate right- and left-side arm--hand actions at each control timestep, leaving cross-hand interactions implicit within a single action vector. We introduce Coordi-$\pi$, a structured action representation for bimanual dexterous manipulation. Coordi-$\pi$ represents the right- and left-side arm--hand actions as individual action tokens and organizes them into an interleaved sequence, explicitly exposing the two sides within the action sequence. To explicitly encode hand identity and temporal synchronization in this interleaved representation, a learnable hand-identity embedding distinguishes the two sides, while sequence--control-timestep factorized rotary positional encoding (RoPE) separates sequence position from control timestep, allowing actions at the same control timestep to share a temporal coordinate while retaining distinct sequence positions. Across all five bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks in DexJoCo, Coordi-$\pi$ achieves state-of-the-art performance under both \textit{rand-obj} and \textit{rand-full}, improving the average success rate over $\pi_{0.5}$ from 31.9\% to 51.3\% and from 18.3\% to 32.3\%, respectively. Coordi-$\pi$ also consistently outperforms $\pi_{0.5}$ across four real-world bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks.
authors: Yiming Meng, Yanming Shao, Weijie Shen, Kunyang Lin, Jiayu Sun, Ping Luo, Yao Mu
bullets: Targets the high-dimensional, structured action space of bimanual VLA policies, where cross-hand interactions are often implicit.
Represents right- and left-side arm–hand actions as separate, interleaved action tokens.
Uses learnable hand-identity embeddings and factorized RoPE to encode hand identity, sequence position, and shared control timing.
On five DexJoCo tasks, average success rises from 31.9% to 51.3% under rand-obj and from 18.3% to 32.3% under rand-full, compared with π₀.₅.
Also consistently outperforms π₀.₅ across four real-world bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Structured interleaved action representation for bimanual dexterous VLA manipulation.
papers.title: Coordi-pi: Coordination-Aware Dual-Hand Action Representation for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation
papers.tldr: Coordi-π improves bimanual dexterous manipulation by explicitly modeling the two hands as coordinated action sequences rather than a single concatenated vector.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have recently achieved remarkable progress by leveraging large-scale robot datasets and foundation models for general-purpose robot manipulation. However, their ability to rapidly adapt to novel manipulation tasks beyond the training distribution remains limited. Existing approaches often require task-specific robot demonstrations and additional training, which are labor- and compute-intensive, limiting the scalability of VLA adaptation to open-world scenarios. To reduce this dependence on target-task robot data, we propose CapPro, a framework that enables a VLA policy to adapt to previously unseen manipulation tasks using only a single human demonstration video. CapPro consists of two components. First, a phase-aware human video representation module constructs a compact video representation through learned visual token selection and learns task-relevant query representations under phase-caption supervision. Second, a video-conditioned adaptation module jointly incorporates the compact video and query-derived representations into the action-conditioning context of the pretrained VLA policy. % This design introduces task-specific guidance while largely preserving the original VLA action-generation backbone. In this way, the human demonstration provides task-specific execution guidance rather than an embodiment-aligned trajectory to imitate, without requiring target-task robot demonstrations or target-task fine-tuning. Experiments across source and unseen target tasks show that CapPro improves average performance across unseen target groups while maintaining comparable performance on the source tasks. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of human-video guidance for cross-task VLA adaptation.
authors: Qi Chen, Yuwei Wu, Quan Chen, Kunpeng Gao, Jin Chen, Che Sun, Zhi Gao, Yunde Jia
bullets: Addresses the costly, poorly scalable need for task-specific robot demonstrations and retraining when adapting VLAs to novel tasks.
Builds a compact, phase-aware video representation using learned visual-token selection and task-relevant queries supervised by phase captions.
Conditions the pretrained VLA policy on the video and query representations to provide task-specific execution guidance while preserving its action-generation backbone.
Experiments on source and unseen target tasks show improved average performance across unseen target groups with comparable source-task performance.
The approach is scoped to cross-task manipulation adaptation guided by human videos; the abstract does not establish broader settings or limitations.
papers.selection_reason: One-shot human video-guided adaptation of VLA policies to unseen manipulation tasks without robot demonstrations.
papers.title: One-shot Human Video-Guided Adaptation for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: CapPro adapts pretrained vision-language-action policies to unseen robot manipulation tasks using a single human demonstration video, without target-task robot data or fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation of planetary rovers is challenged by visually repetitive, featureless terrain. SLAM systems based on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) offer dense mapping but rely on RGB appearance descriptors that degrade under perceptual aliasing - a common failure mode in extraterrestrial environments where physically distinct locations appear visually identical. This paper presents HyperLoop, the first framework integrating hyperspectral imaging (HSI) into the loop closure module of a 3DGS-based SLAM system. Hyperspectral descriptors encode material-level spectral signatures complementing RGB features, providing robustness to illumination changes and visual repetitiveness. Two HSI descriptor families are introduced: Bag-of-Spectral-Words (BoSW), encoding spectral material distributions via TF-IDF weighted histograms, and PCA-K VLAD (PCAK-VLAD), capturing first-order residual statistics of PCA-compressed spectral signatures. Both are evaluated with SIFT-VLAD and NetVLAD RGB descriptors under Strict-AND and Weighted fusion strategies on a custom dataset from the Moon-Mars Outdoor Test Site (MMOTS) at DLR, comprising synchronized RGB-D and hyperspectral sequences across four planetary analog traverses (65.5 m total). A key finding is that the sensor's Red-NIR range (600-860 nm) provides limited discriminability for rock terrain: the best HSI fusion (SIFT-VLAD + BoSW, Strict-AND) achieves 5.04 cm ATE RMSE, within 1.8% of SIFT-VLAD alone (4.95 cm). The gain over NetVLAD (8.81 cm) is attributable to SIFT-VLAD, not HSI fusion. This motivates future adoption of SWIR sensors capturing diagnostic mineral absorption features absent from the 600-860 nm range for planetary SLAM missions.
authors: Annie Bhalla, Dennis Rotondi, Riccardo Giubilato, Kai O. Arras, Wolfgang Stuerzl
bullets: Addresses perceptual aliasing in visually repetitive, featureless planetary environments.
Introduces BoSW and PCAK-VLAD hyperspectral descriptors for material-aware loop closure.
Evaluates HSI fusion with SIFT-VLAD and NetVLAD RGB descriptors using Strict-AND and Weighted strategies.
On the MMOTS dataset, the best HSI fusion achieved 5.04 cm ATE RMSE, nearly matching SIFT-VLAD alone at 4.95 cm.
Results suggest future systems need SWIR sensing to capture diagnostic mineral absorption features.
papers.selection_reason: Improves loop closure detection for autonomous planetary rover navigation in SLAM.
papers.title: HyperLoop: Hyperspectral-Assisted Loop Closure Detection in 3D-SLAM for Planetary Exploration
papers.tldr: HyperLoop integrates hyperspectral descriptors into 3DGS-based SLAM, but Red-NIR sensing provides little loop-closure benefit for the tested rocky planetary terrain.

papers.abstract: Visible reasoning traces of Chinese reasoning-oriented LLMs are typically written in modern vernacular Chinese, which may be verbose under limited decoding budgets. We ask whether the linguistic register of reasoning can be used to improve efficiency. We propose Wenyan Thinking, which emits intermediate reasoning in Classical Chinese (wenyanwen) while retaining a short direct-answer output. Starting from modern-Chinese reasoning traces, we rewrite only the reasoning field into wenyan and fine-tune Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 on the rewritten supervision. To distinguish register shift from generic compression, we construct a compact modern-Chinese control using the same source data, teacher family, base model, and SFT recipe. Across budget-sensitive evaluations on MMLU-ProX-Lite-ZH, CEVAL, and AGIEval-CN, Wenyan Thinking substantially reduces reasoning length and missing-answer rates under constrained decoding. Compact rewriting explains much of the efficiency gain, while wenyan consistently outperforms the compact modern-Chinese control on the primary benchmark and remains competitive across the additional benchmarks. These results identify linguistic register as a practical design axis for efficient visible reasoning in Chinese LLMs.
authors: Minghan Li, Guodong Zhou
bullets: Modern vernacular reasoning traces can be verbose, motivating a more compact linguistic register.
The method rewrites only reasoning traces into wenyan while preserving short direct answers, then fine-tunes a Chinese reasoning model.
A compact modern-Chinese control separates register effects from generic compression.
Across three Chinese reasoning benchmarks, wenyan reduces reasoning length and missing-answer rates under constrained decoding.
Wenyan outperforms the compact modern-Chinese control on the primary benchmark and remains competitive elsewhere.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates linguistic register for efficient LLM reasoning, relevant to LLM training and efficiency.
papers.title: Does the Linguistic Register of Thinking Matter? Wenyan as a Compact Reasoning Register for Chinese LLMs
papers.tldr: Wenyan Thinking uses Classical Chinese for intermediate reasoning to make Chinese LLM outputs more compact and effective under limited decoding budgets.

papers.abstract: Large protein language models provide a powerful framework for learning sequence-function relationships and guiding experimental design. However, architectural improvements are underexplored, especially in low-compute regimes of relevance for resource-constrained research laboratories. We show that the training cost for encoder-only transformer architectures can be reduced by leveraging modern architectural refinements, offering an encouraging performance / compute-efficiency trade-off. We introduce ProtModernBERT, a modernized BERT-style model pre-trained on amino acid sequences, and compare it with ProtBert, Amplify, and ESM2 across a set of supervised structural tasks -encompassing secondary structure prediction, disorder prediction, and subcellular localization- and ProteinGym's zero-shot functional benchmark. We find that ProtModernBERT matches or closely tracks the performance of Amplify-120M and ProtBert with up to 80-90\% reduction in pre-training FLOPs, and narrows the gap to ESM2 when controlling for pre-training. Our analysis using a cluster-based validation protocol for hyperparameter selection and randomly initialized models disentangles the contributions of architecture and data, showing that modern components provide stronger inductive biases that are more consequential than parameter count in low-compute regimes.
authors: Alberto Mart\'inez, Natalia Flechas Manrique, Lloren\c{c} Espinosa-Portal\'es, Luc Andrea
bullets: Targets compute-efficient protein language modeling for resource-constrained research.
Introduces ProtModernBERT, an encoder-only model with modern architectural refinements, and evaluates it on structural, localization, and zero-shot functional tasks.
Matches or closely tracks Amplify-120M and ProtBert while reducing pre-training FLOPs by up to 80–90%.
Narrows the performance gap to ESM2 under controlled pre-training budgets.
Finds that modern architectural inductive biases matter more than parameter count in low-compute regimes.
papers.selection_reason: Compute-efficient protein language modeling with architectural refinements; fits efficiency-focused AI methods.
papers.title: ProtModernBERT: Compute-Efficient Protein Language Modeling
papers.tldr: ProtModernBERT modernizes BERT-style protein language modeling to achieve comparable task performance with substantially lower pre-training compute.

papers.abstract: Goal misgeneralization is a common failure mode in which an agent behaves competently out of distribution but does not pursue the intended goal. However, we still have a weak understanding of what happens to the intended goal in misgeneralizing agents. Across three Procgen environments and five robot tasks, we find three distinct forms of policy-goal misalignment: (1) functional target substitution, where behavior follows an alternative goal, (2) a policy shortcut, where behavior follows a learned action strategy, and (3) cue competition between intended and proxy goal cues. We distinguish these regimes by tracing where goal information remains available internally, how strongly it influences the policy, and what role it plays in action selection, and find that the goal is lost at different depths. Where the goal reaches the decision, as in cue competition, steering redirects the policy to the goal's location, raising intended-goal reach from 16.0% to 95.3%. Where it reaches the policy but not the decision, only new downstream wiring recovers goal reach, from 31.6% to 84.3% in the environment with the action shortcut. Where it is inert, neither works. Our results show that goal misgeneralization is not a single failure of goal representation, but distinct failures of policy alignment at different depths, tightly connected to which recovery works.
authors: Julia Barth, Armin Sommer, Kunvar Thaman, Jannik Schilling
bullets: Identifies functional target substitution, policy shortcuts, and cue competition across Procgen and robot tasks.
Traces whether goal information is retained internally, influences the policy, and reaches the final decision.
Shows that steering can recover behavior when the goal reaches the decision, while new downstream wiring is needed when it does not.
Recovery fails when the goal is inert, linking intervention effectiveness to the depth of misalignment.
Frames goal misgeneralization as multiple policy-alignment failures rather than a single representation failure.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes goal misgeneralization in learned policies across robot tasks, relevant to embodied robot learning and alignment.
papers.title: What Happens to the Goal? Distinct Failures of Policy Alignment in Goal Misgeneralization
papers.tldr: Goal misgeneralization arises from three distinct alignment failures, and recovery depends on how deeply the intended goal is disconnected from action selection.

papers.abstract: Video large language models (Video LLMs) often generate responses unsupported by the input video. Contrastive decoding (CD) can mitigate these hallucinations, but its effectiveness depends on how the negative branch weakens visual evidence. Existing methods rely on predefined perturbations or masking guided by question reconstruction, offering limited control over the model's visual reliance during answer generation. We introduce Attention-guided Representation Perturbation for Contrastive Decoding (ARP-CD), a training-free framework for constructing contrastive negatives directly in representation space. ARP-CD uses the attention mass assigned to visual tokens at the answer-prediction position to guide bounded gradient updates of the language model's input visual hidden states. These updates reduce visual attention and produce a negative input, whose predictions are contrasted with those of the original branch throughout generation. Experiments across four Video LLMs and four benchmarks show that ARP-CD outperforms representative training-free baselines in most model--benchmark settings, reducing hallucinations while improving general video understanding. Further analyses show that attention-guided perturbation directions improve negative quality and that the resulting negatives provide effective contrastive references for correcting the original predictions.
authors: Zhixin Cai, Ruoqi Yuan, Xinchen Yang, Zhuofan Chen, Jun Bai, Chuantao Yin, Wenge Rong
bullets: Targets unsupported video-grounded responses in Video LLMs.
Uses visual-token attention at the answer position to guide bounded gradient updates to visual hidden states.
Contrasts predictions from the perturbed negative branch with the original branch during generation.
A training-free method evaluated across four Video LLMs and four benchmarks.
Outperforms representative training-free baselines in most model–benchmark settings while improving general video understanding.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses hallucination reduction and video understanding in Video LLMs via contrastive decoding.
papers.title: Mitigating Video Hallucinations via Attention-Guided Representation Perturbation
papers.tldr: ARP-CD reduces Video LLM hallucinations by using attention-guided, representation-space perturbations to create stronger contrastive negatives during decoding.

papers.abstract: We present a Generative World Simulation framework that couples persistent shared world state with continuous first-person audiovisual generation. The framework integrates DAO, a computable world engine, and JING, an Egocentric Interactive Experience Model, to support sustained interaction for humans and agents. DAO maintains the states of characters, objects, and spaces and their relationships, advancing the world according to interaction rules and world time while preserving the consequences of past actions. From this evolving state, DAO derives observer-specific conditions for JING, which combines these conditions with character, object, and scene references, observation history, and current actions to generate each observer's audiovisual experience. Users can explore environments, manipulate objects, and communicate with characters through viewpoint control and text instructions, with their actions shaping both the shared state and subsequent experiences. By connecting world-state evolution with experience generation in a continuous interaction loop, the framework offers an approach to building interactive worlds that retain their history, evolve through action, and persist beyond any individual observer.
authors: XGEN Team, Guohao Cai, Haoxuan Che, Frank Fan, Chenran Huang, Junjia Huang, Jiayi Jiang, Yanheng Li, Leon Liu, Shaoteng Liu, Xi Liu, Feng Nie, Zhefan Rao, An Wang, Hanwen Wang, Pengxiang Yan, Jieming Yu, Qian Zha, Wentao Zheng
bullets: Targets interactive worlds that retain history and persist beyond any individual observer.
DAO tracks characters, objects, spaces, relationships, interaction rules, and world time.
JING generates observer-specific audiovisual experiences from world state, references, history, and actions.
Users interact through viewpoint control and text instructions, with actions updating the shared world.
The abstract presents a framework and interaction loop but reports no quantitative evaluation or specific limitations.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a framework for generative world simulation with persistent shared state and egocentric audiovisual generation, a direct fit for Interactive World Models.
papers.title: Generative World Simulation with DAO and JING
papers.tldr: A framework combines a persistent, shared world engine with continuous first-person audiovisual generation to create interactive worlds that evolve and remember past actions.

papers.abstract: Interpreting an ambiguous utterance in real-world interactions often requires context beyond a single utterance. When the utterance refers to objects in a visual scene, it is necessary to maintain and update the set of plausible referents as context accumulates, without assuming that the available information identifies a unique object. However, prior work on interactive visual grounding, which localizes objects referred to by linguistic expressions, has focused on identifying a unique object once sufficient dialogue context becomes available. To address this gap, we propose Candidate Set Visual Grounding (CSVG), a task for estimating the set of objects consistent with the given dialogue context. We further introduce CandVG, a benchmark that evaluates how the candidate set changes across dialogue turns. Our evaluation of vision-language models shows that stronger visual grounding capability does not necessarily yield better CSVG performance. In particular, models have difficulty predicting the complete candidate set, owing to challenges in candidate generation and premature commitment to a small set of candidates in early turns. Nevertheless, we find that this limitation can be partially mitigated in the evaluated large-scale models using instructions designed for CSVG.
authors: Shun Inadumi, Lee Sangmyeong, Koichiro Yoshino
bullets: Ambiguous referring expressions may remain compatible with multiple scene objects as dialogue unfolds.
Candidate Set Visual Grounding (CSVG) estimates the full set of plausible referents rather than selecting one object.
CandVG benchmarks how candidate sets change across dialogue turns.
Stronger conventional visual grounding does not necessarily improve CSVG performance.
CSVG-specific instructions partially mitigate incomplete candidate generation in evaluated large-scale models.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a visual grounding task for ambiguous dialogue, evaluating vision-language models and spatial referent understanding.
papers.title: Recognizing Dialogue Ambiguity via Candidate Set Visual Grounding
papers.tldr: CSVG reframes visual grounding as tracking all objects consistent with ambiguous dialogue, revealing that current vision-language models often miss candidates and commit too early.

papers.abstract: Learning robust driving policies that generalize beyond their training domain remains a central challenge in motion planning. We propose an uncertainty-driven self-play scheme, in which half of the agents are rewarded for increasing their neighbors' epistemic uncertainty, while the other half learn to drive safely as the exploring agents continuously seek out their weaknesses. Epistemic uncertainty indicates where the policy is least confident and serves as an automatic proxy for scenario difficulty. Exploring agents use this signal to seek out hard cases, generating a challenging curriculum without manual scenario design. The resulting policy outperforms standard self-play, achieving best-in-class zero-shot transfer to nuplan Val14 (99.12% vs. 97.97%) and Argoverse 2 (82.39% vs. 78.03%) without fine-tuning, while also improving performance over standard self-play on Waymo. Our diversity-driven approach achieves 85% higher LSTM hidden-state coverage than the baseline, indicating a much richer set of behaviors. Further analysis shows that epistemic uncertainty serves as a calibrated difficulty detector, with highest-uncertain agents exhibiting 14.8 times the combined failure rate across collision, off-road, and DNF, of lowest-uncertain agents, enabling automatic prioritization of challenging scenarios without ground-truth labels.
authors: Sajad Marvi, Julian Schmidt, Alessandro Canevaro, Julian Jordan, Abhinav Valada
bullets: Exploring agents seek states that increase neighboring policies’ epistemic uncertainty, while other agents learn to drive safely through these challenges.
Epistemic uncertainty acts as an automatic difficulty signal, enabling curriculum generation without manual scenario design or ground-truth labels.
The approach improves zero-shot transfer on nuPlan Val14 and Argoverse 2 and also outperforms standard self-play on Waymo.
It produces 85% higher LSTM hidden-state coverage, suggesting a broader range of learned behaviors.
Highest-uncertainty agents have a 14.8× higher combined collision, off-road, and DNF failure rate than lowest-uncertainty agents.
papers.selection_reason: Uncertainty-driven self-play curriculum for robust multi-agent driving policies and motion planning.
papers.title: Uncertainty-Driven Self-Play for Robust Multi-Agent Driving Policies
papers.tldr: Uncertainty-driven self-play automatically focuses training on difficult driving scenarios, producing more robust policies with stronger zero-shot transfer than standard self-play.

papers.abstract: Multi-session agents can switch between LLMs to balance performance and inference cost. Such switches require transferring a history for continuity, yet their effects on the recipient remain underexplored. Through controlled experiments with multi-session tasks, we uncover behavior transfer: recipients tend to adopt reasoning and action patterns from the models that generated their histories. This effect is most evident with raw-history transfer but is substantially reduced by summarization. Based on these findings, we propose Direction- and Authorship-aware Summarization of History (DASH) that preserves stronger-model behavior while minimizing weak-to-strong transfer via summarization. Experiments with repeated swaps show that DASH outperforms raw-history transfer and naive summarization baselines. These results suggest that effective multi-model orchestration requires considering not only which model to use, but also which behavioral patterns to carry forward.
authors: Youngbin Choi, Sehyun Hwang, Suhyeon Jun, Seoyeon Lee, Sunghyun Choi, MoonJeong Park, Dongwoo Kim
bullets: Model swaps can cause recipient LLMs to adopt the reasoning and action patterns embedded in prior histories.
Behavior transfer is strongest with raw-history sharing and is substantially reduced by summarization.
DASH uses direction- and authorship-aware summarization to preserve desirable behavior and limit weak-to-strong transfer.
Across repeated swaps, DASH outperforms raw-history transfer and naive summarization baselines.
The findings highlight behavioral history—not just model selection—as a key factor in multi-model orchestration.
papers.selection_reason: Studies history transfer and summarization in multi-session LLM agents, relevant to LLM deployment and agent behavior.
papers.title: New Model, Old Habits: Behavior Transfer under Model Swapping in Multi-Session LLM Agents
papers.tldr: Switching LLMs in multi-session agents transfers behavioral patterns through shared histories, and DASH reduces unwanted transfer while preserving stronger-model behavior.

papers.abstract: Mamba models underperform Transformers on in-context retrieval. This gap is usually attributed to Mamba's fixed-size recurrent state, which loses information as the context grows. We challenge this assumption by focusing on query-first retrieval, a setup in which the query precedes the context and state capacity should not be the binding constraint. We show that even in this setting Mamba lags substantially behind Transformers, despite its selection mechanism, which was designed to distinguish relevant content from distractors. We then demonstrate that the Mamba selection gates have sufficient control over the state updates to influence the model output: intervening on specific gates alone can swing accuracy between extremes. However, as gates are input-dependent, they require the incoming token's representation to encode its relevance to the query. We therefore probe token representations across layers, and find that the relevance signal emerges only gradually with model depth, and that the gates begin to reflect it only several layers deeper. Crucially, we find that gates in retrieval-critical layers are not yet aligned with relevance. The selection mechanism is thus expressive enough to solve the task, but it commonly operates on a relevance signal that has not yet arrived. Mamba's retrieval bottleneck therefore extends beyond state capacity: even when capacity is sufficient, the delayed emergence of relevance information across depth often prevents successful retrieval.
authors: Nir Yarden, Amit Ben-Artzy, Roy Schwartz
bullets: Query-first retrieval removes state-capacity pressure, yet Mamba still substantially trails Transformers.
Mamba’s selection gates can strongly control outputs, showing that the mechanism is expressive enough for retrieval.
Gate decisions depend on token representations encoding relevance to the query.
Relevance signals emerge gradually across layers, while retrieval-critical gates often act before those signals are available.
The bottleneck is therefore delayed cross-layer relevance alignment, not capacity alone.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes Mamba's retrieval bottleneck and selection gates, relevant to LLM architecture.
papers.title: Beyond State Capacity: Why Retrieval Breaks in Mamba
papers.tldr: Mamba’s retrieval failures are not just caused by limited state capacity: relevance information often reaches its selection gates too late for effective retrieval.

papers.abstract: Recent video world models have increasingly adopted 3D memory mechanisms to integrate historical observations into a lightweight and persistent scene representation. This naturally raises a complementary question: if 3D representations can serve as an effective mechanism for memorizing observed scenes, can they also be directly used as the latent space for reconstructing and generating scenes? Motivated by this idea, we represent a scene as a compact and unstructured 3D-anchored latent space (\textbf{SceneAE}). Each latent combines an explicit 3D position with an implicit content feature and is spatially grounded to describe its local scene region, forming a sparse latent point cloud. Unlike conventional video-VAE latents that describe how a scene appears from particular viewpoints, our representation directly describes the scene itself, making it naturally applicable to both reconstruction and generation. For reconstruction, once the scene has been generated, our persistent 3D representation can be projected and decoded into RGB-D observations by different target cameras, without the need to regenerate a video for each new camera trajectory. For generation, we leverage the geometry-content separation to first generate camera-controlled 3D geometry and then synthesize content conditioned on it, reducing camera-appearance entanglement and improving camera controllability. Experiments show that this 3D latent achieves superior generation quality, computational cost, and camera controllability.
authors: Shuofeng Sun, Wenzhao Zheng, Yunpeng Zhang, Yi Wu, Linqing Zhao, Haibin Yan
bullets: Addresses whether 3D memory representations can serve directly as latent spaces for scene reconstruction and generation.
Represents each scene with spatially grounded 3D positions plus implicit content features, forming a sparse latent point cloud.
Projects the persistent representation into RGB-D views from new cameras without regenerating videos for each trajectory.
Separates geometry generation from content synthesis to reduce camera–appearance entanglement and improve camera control.
Experiments report improved generation quality, computational cost, and camera controllability.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a 3D-anchored latent space for scene generation and reconstruction, fitting World Models (interactive generation) and 3D Vision.
papers.title: SceneAE: Scene Generation and Reconstruction in Queryable 3D-Anchored Latent Space
papers.tldr: SceneAE represents scenes as sparse, queryable 3D-anchored latents that support both camera-flexible reconstruction and controllable generation.

papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning by learning low-rank weight updates. Increasing rank expands adaptation capacity, but does not guarantee that all learned directions improve downstream performance. In a diagnostic experiment with rank-16 LoRA, we show that retaining only the top singular components achieves the best performance, whereas adding further components degrades it. Motivated by this, we propose Residual-Gradient Adaptation (ReGRA), a two-stage method for making more effective use of a fixed rank budget. After the first stage, ReGRA estimates task gradients on a calibration set and removes their projections onto the two-sided subspace induced by the first-stage update. It then aggregates the residual-gradient directions to initialize a second-stage adapter without changing the first-stage update. An orthogonality regularizer encourages the two updates to capture complementary directions. Both updates can be merged into the pretrained weights, incurring no additional inference overhead. Across diverse benchmark sets, ReGRA achieves stronger performance than alternatives with the same total rank and even matches LoRA adapters with twice the rank. Ablation studies and further analysis support the contribution of its core design choices. Code is available at https://github.com/Fanyao-Li/ReGRA.
authors: Fanyao Li, Yuxi Liu, Xiaohao Liu, He Chang, Zhaoxin Wang, Zhulin Tao
bullets: Higher LoRA rank can introduce harmful directions: in a rank-16 diagnostic, keeping only top singular components performed best.
ReGRA uses a two-stage process: it projects calibration-set task gradients away from the first adapter’s induced subspace, then initializes a second adapter from residual directions.
An orthogonality regularizer encourages the two updates to learn complementary information.
Across diverse benchmarks, ReGRA outperforms same-total-rank alternatives and matches LoRA with twice the rank.
The two adapters can be merged into pretrained weights, adding no inference overhead.
papers.selection_reason: Low-rank fine-tuning method for pretrained models, transferable to LLM adaptation.
papers.title: ReGRA: Residual-Gradient Adaptation for Complementary Low-Rank Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: ReGRA improves fixed-rank LoRA fine-tuning by adding a gradient-derived, complementary adapter without increasing inference cost.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) improves reasoning in language models, but scalar outcomes provide coarse supervision over response trajectories. Self-distillation offers denser token-level guidance by comparing an unassisted policy with a feedback-informed self-teacher, yet the teacher evolves with the student, creating unstable targets and motivating additional regularization. We introduce Function-Space Policy Optimization (FSPO), a single-policy framework that combines current privileged adaptation with function-space temporal consolidation. FSPO stores sparse historical next-token distributions as fixed temporal targets, providing temporal separation without maintaining a persistent teacher model. It further introduces privileged disagreement correction to explicitly suppress locally overvalued actions, reliability-adaptive grounding that strengthens reference supervision when self-generated evidence repeatedly fails, and quality and coverage-aware temporal memory that retains verified behaviors and improves privileged demonstrations. Across reasoning and tool-use benchmarks, FSPO achieves the highest average accuracy under a 5-hour training budget, improving over the strongest baseline by approximately 4% points on average while reducing peak memory from about 70 GB to 56 GB on Olmo3-7B-Instruct.
authors: Aryan Das, Arnab Bhattacharya, Vinay Kumar Verma
bullets: Addresses coarse scalar supervision and unstable moving targets in RL with Verifiable Rewards.
Uses a single policy with sparse historical next-token distributions as fixed temporal targets, avoiding a persistent teacher model.
Adds privileged disagreement correction, reliability-adaptive grounding, and quality- and coverage-aware memory.
Reports the highest average accuracy under a 5-hour budget, with roughly 4 percentage points over the strongest baseline.
Reduces peak memory from about 70 GB to 56 GB on Olmo3-7B-Instruct.
papers.selection_reason: RLVR policy optimization for LLM reasoning with temporal self-distillation; relevant to LLM training methods.
papers.title: Function-Space Temporal Self-Distillation for Policy Optimization
papers.tldr: FSPO stabilizes self-distillation for reinforcement learning by using sparse historical policy targets and adaptive correction, improving reasoning and tool-use performance with lower memory use.

papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) changes logit margins among non-target tokens at teacher-forced prefixes. Matching a local reference distribution keeps those probabilities and also penalizes margin expansions. We ask whether a soft auxiliary can preserve selected local non-target margin relations without freezing that distribution. We introduce \textbf{Selective Rank-Preserving SFT (SRP-SFT)}, a soft margin target: a hinge on reference-scaled lower bounds for pairs from the reference's top-$K$ non-target tokens, applied at fixed teacher-forced prefixes. The hinge stops once the requested bound is met. We derive the KL cost of violating a margin, characterize the feasible region and its conditional utility, and give a finite-step condition for reducing aggregate violations. In one-epoch experiments on Qwen3-4B-Base and UltraFeedback, this target raises MATH-500 and code-generation scores over CE and LP-SFT at all three training seeds. At seed 1234, MATH-500 pass@1 rises from 49.56\% to 54.56\% and the four-metric code mean rises from 65.91\% to 69.50\% relative to LP-SFT. Ranking controls, held-out cache diagnostics, sensitivity sweeps, and six additional backbones show where these score changes appear.
authors: Yuxuan Wang, Guangxiang Zhao, Xinyu Tan, Yahui Han, Xinxiang Yin, Zhonghai Wu, Xiangzheng Zhang, Lin Sun, Tong Yang
bullets: SFT can alter non-target logit margins even when matching a local reference distribution.
SRP-SFT applies a hinge loss to reference-scaled lower bounds for pairs among the reference model’s top-K non-target tokens at teacher-forced prefixes.
The hinge stops penalizing a pair once its requested margin bound is satisfied, allowing distributional flexibility.
The paper derives the KL cost of margin violations, characterizes feasibility and utility, and provides a finite-step condition for reducing aggregate violations.
On Qwen3-4B-Base with UltraFeedback, SRP-SFT outperformed CE and LP-SFT across three seeds in the reported MATH-500 and code-generation evaluations.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a margin-preserving SFT objective for LLMs, directly relevant to LLM fine-tuning and training.
papers.title: Beyond Distribution Matching: Selective Margin Preservation for Supervised Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: SRP-SFT preserves selected non-target logit margins without forcing the full reference distribution, improving math and code-generation scores in reported one-epoch experiments.

papers.abstract: World models trained via latent dynamics offer a scalable path for embodied planning, yet existing methods suffer from representational collapse, computational overhead, and limited long-horizon capability. We introduce a memory-enhanced latent world model that augments JEPA-style prediction with a content-addressable memory bank. Our approach learns high-level representations directly from observations, operating at multiple temporal scales within a shared latent space, and conditions predictions via adaptive layer normalization. To prevent collapse and ensure effective memory usage, we design two complementary losses that encourage slot diversity and balanced temporal utilization. Experiments on PushT, Tworoom, Reacher, and OGBCube demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance with a lightweight architecture, outperforming conventional latent world models on long-horizon planning tasks.
authors: Yuwei Sun, Siyu Zhu
bullets: Targets representational collapse, computational overhead, and weak long-horizon performance in latent world models.
Uses a content-addressable memory bank with multi-timescale representations in a shared latent space.
Conditions predictions through adaptive layer normalization.
Introduces losses promoting memory-slot diversity and balanced temporal utilization.
Evaluated on PushT, Tworoom, Reacher, and OGBCube, achieving state-of-the-art performance with a lightweight architecture.
papers.selection_reason: Memory-augmented latent world model for long-horizon embodied planning.
papers.title: Enhancing Latent World Models with Associative Memory
papers.tldr: A memory-augmented JEPA-style latent world model improves long-horizon embodied planning while addressing representation collapse and computational cost.

papers.abstract: Accurate 3D reconstruction in real-world environments remains a significant challenge due to the coexistence of reflective and non-reflective surfaces, which pose distinct modeling demands. Existing methods often treat these surface types separately, limiting their generalizability and physical plausibility. To bridge this gap, we propose MicroSDF, a novel neural implicit framework that facilitates geometry and reflectance modeling through microfacet theory. Our approach incorporates three core innovations: (i) a microfacet-guided geometry model that extracts multi-scale surface normals (macroscopic and microfacet) from a signed distance field (SDF), regularized by a proposed microfacet normal consistency loss to enforce physically plausible surface orientations; (ii) an enhanced dual-branch color model, where the specular branch leverages the microfacet normals to model high-frequency reflectance, and the vanilla branch, unlike prior works, uses reflection direction (instead of viewing direction) to better model diffuse and low-frequency specular components; and (iii) a detection-guided color blending strategy that adaptively fuses the color outputs based on reflection priors, providing more physically intuitive blending than implicitly learned blending weights. Combined with a tailored multi-stage optimization scheme, the proposed MicroSDF achieves robust and high-fidelity reconstruction across reflective and non-reflective surfaces. Extensive experiments on DTU, Shiny Blender, Ref-NeRF, and DeepVoxels datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, establishing a new direction for physically grounded neural reconstruction.
authors: Lejia Ye, Yuhua Xu, Yulan Guo, Lian Xu, Xiaohu Zhang
bullets: Targets the difficulty of modeling mixed-reflectance scenes with a unified neural implicit framework.
Extracts macroscopic and microfacet normals from the SDF and enforces their consistency for physically plausible geometry.
Uses dual color branches: microfacet normals for high-frequency specular effects and reflection direction for diffuse and low-frequency components.
Adaptively blends color predictions using reflection priors rather than implicitly learned weights.
Reports robust, high-fidelity reconstruction and state-of-the-art performance across DTU, Shiny Blender, Ref-NeRF, and DeepVoxels.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a novel neural SDF framework for mixed-reflectance surface reconstruction, contributing to 3D Vision techniques relevant to robotics and simulation.
papers.title: MicroSDF: Microfacet-Driven Hybrid Neural SDFs for Mixed-Reflectance Surface Reconstruction
papers.tldr: MicroSDF reconstructs both reflective and non-reflective surfaces by combining SDF geometry with microfacet-based reflectance modeling and physically guided color blending.

papers.abstract: Executing a vision-language-action (VLA) policy involves deciding when to continue an attempt and when to intervene to improve its chances of success. We introduce ACRO, an Actor--Critic rollout orchestration layer that makes these decisions for a fixed VLA. ACRO seeks interventions that offer a more promising continuation, are physically feasible, and leave sufficient time to complete the task. A Critic learned from policy rollouts estimates success prospects to decide when to intervene and select a re-entry target along the executed trajectory. Trajectory Retraction shortcuts the visited path to return the robot to that target, where the same VLA resumes execution from a fresh observation. We evaluate ACRO with GR00T N1.7 and $\pi_{0.5}$ across SimplerEnv, RoboCasa, and real-robot manipulation. Under the same physical execution budget, including all return motion, ACRO improves success by 10.4, 7.3, and 21.7 percentage points, respectively. It also completes additional tasks as the execution budget grows. These results show that controlling when and where a policy resumes can turn its existing capabilities into more successful task executions. Project page: https://junhoo.me/acro
authors: Junhoo Lee, Seungyeon Kim, Baekseung Kim, Minkyu Kim, Suhyun Jeon, Jimyeong Kim, Nojun Kwak
bullets: Addresses failures caused by poor decisions about continuing versus intervening during VLA policy execution.
Uses a rollout-trained Critic to assess success prospects, choose intervention times, and select re-entry targets.
Applies Trajectory Retraction to return the robot to a selected point before resuming the same VLA with a fresh observation.
Evaluated with GR00T N1.7 and π₀.₅ in simulation and real-robot manipulation, improving success by 10.4, 7.3, and 21.7 percentage points across the reported settings.
Also completes additional tasks when the available execution budget increases.
papers.selection_reason: Actor-critic rollout orchestration deciding when to intervene and where to resume for fixed VLA policies.
papers.title: ACRO: Actor-Critic Rollout Orchestration
papers.tldr: ACRO improves fixed vision-language-action policies by deciding when and where to intervene and resume execution, increasing task success under the same physical execution budget.

papers.abstract: Geometry foundation models estimate camera poses and 3D scene structure from video sequences, but maintaining consistent reconstructions over long horizons remains challenging. Feed-forward models process long sequences as independent, fixed-length frame windows and align their predictions, causing pose and reconstruction errors to accumulate across windows. Streaming models retain information from past frames to inform future predictions, but cannot revise earlier estimates when later observations reveal errors. To address this, we introduce Scaffold MemOry for Revision (SMORE), a framework equipping frozen geometry foundation models with a revisable external memory for long-horizon inference. Inspired by hippocampal associative memory in biological brains, which links spatial context with sensory experience, SMORE associates where an observer is with what it observes, enabling past observations to be stored, retrieved, verified against new evidence, and revised when inconsistencies are detected. We evaluate SMORE with eight competitive geometry models on five datasets spanning camera pose estimation, multi-view depth estimation, 3D point-cloud reconstruction, simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), and novel view synthesis. Across all evaluated models, SMORE consistently improves long-sequence pose estimation, reduces multi-view depth error by up to 58%, reduces Chamfer distance for 3D point-cloud reconstruction by up to 43%, and achieves average trajectory error as low as 2.9 cm in long-horizon SLAM. By retaining corrected poses and observations, SMORE further improves the fidelity and spatial consistency of large-scale 3D scene reconstruction. These results establish revisable external memory as a flexible interface for extending pretrained geometry models beyond fixed-context prediction toward iterative, error-correcting inference over long visual sequences.
authors: Soumick Sarker, Mengmi Zhang
bullets: Addresses error accumulation from fixed-window and non-revisable streaming inference on long video sequences.
Associates spatial context with observations so past geometry can be stored, retrieved, checked against new evidence, and revised.
Evaluated with eight geometry models across five tasks, including pose, depth, point-cloud reconstruction, SLAM, and novel view synthesis.
Consistently improves long-sequence pose estimation, with reported reductions of up to 58% in depth error and 43% in Chamfer distance.
Achieves trajectory error as low as 2.9 cm in long-horizon SLAM and improves large-scale scene consistency.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a revisable external memory (SMORE) for long-horizon 3D geometry, fitting World Models (long-horizon prediction) and Adaptation and Memory.
papers.title: Remember, Revisit, Revise: Scaffold Memory for Long-Horizon 3D Geometry
papers.tldr: SMORE adds revisable external memory to frozen 3D geometry models, enabling long-horizon predictions to retrieve, verify, and correct past estimates for more consistent reconstructions.

papers.abstract: Action-chunking vision-language-action (VLA) models predict sequences of future robot actions. Under fixed-horizon execution, the robot executes a fixedlength prefix of each predicted chunk before invoking the policy again, leaving the remaining predictions unused. For a given number of executed actions, short execution horizons require more policy calls. Extending the execution horizon amortizes policy inference cost over more actions. However, uniformly applying long horizons across episodes can limit opportunities for precise corrections. To address this limitation, we propose PICES (Perturbation-Informed Chunk and Execution Horizon Selection), a training-free method that jointly selects an action chunk and the number of actions executed before the next policy call. Within a single policy call, the action expert generates a batch of action chunks from multiple initial noise samples and their locally perturbed counterparts, using the same conditioning features across all samples. PICES exploits differences between corresponding actions in each nominal chunk and its counterpart to determine candidate-specific execution horizons and select a nominal chunk for execution. Experiments on simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that PICES achieves speedup by up to 2.3x in wall-clock policy inference time on Jetson Orin and Thor relative to fixed horizon baselines while improving the success rate.
authors: Jehun Lee, Hajun Lee, Jimin Ryu, Youhan Lee, Beomseok Kang, Jonghyun Choi, Jae-Joon Kim
bullets: Fixed-horizon execution can waste predicted actions and incur excessive policy calls at short horizons.
PICES is training-free and jointly selects an action chunk and how many actions to execute before replanning.
It compares nominal action chunks with versions generated from locally perturbed noise samples under shared conditioning features.
Experiments in simulation and real-world manipulation show up to 2.3× faster wall-clock inference on Jetson Orin and Thor, with improved success rate.
The method targets adaptive execution: longer horizons for stable predictions and shorter horizons for precise corrections.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free action chunk and execution horizon selection that accelerates VLA inference while improving manipulation success.
papers.title: Accelerating VLA Inference with Perturbation Informed Execution
papers.tldr: PICES accelerates VLA robot control by adapting both the selected action chunk and execution horizon using perturbation-based uncertainty cues, improving speed and success.

papers.abstract: Hyperspectral imaging distinguishes RGB-similar objects, but a pretrained vision-language-action model needs a state its frozen decoder can use. SPECTRA-VLA provides a native-width spectral upgrade without retraining the visual encoder or action decoder. A learned continuous residual enriches each target token through its own normalized false-color reference; projection, norm control and validation-calibrated injection regulate the change. Across 86 held-out acquisitions, category balanced accuracy rises from 0.812 to 0.883. With identical residuals and scale, own-token addition improves reuse of an external category-derived probe on frozen decoder logits: 0.701 versus 0.590 with pooled replacement, at similar image-disjoint recognition. Five grouped tests covering the same 86 acquisitions recover within-category spectral shape with $R^2=0.802/0.337$ from continuous and posterior-code states. Category-matched spectral swaps further show that own-token composition approximately doubles the target-specific recovery increment after frozen decoding. Spectral enrichment and receiving-token preservation thus work together at the pretrained interface.
authors: Chih-Chung Hsu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of making hyperspectral distinctions usable by a pretrained model without retraining its visual encoder or action decoder.
Uses native-width residual enrichment based on each token’s normalized false-color reference, with projection, norm control, and validation-calibrated injection.
Across 86 held-out acquisitions, category-balanced accuracy increases from 0.812 to 0.883.
Own-token addition improves external category-probe reuse over pooled replacement (0.701 vs. 0.590) under identical residuals and scale.
Grouped tests recover within-category spectral shape, while spectral swaps indicate that own-token composition approximately doubles target-specific recovery after frozen decoding.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, adapting frozen interfaces to hyperspectral data without retraining, a core interest in Embodied AI.
papers.title: SPECTRA-VLA: Base-Fine Hyperspectral Token Transfer at Frozen Vision-Language-Action Interfaces
papers.tldr: SPECTRA-VLA transfers hyperspectral information into a frozen vision-language-action model by enriching each visual token with a calibrated, token-specific residual.
