papers.abstract: Typed decision models need an interface that can use additional reasoning while retaining candidate outputs. We train a shared candidate-answer reader on a frozen Qwen3.5-4B backbone to unify direct decisions with on-demand, interruptible reasoning. The reader returns distributions from empty and partial reasoning prefixes. A benefit gate starts reasoning, a natural-state trigger requests explicit reads, and an entropy rule accepts acquired answers and cancels generation. Measurements distinguish answer-query work, generated output, and pipeline time. Across 768 questions from ProofWriter, LogiQA 2.0, and ARC-Challenge, accuracy rises from 70.96% for direct reading to 84.38%. Relative to 512-token terminal reading, accuracy improves by 7.29 percentage points with 2.25% more mean output work. Relative to 1,024-token terminal reading, pipeline time falls by 46.30% with an accuracy difference of -1.17 points. Exact-prefix controls isolate the saving from interruption, while read-scheduling controls distinguish reduced observation work from shorter response time.
authors: Bin Zheng, Zheng Chen
bullets: Addresses how typed decision models can invoke additional reasoning without discarding candidate outputs.
Uses a shared candidate-answer reader over a frozen Qwen3.5-4B backbone, supporting direct decisions and partial reasoning prefixes.
A benefit gate starts reasoning, a natural-state trigger requests reads, and an entropy rule accepts answers or interrupts generation.
Across 768 ProofWriter, LogiQA 2.0, and ARC-Challenge questions, accuracy increases from 70.96% to 84.38%.
Compared with 1,024-token terminal reading, pipeline time drops 46.30% with a 1.17-point accuracy decrease.
papers.selection_reason: Selective reasoning controller for typed decision models; improves reasoning efficiency.
papers.title: Selective Reasoning for Typed Decision Models: When to Start, Read, and Stop
papers.tldr: A selective reading-and-stopping interface improves typed decision accuracy while reducing unnecessary reasoning and pipeline time.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning provides a direct mechanism for optimizing task objectives in large language model-driven agents, but task rewards are typically sparse trajectory-level signals that only evaluate task success, without directly supervising action-conditioned environment transitions, leaving the model with limited explicit understanding of action consequences and environment dynamics. Recent work introduces auxiliary supervision through policy and world modeling co-training, yet typically treats complete environmental observations uniformly as world modeling targets, overlooking the varying decision relevance of observation content. We propose DGS-WM (Decision-Guided Selective World Modeling), a decision-guided policy-world modeling co-training approach for language agents. DGS-WM employs a Decision-Guided Observation Selection component that filters observation units with decision value as world modeling targets based on their support for subsequent policy responses, and a Confidence-Adaptive Weighting component that adaptively adjusts supervision strength according to the model's prediction confidence on selected targets. Together, these components form a decision-aware auxiliary world modeling loss, jointly optimized with the RL loss on the same policy model. Across multiple benchmarks covering single-hop/multi-hop question answering and interactive web tasks, DGS-WM achieves consistent improvements under different model scales and RL algorithms, demonstrating more stable and effective performance compared to full-observation world modeling methods.
authors: Maolin Ran, Minda Chen, Di Huang, Wei Xiong, Fei Huang, Weiwen Liu
bullets: RL agents receive sparse task-level rewards, which provide limited supervision about action consequences and environment dynamics.
DGS-WM selects observation units for world-model training based on their value for subsequent policy decisions.
It adaptively weights selected targets according to the model’s prediction confidence.
The decision-aware world-modeling loss is jointly optimized with the RL objective on the same policy model.
Experiments across question-answering and interactive web tasks show consistent, more stable improvements across model scales and RL algorithms versus full-observation modeling.
papers.selection_reason: Decision-guided selective world modeling for language agents; directly relevant to world models.
papers.title: Model What Matters: Decision-Guided Selective World Modeling for Language Agents
papers.tldr: DGS-WM improves language-agent reinforcement learning by selectively modeling only observation details that inform future decisions and weighting them by prediction confidence.

papers.abstract: Gaze coordinates attention in human interaction through coupled eye, head, and eyelid motion. A humanoid robot must choose where to look while generating a suitable movement toward that target; fixed tracking rules alone do not model the temporal structure of human gaze. We separate these tasks with an asynchronous vision-language model that selects a scene referent, a reactive perception module that maintains fixation, and a Realistic Gaze Transformer (RGT) that generates target-conditioned motion. RGT is a Transformer-VAE trained on markerless human recordings retargeted to the robot's 11-DoF joint space: self-supervised pretraining encodes recent full-head history, and autoregressive fine-tuning exposes the model to its own predictions during rollout. At inference, a four-dimensional binocular-eye trajectory conditions coordinated neck and eye motion; an auxiliary blink predictor triggers eyelid templates during playback. On a two-second benchmark in which all controllers receive the same ground-truth target, RGT-Base obtains the lowest reported overall seven-joint MSE, and physical demonstrations show the integrated targeting and control pipeline. The evidence establishes robot-space kinematic fidelity and real-time RGT inference; perceived naturalness and open-vocabulary target-selection accuracy remain questions for controlled evaluation.
authors: Yuhang Hu, Junlin Lyu, Yuan Fang, Xiaoying Shen, Lechen Zhang, Jiong Lin, Judah Goldfeder, Steven Tian, Hod Lipson
bullets: Separates gaze target selection, fixation, and target-conditioned motion generation.
RGT uses a Transformer-VAE trained on retargeted markerless human gaze recordings in an 11-DoF robot joint space.
Self-supervised history encoding and autoregressive fine-tuning support realistic rollout behavior.
On a two-second shared-target benchmark, RGT-Base achieves the lowest reported overall seven-joint MSE.
Physical demonstrations show integrated targeting and control, while perceived naturalness and open-vocabulary selection remain unevaluated.
papers.selection_reason: Humanoid gaze generation from human video recordings with VLM-guided target selection, relevant to embodied visuomotor control.
papers.title: Eye, Robot: Learning Expressive Gaze Dynamics via a VLM-Guided Transformer-VAE
papers.tldr: A VLM-guided Transformer-VAE enables humanoid robots to select gaze targets and generate coordinated, expressive eye, head, and eyelid movements in real time.

papers.abstract: Recent work has explored visual reasoning through image generation, where models solve visual-reasoning problems by directly generating solution images. Intuitively, iterative samplers such as flow matching are well suited to this task, since each sampling step may resemble one reasoning step. However, in this work, from a circuit complexity perspective, we show that this intuition is misleading. We prove that as long as the model outputs satisfy certain mild regularity conditions, the trajectory of the vanilla flow-matching sampler can be simulated by a constant number of sequential rounds of parallel model evaluations. Consequently, additional sampling steps cannot increase the expressive power of a constant-depth backbone model under the standard complexity-theoretic model of transformers. We then reveal that self-conditioning, which conditions the model on the previous step's estimate of the final image, plays a previously unrecognized role in removing this bottleneck. Controlled experiments on diverse visual-reasoning tasks show that flow matching with self-conditioning achieves higher accuracy and greater reasoning depth than vanilla flow matching, and its performance improves with more sampling steps. Theoretically, we prove that with self-conditioning, a constant-depth backbone can achieve expressive power equivalent to that of space-bounded Turing machines. Our study suggests a design principle for future visual reasoning research: carry more information between sampling steps, so that additional steps translate into deeper reasoning.
authors: Zeyang Zhang, Linxiang Gao, Meiqi Gu, Xingyan Chen, Minrui Luo, Kaifeng Lyu, Tianxing He
bullets: Vanilla flow-matching trajectories can be simulated with only a constant number of parallel model-evaluation rounds under mild regularity conditions.
Therefore, adding sampling steps alone does not increase the expressive power of constant-depth transformer backbones.
Self-conditioning passes the previous estimate of the final image between steps, removing this computational bottleneck.
Experiments across diverse visual-reasoning tasks show higher accuracy, greater reasoning depth, and continued improvement with more sampling steps when self-conditioning is used.
The theory shows that self-conditioned constant-depth backbones can match the expressive power of space-bounded Turing machines.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes self-conditioning in flow matching for visual reasoning, providing a transferable technical insight for deep sequential reasoning in generative models.
papers.title: Self-Conditioning Enables Deep Sequential Reasoning in Flow Matching
papers.tldr: Self-conditioning allows flow-matching samplers to use additional steps for genuinely deeper visual reasoning, overcoming a limitation of vanilla flow matching.

papers.abstract: Differentiable reinforcement learning shows strong promise for robot policy learning, but its application to legged locomotion has remained limited to blind walking or simulated 2D tasks. Extending it to end-to-end visual obstacle avoidance is challenging because hard collision constraints and early termination upon contact corrupt first-order gradients, trapping optimizers in local minima. We present E2DRL, which addresses this with a soft differentiable obstacle-interaction formulation: penetration penalties across multiple body keypoints with velocity-conditioned stop-gradient shaping to provide the first-order training signals for 3D obstacle avoidance. To realize a deployable perception-control system, a privileged teacher trained via Soft Analytic Policy Optimization (SAPO) in a differentiable simulator is distilled into a recurrent depth-based student via DAgger, then blended with a base locomotion policy using a terrain-aware gating module for deployment. In simulation, E2DRL achieves higher sample efficiency than PPO and demonstrates superior velocity-tracking performance and 3D obstacle-avoidance capability compared with both PPO and Duality-based DCBF NMPC. We present the first sim-to-real validation of end-to-end differentiable RL for 3D obstacle avoidance on a Unitree Go2 in static and dynamic environments.
authors: Cheng Fan, Bingyang Zhou, Gang Yang, Zixuan Zhuang, Aoqian Zhang, Pengzhi Yang, Xin Liu, Chunzheng Wang, Yan Rui Tan, Fan Shi
bullets: Addresses gradient corruption from hard collisions and early termination in differentiable RL for legged obstacle avoidance.
Uses velocity-conditioned, stop-gradient shaping with penetration penalties across multiple body keypoints.
Distills a privileged SAPO teacher into a recurrent depth-based student using DAgger, then blends it with locomotion control through terrain-aware gating.
In simulation, shows higher sample efficiency than PPO and improved velocity tracking and obstacle avoidance versus PPO and Duality-based DCBF NMPC.
Demonstrates sim-to-real 3D obstacle avoidance on a Unitree Go2 in static and dynamic environments.
papers.selection_reason: Differentiable RL with soft obstacle interaction for 3D visual obstacle avoidance in quadruped robots, with sim-to-real deployment.
papers.title: E2DRL: End-to-End Differentiable Reinforcement Learning for 3D Obstacle Avoidance in Quadruped Robots
papers.tldr: E2DRL enables end-to-end differentiable visual 3D obstacle avoidance for quadruped robots by replacing hard collision handling with soft, gradient-preserving interaction penalties and deploying a distilled perception-control policy.

papers.abstract: We propose DAGFormer, a Transformer language model whose cross-layer connections are planned by a jointly trained topology predictor. Beyond the residual connections in a standard Transformer, DAGFormer adds direct connections from earlier layers to later ones, and the predictor controls the strength of every connection based on input tokens. Unlike existing cross-layer routing architectures, which set each layer's connections separately, DAGFormer plans the routing of the whole model at once. On matched OLMo-2 pairs from 75M to 1B parameters, DAGFormer lowers WikiText-2 perplexity by 17% to 25% over the vanilla Transformer, and a 1B DAGFormer trained on 5B tokens outperforms the vanilla model trained on 10B. Against four routing baselines with the same data and budget, it reaches the lowest perplexity at 75M, 300M and 1B. The gain carries over to 13 commonsense, science, reading and math evaluation tasks (2.0 to 2.5 points higher mean accuracy at 300M and 1B) and to instruction finetuning (63% to 70% AlpacaEval win rate against the vanilla Transformer, leading every routing baseline), and under structured pruning DAGFormer degrades the least in five of six settings.
authors: Xiaocong Yang, Yuren Hao, ChengXiang Zhai
bullets: Adds direct connections from earlier to later layers beyond standard residual links.
A jointly trained topology predictor plans the full model’s routing at once, rather than layer by layer.
Reduces WikiText-2 perplexity by 17–25% over matched vanilla Transformers from 75M to 1B parameters.
Improves mean accuracy on 13 downstream tasks and achieves higher AlpacaEval win rates after instruction finetuning.
Shows greater robustness to structured pruning in five of six tested settings.
papers.selection_reason: Novel Transformer topology predictor for language models; directly relevant to LLM architecture.
papers.title: DAGFormer: Global Topology Prediction for Transformer Cross-Layer Connections
papers.tldr: DAGFormer jointly plans token-dependent cross-layer connections across the entire Transformer, substantially improving language modeling and downstream performance over standard and routed Transformers.

papers.abstract: Single-image 3D reconstruction has advanced rapidly, yet standalone garments remain challenging due to thin-shell geometry, open boundaries, and layered structures. Existing datasets and evaluation protocols provide limited support for systematic evaluation in this setting. We introduce MagicGarment, a benchmark for single-image standalone 3D garment reconstruction with 1,518 professionally constructed assets across 17 composite garment types, aligned multimodal annotations, and a unified evaluation protocol. We further establish a garment-aware reference baseline by adapting a pretrained image-to-3D backbone at two levels: Grounded Semantic Refinement (GSR) provides garment-focused visual conditioning, while Flow-Time-Route LoRA (FTR-LoRA) adapts the frozen 3D generative backbone using flow-timestep, token-routing, and expert-load information. Experiments demonstrate MagicGarment's benchmark utility and the effectiveness of garment-aware adaptation. Project page: https://1019538157.github.io/MagicGarment/.
authors: Jia Chen, Ruyang Zhao, Jun Bai, Chao Huang, Saishang Zhong, Xinrong Hu
bullets: Addresses challenges from thin-shell geometry, open boundaries, and layered garment structures.
Provides 1,518 professionally constructed assets spanning 17 composite garment types.
Includes aligned multimodal annotations and a unified evaluation protocol.
Adapts a pretrained image-to-3D model with garment-focused visual conditioning and flow-aware LoRA refinement.
Experiments show the benchmark is useful and the garment-aware adaptation is effective.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a benchmark and adaptation method for single-image 3D garment reconstruction using a pretrained backbone, fitting 3D Vision and 3D Foundation Models.
papers.title: MagicGarment: Benchmarking Single-Image Standalone 3D Garment Reconstruction
papers.tldr: MagicGarment introduces a benchmark and garment-aware baseline for evaluating single-image 3D reconstruction of standalone garments.

papers.abstract: Object-goal navigation requires an embodied agent to explore an unfamiliar environment, identify a target object, navigate toward candidate instances, and reliably determine whether the observed object satisfies the mission goal. This work investigates this problem through a two-stage development process. In Stage I, a fixed modular framework is used to examine combinations of exploration, object detection, and target validation methods. The results reveal clear trade-offs among navigation performance, validation reliability, execution time, and model-related cost, with no single fixed configuration remaining preferable across all evaluated conditions. These observations motivate F2A-ObjectNav (Fixed-to-Adaptive Object-Goal Navigation), an adaptive agentic architecture in which a rule-based Supervisor coordinates specialized components for navigation and exploration, object detection, target validation, semantic guidance, and Mission Memory. The architecture uses event-driven recovery, strategy revision, candidate management, and conditional semantic guidance while retaining lightweight execution during normal operation. F2A-ObjectNav is evaluated over 25 episodes in each of AI2-THOR, RoboTHOR, and ProcTHOR, achieving success rate (SR) / success-weighted path length (SPL) values of 0.84/0.52, 0.40/0.22, and 0.44/0.37, respectively. In addition to task-level metrics, architecture-specific behavioral metrics are used to characterize semantic-guidance usage, strategy switching, recovery activation, memory-supported behavior, and decision stability. The results show different patterns of adaptive intervention across the three environments, with higher intervention frequencies observed in RoboTHOR and ProcTHOR than in AI2-THOR.
authors: Seyed Ali Mirghasemi, Alireza Taheri
bullets: Object-goal navigation requires exploration, object detection, target validation, and reliable mission completion in unfamiliar environments.
A fixed modular study found trade-offs among navigation performance, validation reliability, execution time, and model cost, motivating adaptive coordination.
A rule-based Supervisor dynamically manages navigation, exploration, detection, validation, semantic guidance, and Mission Memory.
Event-driven recovery, strategy revision, candidate management, and conditional guidance support adaptive behavior while keeping normal execution lightweight.
Across AI2-THOR, RoboTHOR, and ProcTHOR, SR/SPL were 0.84/0.52, 0.40/0.22, and 0.44/0.37; adaptive interventions were more frequent in RoboTHOR and ProcTHOR.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive agentic architecture for object-goal navigation with mission memory and recovery.
papers.title: F2A-ObjectNav: An Adaptive Agentic Architecture for Object-Goal Navigation
papers.tldr: F2A-ObjectNav adaptively coordinates specialized navigation components to improve object-goal navigation across varied environments.

papers.abstract: Instruction-Conditioned Motion Control (ICMC) separates parameter specification, instruction generation, and code synthesis for language-driven robot control, making execution outcomes traceable to instructions and programs. We compare one-shot generation with ICMC under o1 and o4-mini on cube pick-and-place and letter-reshaping tasks for a UR5e arm in MuJoCo. We then train an open-weight instruction policy by GRPO through a frozen code generator on cube placement onto two- and five-cube letter layouts, averaging the rewards of five programs per instruction. The logged positive-reward rate rose from 31.6% to 35.3% (253/800 to 282/800) between the first and last five training steps. A log audit identifies positive binary labels associated with geometric-failure messages: at least 19 in that run, 18 in the dense-reward run, and 5 in the run with one program per instruction. In one case, all five rewards were 1.0 while the log reports a 0.9515 m miss against a 0.05 m tolerance; the verdict came from the program's own output stream. We distinguish logged reward rates from independently verified task success and report descriptive results for each configuration's single training trajectory. We introduce an independent evaluation protocol that checks task completion against fixed specifications, separating robot control from success assessment to support reproducible evaluation.
authors: Fan Huang, Dezhong Tong, Changyu Chen, Haewoon Kwak, Jisun An
bullets: Evaluates one-shot generation versus ICMC on UR5e cube pick-and-place and letter-reshaping tasks in MuJoCo using o1 and o4-mini.
Trains an open-weight instruction policy with GRPO through a frozen code generator, averaging rewards from five programs per instruction.
Logged positive-reward rates increased from 31.6% to 35.3% over the reported five-step trajectory, but these rates were not always consistent with independently verified task success.
Audits found positive labels for geometric failures, including a case where all five rewards were 1.0 despite a 0.9515 m miss against a 0.05 m tolerance.
Proposes independent evaluation against fixed task specifications to separate robot control from success assessment.
papers.selection_reason: Language-conditioned robotic arm control via code decomposition and reinforcement learning.
papers.title: Instruction-Conditioned Motion Control for Robotic Arms: Language-to-Code Decomposition and Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: ICMC makes language-driven robot motion more traceable by separating instructions, parameters, and code, while exposing limitations in reward-based success evaluation.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has enabled robust locomotion for legged robots, but learned policies are typically tied to a specific robot morphology and require additional engineering when the number of legs, actuators, or mechanical properties change. We present PolyMorph, a morphology-conditioned framework that learns a single locomotion policy for heterogeneous legged robots. PolyMorph converts each robot's URDF into joint-link modules and combines a recurrent encoder, graph-based Transformer, and per-joint decoder to generate actions across variable leg counts and joint configurations. To improve training stability, PolyMorph uses morphology-normalized rewards, adaptive robot sampling, and URDF-derived PD-gain initialization. We evaluate PolyMorph in simulation across bipedal, tripedal, and quadrupedal robots, including unseen morphology variants and platforms, and deploy the policy on real quadruped platforms operated in multiple configurations. The results show that a single PolyMorph policy generalizes across diverse robot morphologies without per-robot policy retraining.
authors: Hyunsik Oh, Seunghun Jeon, Donghoon Youm, Jungwoo Hur, Hyeongjun Kim, Jeong Hyun Lee, Moonkyu Jung, Jemin Hwangbo
bullets: Targets the need to retrain or re-engineer locomotion policies when robot morphology changes.
Encodes URDF-derived joint-link modules with a recurrent encoder, graph Transformer, and per-joint action decoder.
Improves training stability using morphology-normalized rewards, adaptive robot sampling, and URDF-based PD-gain initialization.
Evaluated in simulation on bipedal, tripedal, and quadrupedal robots, including unseen morphologies and platforms.
Demonstrates real-world deployment on quadrupeds in multiple configurations without per-robot policy retraining.
papers.selection_reason: Morphology-conditioned locomotion policy learning across heterogeneous legged robots.
papers.title: PolyMorph: Learning Locomotion Policy for Cross-Embodiment Adaptation
papers.tldr: PolyMorph learns one morphology-conditioned locomotion policy that transfers across legged robots with different body designs, including unseen variants and real quadruped configurations.

papers.abstract: Modern vision-language models can accept multi-image contexts, but aggregate accuracy rarely reveals where a multi-image reasoning pipeline fails. We study a controlled schema-application task in which a model must locate two target characters in a 16-image sequence, identify their visual attributes, consult an item-specific visual codebook, and compose two ordered nonce code names. We introduce a within-item 2-by-2 factorial Oracle design: Oracle-A supplies a verified textual schema, Oracle-B supplies a verified ordered target-appearance representation, and both interventions retain the original images and final question. Across 72 new items and 1,188 analyzed model responses, Oracle-B increased strict exact accuracy by 54.6 percentage points (95% confidence interval: 46.3 to 63.0) and outperformed Oracle-A by 60.6 points (Holm-adjusted p-value no greater than .0002). An auxiliary retrieval diagnostic reached only 49.1% ordered-appearance accuracy even after removing code-name generation. Providing both Oracle sources yielded 100% accuracy across all models. These results localize the dominant recoverable deficit to upstream ordered instance recovery rather than primarily to downstream schema use and composition.
authors: Yiliu Xu, Xinjin Li, Yu Ma
bullets: The task requires locating two characters across 16 images, identifying their attributes, consulting a visual codebook, and composing ordered nonce names.
A within-item 2×2 design independently supplied a verified textual schema and verified ordered target-appearance representation while retaining the original images and question.
Providing ordered target appearances increased strict exact accuracy by 54.6 percentage points; it outperformed schema provision by 60.6 points.
An auxiliary diagnostic achieved only 49.1% ordered-appearance accuracy, while supplying both Oracle sources produced 100% accuracy across all models.
Findings are scoped to this controlled schema-application task and its 72 new items and 1,188 analyzed responses.
papers.selection_reason: Oracle-intervention analysis of multi-image VLM schema application; fits multimodal LLM understanding.
papers.title: What Breaks in Multi-Image Schema Application? Factorial Oracle Interventions Reveal an Instance-Information Bottleneck
papers.tldr: A factorial Oracle study finds that multi-image schema reasoning fails mainly because models cannot reliably recover the ordered appearances of target instances, rather than because they cannot apply the schema.

papers.abstract: Long-output inference in large language models suffers from severe KV cache memory and bandwidth bottlenecks. While KV cache quantization alleviates this issue, low-bit quantization (e.g., 2-bit) severely degrades model accuracy. Recent mixed-precision key-cache quantization methods mitigate this degradation by allocating higher precision to important key channels, but estimate channel saliency using only key statistics. Through attention logit perturbation analysis at the RoPE channel-pair level, we show that quantization errors in channel pairs with large query--key pair-norm products contribute significantly to logit variation. Based on this insight, we propose PN-Mix, a mixed-precision key-cache quantization method for RoPE-based decoder-only LLMs, which allocates higher precision to salient channel pairs identified once during the prefill stage and reused throughout decoding. Across standard reasoning, code-generation, and AIME benchmarks, PN-Mix with 2.26-bit average precision achieves comparable or better average accuracy than prior mixed-precision methods using 2.32--2.39 bits. Furthermore, in our Pareto sweep, PN-Mix degrades gracefully down to 1.5 bits, whereas the compared baselines exhibit sharper performance drops below 2.25 bits.
authors: Gil Jae Song, Sungjoo Yoo
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory and bandwidth bottlenecks in long-output LLM inference.
Uses RoPE channel-pair attention-logit perturbation analysis to identify salient pairs via query–key pair-norm products.
Assigns higher precision to salient key pairs once during prefill and reuses the allocation during decoding.
At 2.26-bit average precision, matches or outperforms prior mixed-precision methods using 2.32–2.39 bits across reasoning, code-generation, and AIME benchmarks.
Degrades more gracefully to 1.5 bits than compared baselines, which show sharper drops below 2.25 bits.
papers.selection_reason: Mixed-precision KV cache quantization for efficient LLM inference.
papers.title: PN-Mix: Pair-Norm Guided Mixed-Precision Key Cache Quantization for Efficient Long-Output LLM Inference
papers.tldr: PN-Mix improves low-bit KV-cache efficiency by assigning precision using query–key pair-norm saliency, enabling strong long-output LLM accuracy at very low bit rates.

papers.abstract: Force feedback provides vision-language-action (VLA) policies with physical observations that can guide action selection and execution. However, differences in tasks, demonstrations, and control settings across existing systems hinder reliable comparisons of force integration designs. We introduce ForceBench, a simulation benchmark for evaluating six-axis wrist-force integration under a unified protocol. ForceBench combines eight tasks spanning physical-property inference, resistance-dependent interaction, and contact-rich assembly with 1,600 synchronized demonstrations and task-specific success criteria. We compare one no-force baseline and six force integration designs on a shared $\pi_{0.5}$ backbone. Prompt Fusion achieves the highest observed mean simulation success of 35.31%, compared with 23.25% for the baseline, and improves success rates across all three task categories. Predictive and temporal gains in simulation concentrate on physical-property inference, while both temporal designs underperform the baseline on assembly. Real-world evaluation of eight systems across five tasks supports the main qualitative trends: Prompt Fusion and Dual-Path Fusion achieve 63.00% mean success, compared with 40.00% for the baseline, but only Prompt Fusion improves every task. These findings support ForceBench's practical value for identifying the benefits and limitations of force integration across manipulation demands. The project page is available at https://forcebench-platform.github.io/.
authors: Xuan Han, Zinuo Jin, Tianlin Li, Yunfan Lou, Xin Liu, Yuchen Xue, Yuanpeng He, Boxian Yao, Shuhan Zhan, Ruihai Wu, Zhibo Pang
bullets: Introduces a unified simulation benchmark covering eight tasks, 1,600 synchronized demonstrations, and task-specific success criteria.
Compares a no-force baseline with six force-integration designs using a shared π0.5 backbone.
Prompt Fusion achieves 35.31% mean simulation success versus 23.25% for the baseline and improves all three task categories.
In real-world tests, Prompt Fusion and Dual-Path Fusion reach 63.00% mean success versus 40.00% for the baseline; only Prompt Fusion improves every task.
Predictive and temporal benefits are strongest for physical-property inference, while temporal designs underperform on assembly.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for force integration in VLA-based robotic manipulation.
papers.title: ForceBench: Benchmarking Force Integration for Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: ForceBench standardizes evaluation of six-axis wrist-force integration for vision-language-action policies, finding that Prompt Fusion performs best across diverse robotic manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong performance on local robot manipulation, yet their success does not readily translate to long-horizon mobile manipulation. In our experiments, a pretrained subtask VLA achieves 80% success rate on atomic manipulation tasks but only 19% when these skills are composed into mobile manipulation. We argue that this gap stems from failures across the execution process rather than from local manipulation capability alone. To uncover these bottlenecks, we systematically diagnose failures in long-horizon mobile manipulation and identify three dominant regimes: task planning, navigation and base positioning, and local manipulation. Based on this diagnosis, we develop failure-guided agentic intervention that augments a fixed subtask VLA with demonstration-based planning guidance, adaptive visual memory, accessibility-aware base adjustment, and local end-effector adjustment. On RoboCasa365, these interventions progressively improve task success from 19% to 47%, with the finalized system reaching 49% on held-out episode seeds, compared with 18% for the baseline. The same design improves performance from 14% to 37% on BEHAVIOR-1K and from 5/20 to 13/20 on real-robot tasks. These results suggest that reliable mobile manipulation can be advanced by diagnosing and intervening on the current bottleneck, rather than uniformly scaling the underlying policy. Our code will be released at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/Cracking-Mobile-Manipulation.git.
authors: Zixuan Wang, Jia-Ning Li, Yinzhou Tang, Yanzhao Yu, Biao Wu, Meng Fang, Xin Li, Yiwu Zhong
bullets: A pretrained VLA succeeds on 80% of atomic manipulation tasks but only 19% when skills are composed for mobile manipulation.
Failures primarily arise in task planning, navigation/base positioning, and local manipulation.
The proposed system adds demonstration-based planning, adaptive visual memory, accessibility-aware base adjustment, and local end-effector adjustment to a fixed subtask VLA.
Success improves from 19% to 47% on RoboCasa365, reaching 49% on held-out seeds versus 18% for the baseline.
The approach also improves results on BEHAVIOR-1K and real-robot tasks, supporting bottleneck-focused intervention over uniform policy scaling.
papers.selection_reason: Failure-guided agentic interventions for long-horizon mobile manipulation with adaptive visual memory.
papers.title: Cracking Mobile Manipulation: From Failure Diagnosis to Agentic Robot System
papers.tldr: Diagnosing bottlenecks across planning, navigation, and manipulation enables targeted agentic interventions that substantially improve long-horizon mobile manipulation.

papers.abstract: Whole-body mobile manipulation suffers from two fundamental challenges: inherent motion heterogeneity across locomotion, arm, and hand modules, and progressive error accumulation over long-horizon multi-stage tasks. Existing teleoperation platforms also lack integrated dexterous tactile sensing to support coordinated whole-body decision-making. This paper presents RoboSpan, a high-DoF whole-body teleoperation and demonstration platform, and the Hierarchical Modular Framework (HMF) for learning modular coordination policies. HMF functionally decouples the 29-DoF action space into fine hand manipulation, arm pose adjustment, and mobile-base spatial configuration branches, and introduces the Coordinated Modular Embodied Transformer (COMET) with inter-modular cross-attention to enable dynamic information exchange and action coordination. Vision-language model driven hierarchical task decomposition structurally suppresses temporal error propagation, while a full-palm 2D tactile representation encodes distributed contact signals for cross-module tactile empowerment. Experiments on a physical 29-DoF robot demonstrate that the proposed method achieves over 20\% higher task success rate than mainstream baselines across a range of long-horizon whole-body tasks, markedly improving stability and robustness in contact-rich manipulation.
authors: Keqiang Ren, Xuecheng Ye, Hanyu Liu, Zhihua Wang, Tao Jian, Yunsheng Ma, Jiayi Wen, Xinran Li, Zhigong Song
bullets: Addresses motion heterogeneity across locomotion, arms, and hands, plus error accumulation in long-horizon tasks.
Decouples the 29-DoF action space into hand, arm, and mobile-base branches within a Hierarchical Modular Framework.
Uses COMET cross-attention for inter-module coordination and vision-language-model task decomposition to limit temporal error propagation.
Adds full-palm 2D tactile sensing to represent distributed contact signals across modules.
On a physical 29-DoF robot, achieves over 20% higher task success than mainstream baselines across varied long-horizon tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Modular coordination policies for high-DoF whole-body mobile manipulation with tactile sensing.
papers.title: RoboSpan: Learning Modular Coordination Policies for High-DoF Whole-Body Mobile Manipulation with Teleoperation
papers.tldr: RoboSpan combines a high-DoF teleoperation platform with hierarchical modular policies to improve long-horizon, contact-rich whole-body mobile manipulation.

papers.abstract: The lasting gains in AI have come from methods that absorb more computation, and language models already scale computation within a call. Useful work, though, happens across calls: over hours or days, through tools and external systems, among many agents and the humans they work for, and increasingly through code the agents write themselves. Whether that work compounds is enabled by the harness around it, and the harness faces a constraint the model does not: of the three participants in such a computation, the human, the model and code, only the human's attention does not scale, so the computation can grow only if the human is not in every loop. L3M is a runtime built on that premise, written in Lean 4 so that one language implements the harness, states its invariants, and is the language agents extend it in. One computation spans humans, agents, models and code, and all of its state lives in Git: a rich state trajectory -- rather than a chat conversation -- is an object the runtime can resume, rewind, fork, compare and merge. Waiting, communication, delegation and undo are primitives, not patterns the model reasons through each time. When an agent works out a procedure, it can write it once as a sealed Lean program whose type is its permission request, and the harness offers it back as a tool -- machinery for the model to use. To take the human out of the loop, L3M uses reversibility to decide where that is safe: a tool's review tier follows from how far its effects can be undone, so agents act freely where the runtime can recover. Because the machinery can change, the properties that make this safe are stated as kernel-checked theorems about the code that runs. On Terminal-Bench, an untuned L3M reaches about two thirds of its (unsafe) shell-equipped pass rate using only safe (not needing human review) tools.
authors: Carson Eisenach, Robert Joseph George, Vincent Quenneville-Belair, Kate Gwimm, Dean Foster
bullets: Targets multi-call agent work involving tools, external systems, other agents, humans, and self-written code.
Stores the full computation state in Git, enabling resume, rewind, fork, comparison, and merge instead of relying on chat history.
Provides primitives for waiting, communication, delegation, and undo; agents can turn procedures into sealed Lean tools whose types specify permissions.
Uses reversibility to assign tool review tiers, allowing autonomous execution where effects can be safely undone.
An untuned system achieves roughly two-thirds of its unsafe shell-equipped pass rate on Terminal-Bench using only safe tools.
papers.selection_reason: Git-based persistent state/memory runtime for LLM agents; directly relevant to agent memory.
papers.title: L3M: A Verifiable Harness and Runtime for Self-Extending and Self-Improving Agents
papers.tldr: L3M is a Lean 4 runtime that enables agents to carry out long-running, collaborative work with less human oversight by making computation stateful, reversible, and formally verifiable.

papers.abstract: State-of-the-art visuomotor policies are increasingly capable of executing complex tasks, yet can fail during deployment in ways they cannot predict or recover from on their own. Improving their performance and robustness typically requires collecting more data, retraining, or modifying the policy architecture, all of which are time- and resource-intensive in practice. We instead propose an offline-trained monitoring-and-intervention framework that improves a policy during deployment using only black-box query access. From a limited set of labeled on-policy rollouts, we learn a policy-conditioned liveness value that measures the nominal policy's progress toward task completion; we additionally train a compact latent world model using these rollouts together with play data. At deployment, the liveness value continuously monitors execution. When it detects a loss of progress, a short-horizon planner searches the world model for corrective actions using the same value as its planning objective, after which control returns to the nominal policy. We evaluate our method on the LIBERO-Goal task suite and on a Franka Panda manipulator, using the vision-language-action model $\pi_{0.5}$ and a diffusion policy as nominal policies, and demonstrate significant improvements in task success rates, while supporting real-time control. Additional results and videos are available on the project website (https://policy-improvement-wm.pages.dev/).
authors: Colton Crosby, Hao Wang, Mac Schwager, Somil Bansal
bullets: Addresses deployment-time failures that nominal policies cannot predict or recover from without retraining or new data collection.
Learns a policy-conditioned liveness value from labeled on-policy rollouts to measure progress toward task completion.
Trains a compact latent world model from on-policy rollouts and play data, then plans short corrective interventions when progress is lost.
Evaluated on LIBERO-Goal and a Franka Panda using π₀.₅ and a diffusion policy, with reported task-success improvements and real-time control.
Scope: interventions rely on offline training data and black-box query access to the nominal policy.
papers.selection_reason: Deployment-time policy improvement via latent world model planning and liveness monitoring.
papers.title: Back on Track: Deployment-time Policy Improvement via World Model Planning
papers.tldr: An offline-trained monitor and world-model planner can improve black-box visuomotor policies during deployment by detecting stalled progress and intervening with corrective actions.

papers.abstract: Real-world engineering drawings are often large-format and information-dense. Answering practical engineering questions therefore requires both fine-grained understanding of engineering information and complex reasoning over objects, relations, and evidence distributed across different regions or views. Existing benchmarks cover a range of engineering-drawing understanding tasks involving local regions, individual views, specific elements, or more constrained visual settings. However, systematic evaluation of understanding over realistic, large-format engineering drawings remains limited. To address this gap, we introduce LED-BENCH, a multidisciplinary benchmark designed to evaluate fine-grained understanding and complex reasoning over large-format engineering drawings, spanning the mechanical, architectural, and transportation domains. Extensive evaluation of 11 representative multimodal large language models, including 8 proprietary models and 3 open-source models, reveals substantial remaining difficulty: GPT-5.6 Sol achieves 52.65% average accuracy, performance varies across engineering domains, and all evaluated models perform worse on questions requiring broader evidence integration. These results highlight fine-grained understanding, evidence integration, and complex reasoning over large-format engineering drawings as persistent challenges for current multimodal models.
authors: Ke Li, Tianyi Wang, Enning You, Chaoqun Wan, Zhen Huang, Shuxian Liang, Xian-Sheng Hua
bullets: Covers mechanical, architectural, and transportation engineering domains.
Tests reasoning over objects, relations, and evidence distributed across regions and views.
Evaluates 11 multimodal large language models, including proprietary and open-source systems.
Models struggle particularly with questions requiring broad evidence integration; GPT-5.6 Sol reaches 52.65% average accuracy.
Results identify fine-grained understanding, evidence integration, and complex reasoning as persistent challenges.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for MLLM understanding of large-format engineering drawings; fits multimodal LLM evaluation and spatial reasoning.
papers.title: LED-BENCH: A Benchmark for Large-format Engineering Drawing Understanding
papers.tldr: LED-BENCH evaluates multimodal models on fine-grained understanding and complex reasoning over realistic, large-format engineering drawings.

papers.abstract: A spatial answer depends on the reference frame specified in language and its supporting visual evidence. Item accuracy alone obscures whether correctness persists when either changes. We introduce Frame Evidence, a benchmark of 320 matched triplets and 960 Chinese multiple-choice questions from captured and rendered scenes. One family compares three grounded reference frames over fixed images. The other pairs image deletion annotated as insufficient with answer-preserving addition. Joint metrics require correct answers across all three frames and paired evidence variants. Across 20 configurations on 288 held-out questions, GPT three-shot reaches 50.00\% item accuracy, but the best three-frame group accuracy is 5/48 (10.42\%), reached by GPT two-shot. Few-shot prompting and task-specific adaptation improve item accuracy without consistently improving joint correctness. Input controls show where images support matched success, while repeated executions reveal answer instability beneath similar scores.
authors: Chunxi Luo, Qishuai Ding, Xingchen Peng, Hengwei Ye, Ke Zhang, Wenxin Lian, Tianyi Lu, Chunlong Yu, Zhenya Lin
bullets: Introduces 320 matched triplets and 960 Chinese multiple-choice questions from captured and rendered scenes.
Tests three grounded reference frames with fixed images, plus image deletion and answer-preserving addition variants.
Uses joint metrics requiring correct answers across all reference-frame and evidence variants.
Across 20 configurations, GPT’s best three-frame group accuracy was 5/48 (10.42%), despite 50.00% item accuracy in one setting.
Few-shot prompting and task adaptation improved individual answers but did not consistently improve joint correctness; repeated runs exposed instability.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for reference frames and visual evidence in multi-image spatial reasoning; fits spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Frame Evidence:A Benchmark for Reference Frames and Visual Evidence in Multi-Image Spatial Reasoning
papers.tldr: Frame Evidence shows that high item accuracy can hide poor consistency across reference frames and supporting visual evidence in multi-image spatial reasoning.

papers.abstract: An early mistake in the generated reasoning can constrain all subsequent reasoning. Repeated-generation methods, like MCMC-based approaches, attempt to improve output quality by sampling multiple generations, but their effectiveness can be limited by randomly selecting where to regenerate. On MATH500 with Qwen2.5-Math-7B, we find that incorrect responses have substantially higher mean token entropy than correct responses, with an average within-question relative increase of approximately 112%, suggesting that entropy can signal reasoning errors. Motivated by this finding, we introduce REWIND, a training-free controller that uses entropy dynamics to propose targeted suffix regenerations. Across three model families and five benchmarks, REWIND outperforms all baselines, with gains of 0.51-10.00 percentage points over the strongest baseline. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of targeted, uncertainty-guided trajectory repair across models and tasks. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/rewind-D310.
authors: Yi Ding, Mengyu Wang, Min Zhou, Menglin Yang
bullets: Early reasoning mistakes can constrain all later generated steps.
Incorrect responses show substantially higher mean token entropy than correct ones, motivating entropy-based error detection.
REWIND is a training-free controller that uses entropy dynamics to target suffix regeneration instead of choosing regeneration points randomly.
Across three model families and five benchmarks, it outperforms baselines by 0.51–10.00 percentage points over the strongest baseline.
The approach is evaluated for targeted trajectory repair across multiple models and tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Uncertainty-guided trajectory repair for test-time reasoning in LLMs.
papers.title: REWIND: Uncertainty-Guided Trajectory Repair for Test-Time Reasoning
papers.tldr: REWIND uses token-entropy signals to detect likely reasoning errors and selectively regenerate affected suffixes at test time, improving performance across models and benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Lipreading remains challenging due to the inherent ambiguity of visual speech cues and their sensitivity to head pose and video resolution. In this work, we propose FLARE, a framework for robust visual speech representation learning via cross-modal distillation and joint face-lip modeling. FLARE leverages semantically rich Whisper representations as the acoustic teacher signal, converting them into discrete distillation targets through a random-projection quantizer and pretraining the model with a masked prediction objective. To capture complementary visual information, FLARE employs a dual-stream architecture that jointly processes lip region-of-interest (ROI) and full-face inputs, where the lip stream captures finegrained articulatory motion and the face stream encodes broader facial dynamics. During pretraining, auxiliary audio input is incorporated to facilitate cross-modal alignment, and modality dropout is applied to encourage robust visual-only representations. For downstream lipreading, FLARE serves as a visual encoder coupled with either a lightweight Transformer decoder or an LLM-based decoder. Evaluated on LRS2, LRS3, and the out-of-domain WildVSR benchmark, FLARE achieves strong lipreading performance, with word error rates of 11.7%, 13.2%, and 34.3%, respectively. A progressive design study confirms the contribution of each major component. Further analyses demonstrate that joint face-lip modeling improves robustness under degraded video resolution and large head pose variation, while yielding more phoneme-discriminative visual representations. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/jxzhanggg/FLARE.
authors: Jing-Xuan Zhang, Genshun Wan, Jianqing Gao, Jia Pan, Yumei Zhang, Lichen Zhang
bullets: Addresses ambiguity in lipreading and sensitivity to head pose and video resolution.
Uses Whisper-based cross-modal distillation with random-quantized targets and masked prediction pretraining.
Combines dual-stream lip-ROI and full-face processing, with auxiliary audio and modality dropout for robust visual-only representations.
Supports Transformer or LLM-based decoders and reports 11.7%, 13.2%, and 34.3% WER on LRS2, LRS3, and WildVSR.
Analyses indicate improved robustness to degraded resolution and large pose variation, with more phoneme-discriminative representations.
papers.selection_reason: Visual speech representation learning from video via cross-modal distillation; fits video understanding.
papers.title: Learning Visual Speech Representations via Cross-Modal Distillation and Joint Face-Lip Modeling
papers.tldr: FLARE improves visual speech recognition by distilling speech knowledge from Whisper while jointly modeling lip and full-face video cues.

papers.abstract: Foundation models for dynamical systems can forecast unseen partial differential equations (PDEs), ordinary differential equations (ODEs), and time series during inference. However, it remains an open question whether these foundation models truly learn generalizable in-context forecasting strategies. We show that looped transformers are capable of emulating propagators for dynamical systems in-context by first establishing a link between linear attention and (extended) dynamic mode decomposition. We then generalize this insight into the $\textit{Test-Time Forecasting}$ (TTF) framework in which a one-step forecaster leverages iterations of gradient descent as recurrent depth. We demonstrate that lightweight TTF models trained on ODEs and PDEs generalize to out-of-distribution system dynamics during autoregressive rollout after being trained for one-step prediction. Our results reinforce TTF as a theoretically motivated framework for designing recurrent depth models capable of forecasting unseen dynamical systems at test-time.
authors: Jeffrey B. Lai, John Quinn, Anthony Bao, William Gilpin
bullets: Addresses whether foundation models learn generalizable in-context forecasting strategies for unseen ODEs, PDEs, and time series.
Links looped transformers and linear attention to dynamic mode decomposition, motivating their ability to emulate dynamical propagators.
Introduces TTF, where repeated gradient-descent iterations provide recurrent depth at test time.
Shows models trained only for one-step prediction on ODEs and PDEs can generalize to out-of-distribution dynamics during autoregressive rollout.
Scope: the abstract does not report specific datasets, numerical gains, or limitations beyond the demonstrated ODE/PDE setting.
papers.selection_reason: Foundation model for forecasting unseen dynamical systems; fits learned predictors of environment dynamics.
papers.title: Test-Time Forecasting: Recurrent Depth Enables In-Context Dynamics Prediction
papers.tldr: Test-Time Forecasting uses recurrent gradient-descent iterations to help lightweight one-step forecasters predict unseen dynamical systems during inference.

papers.abstract: Image-goal navigation requires a global planner that connects visually specified endpoints while providing observations that a local policy can follow. Three-dimensional Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) provides map-registered RGB, opacity, and depth renderings, but does not explicitly encode navigable topology. We introduce \method, a Gaussian visual roadmap whose milestones, local connections, and visual references are constructed directly through 3DGS rendering without deriving an occupancy grid or signed distance field. We define render-based collision-free (RC-free) configurations and paths. Panoramic depth supplies conservative clearance for milestone validation and adaptive coverage, while edge-aligned orthographic rendering tests the robot's swept volume. We establish conditional soundness and sufficient conditions for deterministic query completeness and probabilistic construction completeness of GS-PRM. To validate the performance of GS-PRM, we conduct experiments in both simulated and real-world environments, demonstrating long-horizon navigation using goal-conditioned policies guided by GS-PRM. Compared with a state-of-the-art 3DGS-based navigation system, our GS-PRM-based navigation system achieves up to a twice higher average success rate and reduces travel time by up to 57.2% when both systems complete the navigation task.
authors: Ashraf Siddique, Kyung Min Han, Young J. Kim
bullets: Addresses the gap between 3DGS visual rendering and explicit navigable topology for global planning.
Constructs milestones, local connections, and visual references using 3DGS-rendered RGB, opacity, and depth.
Uses panoramic depth for conservative clearance and adaptive coverage, plus edge-aligned orthographic rendering to test swept-volume collisions.
Provides conditional soundness and completeness guarantees for deterministic queries and probabilistic roadmap construction.
Validated in simulated and real-world environments, achieving up to 2× higher average success and 57.2% shorter travel time than a state-of-the-art 3DGS navigation system when tasks are completed.
papers.selection_reason: 3DGS-based visual roadmap for image-goal navigation with collision-free planning.
papers.title: GS-PRM: Gaussian Visual Roadmap for Image-Goal Navigation
papers.tldr: GS-PRM builds a navigable visual roadmap directly from 3D Gaussian Splatting to support reliable long-horizon image-goal navigation without occupancy grids or signed distance fields.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables high-quality, real-time novel view synthesis but requires significant storage and transmission resources. Mapping Gaussian attributes to 2D representations enables efficient compression using mature image codecs. However, Gaussian representations that achieve comparable rendering quality are generally treated similarly during optimization, despite substantial differences in coding rate, leading to limited rate-distortion (R-D) performance after compression. To address this limitation, we propose RDCompGS, a 3DGS compression method that enables overall R-D optimization of Gaussian representations with respect to subsequent coding. A differentiable estimate of the coding rate is incorporated into the R-D optimization with rendering distortion. The rate constraint adjustment model further regulates the R-D trade-off across different compression conditions. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that RDCompGS achieves average Bj{\o}ntegaard Delta Rate reductions of 37.84% and 49.31% with H.265/HEVC and JPEG XL, respectively. The estimated rate also shows a strong correlation with the actual bit-rate under different compression conditions.
authors: Huiping Ren, Shuai Wan, Luqian Bai, Zhang Chen, Fuzheng Yang
bullets: Targets the high storage and transmission cost of 3DGS while preserving novel-view rendering quality.
Maps Gaussian attributes to 2D representations and incorporates differentiable coding-rate estimates into rate-distortion optimization.
Uses a rate-constraint adjustment model to control the trade-off across compression conditions.
Across three benchmark datasets, reduces average BD-Rate by 37.84% with H.265/HEVC and 49.31% with JPEG XL.
Estimated rates strongly correlate with actual bitrates under varying compression conditions.
papers.selection_reason: 3D Gaussian Splatting compression with rate-distortion optimization; fits 3D scene representation.
papers.title: RDCompGS: Rate-Distortion Optimization for Compression of 3D Gaussian Splatting with Image Codecs
papers.tldr: RDCompGS improves 3D Gaussian Splatting compression by jointly optimizing rendering quality and estimated image-codec bitrate.

papers.abstract: As a lightweight and highly accurate method for nearest-neighbor search in 3D point clouds, approaches based on space-filling curves (SFC) have been proposed. However, due to the inherent properties of SFC, a gap arises between proximity relationships along the SFC and those in the original Euclidean space. In this study, we propose a loss function that reduces the influence of this gap. Specifically, we compute the distances between adjacent points along the SFC and train the model to optimize feature similarity between pairs of points that are distant from each other in the original 3D space. We incorporate the proposed method into a high-performing 3D point cloud segmentation model and evaluate its effectiveness on three datasets. The results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms conventional methods on both indoor and outdoor point cloud datasets.
authors: Konan Sasaki, Junya Komori, Kazuhiro Hotta
bullets: SFC-based neighbor search is efficient but can connect points that are far apart in 3D space.
The method computes distances between adjacent points along the SFC.
It trains feature similarity for point pairs that are distant in Euclidean space but close along the SFC.
The loss is integrated into a high-performing 3D point-cloud segmentation model.
Evaluation on three datasets shows improvement over conventional methods in both indoor and outdoor settings.
papers.selection_reason: 3D point cloud segmentation with space-filling-curve neighbor gap loss; fits 3D vision perception.
papers.title: Reducing the Gap Between Spatial and Space-Filling Curve Neighbors in 3D Point Cloud Segmentation
papers.tldr: A novel loss reduces the mismatch between space-filling-curve and Euclidean neighbors, improving 3D point-cloud segmentation across indoor and outdoor datasets.

papers.abstract: Retrieving external knowledge can improve large language model (LLM) translation by providing supplementary information such as idiom interpretations and terminology. However, existing retrieval-augmented machine translation systems typically apply predefined retrieval strategies uniformly across all inputs. We argue that translation operates in a partial-evidence regime: LLM's parametric knowledge suffices for many inputs, while external evidence benefits a subset and usually supports rather than directly provides the desired translation. This creates two challenges: deciding when to retrieve and what evidence to acquire. We introduce Selective Retrieval-Augmented Translation (SRAT), an agentic reinforcement learning framework that learns when to translate directly or retrieve, what to retrieve, and how to integrate these decisions by optimizing final translation quality. To align evidence retrieval with downstream translation quality rather than simple semantic similarity, we further develop joint Plackett--Luce optimization and translation-quality contrastive training for retriever-training. Experiments on idiom, knowledge-intensive, and document-level translation with offline or online retrieval show that SRAT consistently outperforms never- and always-retrieve baselines, and quality-aligned retriever training provides further gains when similarity-based retrieval is insufficient. The results demonstrate the benefit of treating retrieval as a learnable translation action rather than fixed preprocessing.
authors: Shijun Li, Yang Liu, Najmeh Sadoughi, Dongmei Wang, Xinjie Li, Zhu Liu, Rohith Mysore Vijaya Kumar, Yuzong Liu
bullets: Existing retrieval-augmented translation retrieves uniformly, despite many inputs being solvable from the LLM’s parametric knowledge.
SRAT uses agentic reinforcement learning to decide whether to retrieve, what evidence to seek, and how to use it.
Joint Plackett–Luce optimization and translation-quality contrastive training align retrieval with downstream translation quality rather than similarity alone.
Experiments across idiom, knowledge-intensive, and document-level translation show consistent gains over never- and always-retrieve baselines.
The approach treats retrieval as a learnable translation action, with benefits shown under both offline and online retrieval.
papers.selection_reason: Selective retrieval-augmented MT via RL; relevant to external memory/retrieval.
papers.title: Retrieve What Helps, Only When It Helps: Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Selective Retrieval-Augmented Machine Translation
papers.tldr: SRAT learns to retrieve translation evidence selectively and integrate it when useful, improving translation over fixed never- or always-retrieve strategies.

papers.abstract: We devise a dual-arm cooperative planning framework for wiping table surface in the presence of scattered objects. Unlike conventional surface-cleaning strategies that only cover free areas and detour around obstacles, our framework explicitly assigns one arm to rearrange objects while the other performs coverage wiping, thereby enabling access to previously obstructed regions. Specifically, we first construct a set of wiping and object-rearrangement action primitives. Based on these primitives, we introduce Geo-MILP, a geometry-aware task planner formulated as Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP). By integrating Logic-Based Benders Decomposition (LBBD), Geo-MILP iteratively optimizes action sequencingand timing to resolve geometric conflicts, promoting efficient cooperation between wiping and object rearrangement. We then employ K-Order Markov Optimization (KOMO) to generate smooth, collision-free motions to ensure feasible execution. Simulation and physical experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework not only increases reachable coverage by enabling access to obstructed areas, but also significantly improves time efficiency compared to Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) baselines, reducing planning time by up to 9 times and execution makespan by approximately 40%.
authors: Pengqi Zhang, Longchang Yu, Daohan Li, Liang Yan, Hangxin Liu
bullets: Addresses the limited coverage and detours of wiping methods that avoid scattered objects.
Assigns one arm to move objects while the other performs surface wiping using predefined action primitives.
Uses geometry-aware MILP planning with Logic-Based Benders Decomposition to optimize action order and timing under geometric conflicts.
Applies K-Order Markov Optimization to generate smooth, collision-free executable motions.
Simulation and physical experiments show up to 9× lower planning time and approximately 40% shorter execution makespan than TAMP baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Dual-arm cooperative manipulation planning with geometry-aware MILP for tabletop wiping.
papers.title: Dual-arm Cooperation for Tabletop Wiping with Temporal Object Removal
papers.tldr: A dual-arm planner coordinates object rearrangement and tabletop wiping to clean previously obstructed areas more efficiently.

papers.abstract: Temporal action detection in long untrimmed videos suffers from inaccurate localization and low-quality proposals, especially with sparse annotations and ambiguous boundaries. For open-ended video understanding and LLM-driven event analysis, reliable proposals connect temporal localization, event annotation, and semantic understanding. However, conventional temporal action detection (TAD) pipelines lack explicit modeling of proposal localization quality, cross-representation support, and inter-proposal relations. We propose Hybrid Rank-Calibration of Action Proposals (HyrCap), a proposal-centric query-based TAD framework for temporal event understanding. Hybrid combines complementary video features with different localization cues, while Rank-Calibration adjusts proposal ranking confidence to reflect localization reliability and candidate competition. HyrCap treats dense query-based predictions as an over-complete temporal event hypothesis space. Cross-Representation Consensus Calibration, Localization Quality Estimation, and Proposal Redundancy Suppression improve proposal ranking reliability, localization quality, and candidate discrimination. Inspired by LLMs' capabilities in fine-grained semantic recognition, event description, and reasoning, we introduce HyrCap for Semantic Action Understanding, using calibrated proposals for standard TAD and as inputs to LLM-based semantic understanding. We define a staged evaluation protocol to separately measure event localization, segment-level semantic understanding, and combined event understanding performance. Experiments on public benchmarks show that HyrCap achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple metrics and provides a finer-grained paradigm and evaluation protocol for query-based event segmentation and annotation.
authors: Rui Chen, Xingyu Chen, Pengxin Xu, Kai Chen, Junzhi Yu
bullets: Addresses inaccurate temporal localization and low-quality proposals in long, untrimmed videos, particularly with sparse annotations and ambiguous boundaries.
Uses complementary video representations and treats dense query predictions as an over-complete set of temporal event hypotheses.
Introduces consensus calibration, localization-quality estimation, and redundancy suppression to improve proposal ranking and candidate discrimination.
Supports both standard temporal action detection and LLM-based semantic event understanding through calibrated proposals.
Experiments on public benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance across multiple metrics and propose a staged evaluation protocol for localization, semantic understanding, and their combination.
papers.selection_reason: Proposal-centric temporal action detection framework for event understanding, relevant to video understanding.
papers.title: HyrCap: Hybrid Rank-Calibration of Action Proposals for Temporal Event Understanding
papers.tldr: HyrCap improves temporal event understanding by calibrating and ranking action proposals according to localization quality, redundancy, and semantic reliability.

papers.abstract: Robotic exploration, coverage, and multi-agent deployment algorithms require reproducible environments with controllable geometry and visibility. This paper presents the Dungeon and Visibility World Generator, an open-source framework for constructing two- and three-dimensional environments and evaluating geometric line-of-sight. The framework supports orthogonal, polygonal or polyhedral, and curvilinear geometries, with six construction families covering scattered rooms, clusters, winding passages, caverns, branches, and loops. Room dimensions, passage structures, obstacles, and spatial placement can be controlled through configurable parameters and probability distributions. Each generated environment provides continuous free-space geometry and a corresponding discrete occupancy representation. A Rust-based visibility engine supports line-of-sight queries in both representations, enabling the evaluation of observable regions from arbitrary agent positions. The framework records configurations, generated geometries, occupancy grids, and visibility results to support reproducible experiments. We demonstrate the generator across all six geometry classes, examine how geometry and spatial resolution affect visibility, and evaluate generation time and reproducibility. The resulting framework provides a configurable foundation for evaluating robotic exploration, coverage, and multi-agent deployment algorithms in diverse environments.
authors: Edwin M\'eriaux, Antonio Lor\'ia, Gregory Dudek
bullets: Supports orthogonal, polygonal/polyhedral, and curvilinear environments.
Provides six construction families, including rooms, passages, caverns, branches, and loops.
Offers continuous free-space and discrete occupancy representations with configurable obstacles and spatial placement.
Includes a Rust-based visibility engine for line-of-sight queries from arbitrary agent positions.
Evaluates geometry, resolution, generation time, and reproducibility across the six environment classes.
papers.selection_reason: Configurable environment and visibility generator for evaluating embodied exploration, coverage, and multi-agent deployment.
papers.title: Dungeon and Visibility World Generator
papers.tldr: An open-source generator creates reproducible 2D and 3D environments with configurable geometry and line-of-sight evaluation for robotic exploration and deployment research.

papers.abstract: While multi-fingered dexterous robot hands have the potential to provide human-level dexterity, using them for functional manipulation remains difficult because task success depends on precise contact, coordinated arm-hand motion, and reactive recovery from execution errors. Precise contact depends on complex contact dynamics that are difficult to model accurately in simulation, motivating real-world learning. However, real-world demonstrations in the full arm-hand control space are costly and noisy because each trajectory must coordinate arm motion with high-DoF multi-finger contact. Small execution deviations can further cause slipped contact or premature force application, making recovery from off-nominal contact states important for robust execution. To deal with these challenges, we propose HiFun, a hierarchical real-world RL framework for functional dexterous manipulation tasks. Our key insight is to decouple the control complexity into a functional hand skill for precise contact execution and an arm-hand coordination policy for arm control and hand-skill activation. This design enables effective real-time human intervention for reactive recovery learning and efficient data collection with Dynamic Movement Primitive (DMP) augmentation. Across six real-world tasks on two dexterous hands, HiFun achieves 98.3% average success within one hour of online training and remains robust to dynamic disturbances. The project page is available at https://hly-123.github.io/HiFun/.
authors: Linyi Huang, Guowei Huai, Weibin Liu, Shulong Jiang, Ping Tan, Weixuan Zhang, Hui Zhang, Jie Song
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of learning precise contact, coordinated arm–hand motion, and recovery from execution errors.
Decouples control into a functional hand skill for contact execution and an arm–hand policy for arm control and skill activation.
Uses real-time human intervention for reactive recovery learning and Dynamic Movement Primitive augmentation for data-efficient training.
Achieves 98.3% average success within one hour of online training across six real-world tasks on two dexterous hands.
Remains robust to dynamic disturbances, though its evaluation scope is limited to the reported tasks and hardware.
papers.selection_reason: Hierarchical RL for functional dexterous manipulation directly fits robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: HiFun: a Hierarchical Framework for Efficient Functional Dexterous Manipulation Learning
papers.tldr: HiFun is a hierarchical real-world reinforcement learning framework that enables efficient and robust functional manipulation with multi-fingered dexterous hands.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual perception and language understanding with robot control, providing a foundation for instruction-conditioned manipulation. However, conventional pretrained VLA policies lack a mechanism for gradual adaptation through accumulated interaction experience during deployment. We therefore propose VLRLA, a general framework that equips existing VLA models with \textit{in-context reinforcement learning} capabilities for deployment-time adaptation. Our approach augments a VLA model with a reinforcement learning module that learns from historical observations, actions, rewards, and termination signals. During deployment, the policy gradually refines its action generation and progressively improves task success while keeping model parameters fixed. Our approach is also designed for general applicability and compatibility with diverse learning history construction strategies and model training pipelines. Finally, through extensive experiments, we systematically investigate the learning properties of VLRLA in simulation and demonstrate its ability to adapt to unseen scenarios during real-world deployment.
authors: Diyuan Shi, Yiqi Tang, Hongyin Zhang, You Wu, Donglin Wang
bullets: Addresses the lack of continual adaptation in conventional pretrained VLA policies.
Adds a reinforcement-learning module that uses past observations, actions, rewards, and termination signals.
Refines action generation during deployment without updating the underlying model parameters.
Designed to support diverse history-construction strategies and VLA training pipelines.
Experiments in simulation and real-world deployment demonstrate adaptation to unseen scenarios.
papers.selection_reason: Deployment-time adaptation of VLA models via in-context RL; directly relevant to VLA and test-time/continual learning.
papers.title: VLRLA: Deployment-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language-Action Models through In-Context Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: VLRLA enables fixed vision-language-action models to adapt during deployment by learning from accumulated interaction history through in-context reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Block-diffusion language models denoise a whole block of token positions in parallel so each forward pass can emit many tokens. However, blocks are still denoised in strict sequence, a cost that within-block acceleration leaves untouched. Here, we investigate decoding blocks concurrently and propose One Block Ahead (OBA), a training-free decoding algorithm that denoises the next block alongside the current one. We demonstrate that for uniform-state diffusion LMs, where a block's denoising progress is not visible in its intermediate tokens, concurrent decoding is advantageous if the next block's tokens are promoted together with the corresponding sampler state, including the self-conditioning signal and the denoising time. We also derive a break-even criterion that relates the benefit of OBA to the relative cost of a paired-block forward pass. On DiffusionGemma, a state-of-the-art diffusion LM, OBA increases the tokens per forward pass by 42.3% (from 15.64 to 22.25) and the single-request denoising throughput by 16.3%, averaged over ten benchmarks, with a small accuracy regression.
authors: Yangyi Shen, Pin-Jui Ku, Nicolai Oswald, Jean-Marie Lemercier, Yonggan Fu, Stefano Ermon, Jure Leskovec, Boris Ginsburg, Ante Juki\'c
bullets: Block-diffusion LMs generate tokens in parallel within blocks but traditionally denoise blocks sequentially.
OBA is a training-free decoder that advances the next block alongside the current block.
For uniform-state diffusion LMs, effective promotion requires carrying the next block’s sampler state, including self-conditioning and denoising time.
A break-even criterion relates OBA’s benefit to the cost of paired-block forward passes.
On DiffusionGemma, OBA raises tokens per forward pass by 42.3% and single-request denoising throughput by 16.3% across ten benchmarks, with a small accuracy regression.
papers.selection_reason: Concurrent decoding for diffusion LMs improves throughput; fits efficient inference.
papers.title: One Block Ahead: Promoting Sampler State in Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: One Block Ahead (OBA) accelerates block-diffusion language model decoding by denoising the next block concurrently with the current one, improving throughput with a small accuracy trade-off.

papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence requires scalable 3D environments that are both photorealistic and semantically grounded, yet existing indoor datasets are dominated by room-scale captures and costly LiDAR acquisition. Online real-estate platforms offer abundant panoramas of diverse multi-room homes, but sparse viewpoints and texture-poor regions make reconstruction severely under-constrained. We introduce Holi-Spatial 360, a generative reconstruction and data curation framework for converting these panoramas into annotated multi-room 3D environments. Because reconstruction quality bounds subsequent generation, our Correspondence-Guided Geometric Optimization converts feed-forward reconstruction priors into reliable cross-view constraints and builds a coherent 3D Gaussian Splatting representation as 3D spatial memory. Adapted single-image and video priors then restore appearance and complete continuous trajectories while preserving observed content. The reconstructed scenes support arbitrary RGB-D rendering and an automated curation pipeline that combines end-to-end 3D grounding with VLM-based verification.
