Holi360 contains over 1K multi-room 3DGS scenes, more than 100K instance annotations, and 2M spatial question-answer pairs. We also introduce the Holi360 benchmark to evaluate the spatial understanding of VLMs in real-world, multi-room indoor environments. Experiments demonstrate superior reconstruction and curation quality under sparse panoramic inputs, while fine-tuning VLMs on Holi360 substantially improves spatial reasoning capabilities.
authors: Yuanyuan Gao, Zhirui Liu, Yuning Gong, Yifei Liu, Yifan Zhan, Kuixuan Jiao, Xiaolong Zhou, Yifan Yang, Hongjie Zhang, Xue Yang, Dan Xu, Zhihang Zhong
bullets: Addresses the scarcity of scalable, photorealistic, semantically grounded indoor 3D data and the under-constrained nature of sparse panoramas.
Uses correspondence-guided geometric optimization to turn reconstruction priors into cross-view constraints and build coherent 3D Gaussian Splatting spatial memory.
Applies image and video generation priors to restore appearance and complete continuous trajectories while preserving observed content.
Provides RGB-D rendering and automated 3D curation with grounding and VLM-based verification.
Introduces over 1K scenes, 100K+ instance annotations, 2M spatial QA pairs, and a benchmark; fine-tuning on the data improves VLM spatial reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: Generative reconstruction of multi-room 3D environments and benchmark for VLM spatial reasoning, directly relevant to spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Holi-Spatial 360: Generative Reconstruction from Sparse Panoramas for Spatial Rendering and Intelligence
papers.tldr: Holi-Spatial 360 reconstructs richly annotated multi-room 3D environments from sparse real-estate panoramas and uses them to improve spatial reasoning in vision-language models.

papers.abstract: Retrieving useful context for a robot requires matching its task, execution stage, and the continuation that should follow. We introduce Robota-Embed, to our knowledge the first vision-language-action (VLA) embedding model to jointly encode all three modalities in both current-state queries and recorded future continuations. Predictive retrieval training aligns these endpoints, enabling historical continuations to serve as context at inference time. We construct a multi-source corpus of 1,695,684 cleaned training anchors and introduce Robota-Embed-Bench, with 4,000 queries and a shared 8,000-entry gallery. Robota-Embed achieves 47.33% clip-level and 81.77% episode-level R@1, exceeding action-free Gemini Embedding 2 by 22.09 and 33.47 percentage points. Controlled retrieval studies show that removing native action degrades retrieval more than removing vision. We study two complementary applications. Embed2ICL uses retrieved experience for training-free and training-based policy conditioning, increasing success from 47.0% to 56.3% in DROID-Sim and from 86.4% to 92.8% on the LIBERO difficult subset, while improving task progress on real robots. Embed2Evolve uses execution feedback to grow task-local memory and refine context use around a frozen GPT-6 Astra policy. Across five ManiSkill tasks, it achieves 68% success, compared with 24% for GPT-6 Astra Direct and 33% for a harness independently evolved with Omni-Embed-Nemotron-3B under the same protocol. Relative to the latter, it uses approximately 79.5% fewer policy tokens per test rollout, counting both successes and failures. These results show that a unified, action-aware retrieval space can support robot in-context learning and task-local context evolution.
authors: Yunze Liu, Jing Wang, Shenrui Wu, Wenkun He, Guanqi Zhan, Xianzheng Ma, Junyu Chen, Wenhang Ge, Haozhan Tang, Yuchao Gu, Zhuoyang Zhang, Zekai Wang, Dantong Niu, Zhen Dong, Yuke Zhu, Trevor Darrell, Linxi "Jim" Fan, Song Han, Han Cai
bullets: Jointly encodes task, execution stage, and future action continuations in both current-state queries and recorded experiences.
Uses predictive retrieval training and a corpus of 1,695,684 training anchors; introduces a 4,000-query benchmark with an 8,000-entry gallery.
Achieves 47.33% clip-level and 81.77% episode-level R@1, outperforming the action-free Gemini Embedding 2 baseline in the reported comparisons.
Retrieved experience improves policy success in DROID-Sim and LIBERO, and execution-feedback memory evolution improves performance across five ManiSkill tasks.
Ablations indicate that removing action information harms retrieval more than removing vision; evaluation focuses on the reported simulated and real-robot settings.
papers.selection_reason: Unified VLA retrieval embeddings for robot in-context learning and task-local memory evolution.
papers.title: Robota-Embed: Unified VLA Embeddings for Robot In-Context Learning and Evolution
papers.tldr: Robota-Embed learns a unified vision-language-action retrieval space that helps robots retrieve useful past experience for in-context learning and task-specific evolution.

papers.abstract: Sim-and-real co-training is an effective way to scale robot learning by augmenting limited real-world demonstrations with simulation data. However, existing approaches typically treat simulators as fixed data sources, relying on uniform generation, offline retrieval, or manual parameter alignment by domain experts. We formulate \textit{Active Generative Simulation}: optimizing a simulator's data-generation distribution to maximize downstream real-world performance. To solve this problem, we propose MetaGenSim, a meta-learning framework that trains an auxiliary rater network via meta-gradients to automatically discover high-utility data-generation distributions within a user-specified simulation parameter space, without manual parameter alignment. Across simulation and real-world manipulation tasks, MetaGenSim outperforms uniform generation and retrieval baselines, achieves a 150% relative improvement in real-world full-task success over uniform generation, and matches expert manual alignment. We further show that distributions curated with a lightweight proxy policy transfer to VLA fine-tuning, and that MetaGenSim can exploit partial alignment through atomic skill stitching and object-receptacle composition when exact sim-and-real task alignment is unavailable. Project website: https://meta-gensim.github.io
authors: Liqian Ma, Vaibhav Saxena, Utkarsh Aashu Mishra, Shuo Cheng, Yongxin Chen, Danfei Xu
bullets: Addresses fixed or manually tuned simulator data distributions that may poorly support real-world policy learning.
Uses meta-learning and meta-gradients to train an auxiliary rater that selects high-utility generation distributions within a user-defined parameter space.

Outperforms uniform-generation and retrieval baselines across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, with a reported 150% relative improvement in real-world full-task success over uniform generation.
Matches expert manual parameter alignment and transfers proxy-policy-curated distributions to VLA fine-tuning.
Supports partial sim-real alignment through atomic skill stitching and object-receptacle composition.
papers.selection_reason: Meta-learning simulation data generation for sim-and-real robot policy co-training fits robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Active Generative Simulation: Meta-Learning What to Simulate for Sim-and-Real Policy Co-Training
papers.tldr: MetaGenSim learns which simulation data to generate so that robot policies trained with sim-and-real co-training perform better in the real world.

papers.abstract: Post-training often improves the performance of large audio-language models on audio understanding and reasoning benchmarks. However, these improvements may reflect adaptation to specific question formats, such as multiple-choice questions, rather than genuine advances in audio understanding and reasoning capabilities. To investigate what LALMs actually learn from post-training, we conduct controlled experiments that disentangle improvements in audio understanding from adaptation to specific question formats. Across different models and post-training methods, we find that much of the reported improvement persists even without informative audio, but largely disappears when the question format changes. These findings suggest that post-training often teaches models to exploit task-specific textual cues and answer patterns rather than developing generalizable audio understanding and reasoning capabilities.
authors: Hua-Hsuan Chen, Xuanjun Chen, Wei-Chung Lu, Chih-Kai Yang, Yu-Xiang Lin, Sung-Feng Huang, Haibin Wu, Hung-yi Lee
bullets: Reported benchmark improvements may be driven by adaptation to multiple-choice and other task-specific formats.
Controlled experiments separate audio understanding from question-format adaptation across models and post-training methods.
Much of the improvement persists when informative audio is removed.
The gains largely disappear when the question format changes.
The findings question whether standard benchmarks measure genuine audio reasoning progress.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes post-training of large audio-language models, directly relevant to multimodal LLM understanding and evaluation.
papers.title: What Does LALM Post-training Learn? Rethinking Audio Understanding and Reasoning Capabilities
papers.tldr: Post-training gains in large audio-language models often reflect learning question formats and answer patterns rather than genuine, generalizable audio understanding or reasoning.

papers.abstract: Multimodal in-context learning (ICL) is an important capability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Its performance is closely tied to the demonstrations it uses, making demonstration retrieval a core problem for ICL. Common methods use fixed scoring methods to retrieve all the demonstrations at once, which may introduce redundancy and noise. Context-aware retrieval methods have emerged to address this problem by allowing incremental retrieval from a growing context. However, none of them lets the MLLM learn how to judge what new demonstrations it needs and then carry out progressive retrieval on its own. To this end, we introduce ActICL, which trains an MLLM agent to acquire and use an ICL context via tool-augmented reasoning. An ActICL agent analyzes its own information gaps during iterative reasoning and tool-use actions. Based on these gaps, it performs targeted retrieval to acquire a set of initial candidates. It can then use the existing context to further filter the candidates and refine the context, or it can iteratively perform a new retrieval. When the agent judges that the context is sufficient for the task, or when the resource limit is reached with the user request met, it sends the acquired context to an answering model, either the agent itself or another MLLM. We use a two-stage post-training procedure that jointly optimizes the agent's acquisition and answering. With an adaptive number of demonstrations, ActICL improves average performance by 11.6 percentage points over standard similarity-based retrieval across seven benchmarks and three MLLMs, and by 4.4 points compared to the strongest prior baseline. The contexts acquired by ActICL agents can also be used effectively by frontier models. When GPT-5.6-Sol performs 4-shot ICL, ActICL's contexts improve its performance by 3.5 points over standard retrieval, averaged over three benchmarks.
authors: Yanshu Li, Ruixiang Tang, Junyi Jessy Li, Elias Stengel-Eskin
bullets: Fixed, one-shot demonstration retrieval can introduce redundant or noisy context.
ActICL uses tool-augmented reasoning for adaptive, progressive retrieval and context refinement.
A two-stage post-training procedure jointly optimizes demonstration acquisition and answer generation.
It improves average performance by 11.6 percentage points over similarity-based retrieval across seven benchmarks and three MLLMs, and by 4.4 points over the strongest prior baseline.
ActICL-generated contexts also improve GPT-5.6-Sol’s 4-shot ICL performance by 3.5 points across three benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Trains MLLM agents for progressive demonstration retrieval in multimodal in-context learning, directly relevant to multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: ActICL: Post-Training for Agentic Multimodal In-Context Learning
papers.tldr: ActICL trains an MLLM agent to iteratively identify information gaps and retrieve only the demonstrations needed for effective multimodal in-context learning.

papers.abstract: Native multimodal pre-training trains a single model from scratch on text and multimodal data, enabling it to understand both language and visual inputs. However, how visual signals shape scaling behavior and support capabilities beyond visual understanding remains unclear. We investigate this question through controlled visual-content ablations across model sizes and training budgets. Specifically, we replace image embeddings with content-free padding token embeddings. Retaining visual content improves text prediction on image-text examples without materially changing the lowest text-only loss at a given compute budget, the optimal balance of model size and training data, or aggregate language scores. The relative multimodal loss benefit grows approximately as a power law of compute. To test benefits beyond understanding images, we evaluate spatial reasoning from text descriptions alone. Both conditions improve with model and data scaling. During training of the largest model, visual gains are most sustained in localization, navigation, and symbolic planning, which involve maintaining object configurations or composing spatial updates; gains in spatial relations, geometry, and physical commonsense are less consistent. These findings identify visual content as a scalable anchor for multimodal learning, with benefits that extend beyond visual inputs while preserving aggregate language performance.
authors: Haoyuan Wu, Aoqi Wu, Jiani Hu, Bei Yu
bullets: Controlled ablations replace image embeddings with content-free padding embeddings across model sizes and compute budgets.
Retaining visual content improves text prediction on image-text examples, with benefits growing approximately as a power law of compute.
Visual content does not materially change the lowest text-only loss, optimal model/data balance, or aggregate language scores.
Text-only spatial reasoning benefits most consistently in localization, navigation, and symbolic planning, while gains in geometry and physical commonsense are less consistent.
papers.selection_reason: Native multimodal pretraining analysis showing visual content benefits spatial reasoning, fitting multimodal and spatial intelligence interests.
papers.title: More Than Seeing: Vision as Scalable Anchors in Native Multimodal Pre-Training
papers.tldr: Visual content acts as a scalable anchor in native multimodal pre-training, improving multimodal learning and some text-only spatial reasoning without reducing overall language performance.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies fine-tuned on LIBERO are trained and evaluated on the same ten instruction strings, and rewording the instruction changes base OpenVLA's success by -38.0 points. Test-time prompt ensembling, which improves language models, does not recover this loss in any setting we ran. Paraphrase consensus (the medoid action over K paraphrases) costs base OpenVLA 16.8 points when the training instruction is a member. Without it, the medoid of the paraphrases scores -32.4 points relative to the training instruction, and confidence-based selection scores -28.0. The same medoid over samples of one paraphrase improves on greedy decoding but stays -27.6 points below the training instruction, consistent with aggregation reducing variance without removing the bias the paraphrases share. A wrong-instruction probe measures how much of a policy's success depends on the instruction. Across three policies and four suites, paraphrases cost a policy only where this share is high, and the stronger policies lose a much smaller fraction of it than base OpenVLA. LoRA post-training on paraphrased instructions reduces the one-paraphrase effect to +2.0 points, against -32.0 for a matched control, reproduces across two seeds and on OpenVLA-OFT, transfers to withheld phrasings, and leaves the policy's reliance on the instruction unchanged.
authors: Hanlong Li, Sihan Tan, Takeshi Ashizawa, Benjamin Yen, Kazuhiro Nakadai
bullets: Rewording instructions reduces base OpenVLA success by 38.0 points on LIBERO, despite using semantically equivalent commands.
Test-time prompt ensembling, paraphrase medoids, and confidence-based selection fail to recover the lost performance; aggregation mainly reduces variance while preserving paraphrase bias.
A wrong-instruction probe links paraphrase sensitivity to how much policy success depends on the instruction, with stronger policies losing a smaller fraction.
LoRA training on paraphrased instructions reduces the one-paraphrase effect to +2.0 points versus −32.0 for a matched control, replicating across seeds and OpenVLA-OFT.
The robustness improvement transfers to withheld phrasings without changing the policy’s overall reliance on instructions.
papers.selection_reason: Analysis of instruction paraphrase robustness in VLA policies directly addresses vision-language-action models.
papers.title: Paraphrase Consensus Is Not Self-Consistency: Instruction Reliance and Robustness in VLA Policies
papers.tldr: VLA policies can be highly sensitive to instruction wording, and paraphrase aggregation does not remove this shared bias, whereas paraphrase-focused LoRA training substantially improves robustness.

papers.abstract: This paper presents $S^3$-Nav, a structured spatial-semantic decision-making framework for language-guided robot navigation under partial observability. Rather than assuming a complete environment representation in advance, $S^3$-Nav incrementally constructs persistent spatial-semantic state while exposing only a capacity-controlled, task-conditioned view to the high-level policy. This separation decouples what the robot must retain from what the policy needs to inspect, allowing decision complexity to be controlled without discarding grounded evidence required for subsequent reasoning and validation. High-level navigation outputs remain provisional and are independently grounded and validated against persistent semantic evidence and current geometric observations before physical execution or task termination. Evaluations across multiple environments and object- and relation-goal tasks demonstrate that separating persistent state, decision-facing evidence, and execution authority improves closed-loop navigation reliability while reducing policy reasoning cost.
authors: Chaemin Lee, Hae Min Cho
bullets: Incrementally builds a persistent spatial-semantic representation instead of requiring a complete environment model.
Provides the high-level policy with a compact, task-conditioned view to control decision complexity.
Independently grounds and validates provisional navigation decisions using stored semantic evidence and current geometry.
Evaluations across multiple environments and object- and relation-goal tasks show improved closed-loop reliability with lower policy reasoning cost.
papers.selection_reason: Language-guided robot navigation with structured spatial-semantic state directly fits vision-language navigation.
papers.title: $S^3$-Nav: Structured Spatial-Semantic Decision Making for Language-Guided Robot Navigation
papers.tldr: S³-Nav improves language-guided robot navigation under partial observability by separating persistent spatial-semantic memory from capacity-controlled policy inputs and validating actions before execution.

papers.abstract: LLM system capabilities depend not only on model parameters but also on the executable harnesses that organize information acquisition, tool use, reasoning, and memory. Recursive harness evolution can automate their design, but how it can reliably discover generalizable systems from limited, noisy, and repeatedly reused feedback remains unclear. We study this question in agentic video understanding, where rich multimodal evidence and coupled mechanisms make harness optimization challenging. We first introduce VideoHarness-BRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework that evolves video harnesses around a frozen vision-language model. Analyzing over 4,000 evolved candidates, we find it competitive with hand-engineered systems but identify three interconnected failure modes: validation overfitting, search-budget dilution, and the early-experience trap. We trace all three to a common root: the same imperfect validation evidence drives both harness revisions and the proposer's search strategy. We therefore propose VideoHarness-SRSI, an evidence-governed framework in which every search decision rests on evidence that is transferable, sufficient, and gathered before the search commits. It restricts the proposer to content-free feedback, informs exploration with instrumented warm-up experiments, and develops mechanisms in isolated probe-race branches before factorial composition and joint refinement. Across four video understanding benchmarks, VideoHarness-SRSI improves the equally weighted mean held-out score by 6.2% relative to VideoHarness-BRSI and reduces the mean validation-test gap by 37.9%. Reliable harness evolution thus depends on how search is organized and informed, not only on how well it optimizes validation performance.
authors: Zihao Lin, Haoyu Dong, Haobo Xu, Chi-Chih Chang, Xuying Ning, Yinglong Xia, Shuang Yang, Zhuokai Zhao, Xinying Song, Dongfang Liu, Lifu Huang, Yang Song, Qifan Wang
bullets: Recursive harness evolution is studied for agentic video understanding with a frozen vision-language model.
Analysis of over 4,000 candidates identifies validation overfitting, search-budget dilution, and the early-experience trap.
SRSI uses transferable, sufficient, pre-commitment evidence; content-free proposer feedback; instrumented warm-up experiments; and isolated probe-race branches.
Across four benchmarks, it raises the equally weighted mean held-out score by 6.2% relative to BRSI and reduces the validation-test gap by 37.9%.
The findings suggest that reliable harness evolution depends on search organization and evidence quality, not validation optimization alone.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses video understanding system design via recursive self-improvement of harnesses, relevant to video understanding.
papers.title: VideoHarness-SRSI: Structured Recursive Self-Improvement for Video Understanding Harness
papers.tldr: VideoHarness-SRSI improves reliable recursive evolution of video-understanding harnesses by separating search decisions from noisy validation feedback and organizing evidence before optimization.

papers.abstract: Simulated environments enable scalable training data generation for embodied agents, but more data does not necessarily provide what a particular agent needs to learn. Existing environment-generation pipelines largely optimize generic properties such as realism, diversity, or task coverage, while different pretrained policies can fail for different environmental reasons. We therefore introduce WEDGE, a framework for weakness-guided navigation learning in which the failure modes of a pretrained agent guide the generation of training environments at each adaptation round. Given a pretrained policy, WEDGE uses an LLM to propose executable weakness features from contrasting successful and failed rollouts, automatically validates them on the diagnostic set, and selects the strongest validated weakness based on its success-rate gap. The validated weaknesses are then mapped to the environmental factors that control them. WEDGE varies these factors to construct environments in the difficulty regimes where the policy struggles, producing targeted training experience for adaptation. Across three navigation agents with different adaptation mechanisms, we find that policies exhibit distinct weakness profiles and benefit from different training environments. Weakness-conditioned adaptation consistently outperforms matched random and hard-example alternatives on ProcTHOR, while the resulting gains for Uni-NaVid and Gemini also extend to HM3D after ProcTHOR adaptation. Iterative re-diagnosis further shows that dominant weaknesses can persist or shift as the policy improves, providing updated guidance for subsequent environment construction. Together, these results show that policy failures are not only diagnostic signals, but actionable guidance for constructing training environments that target a policy's current weaknesses.
authors: Yue Zhang, Han Lin, Zun Wang, Yidong Huang, Zaid Khan, Mohit Bansal
bullets: Generic realism, diversity, and task coverage may not target the distinct failure modes of different pretrained navigation policies.
An LLM extracts and validates weakness features from contrasting successful and failed rollouts, then selects the strongest weakness by success-rate gap.
The framework maps validated weaknesses to controllable environmental factors and generates environments in the difficulty regimes where the policy struggles.
Across three navigation agents, weakness-conditioned adaptation outperforms matched random and hard-example alternatives on ProcTHOR; gains for Uni-NaVid and Gemini transfer to HM3D.
Iterative re-diagnosis tracks weaknesses that persist or shift as policies improve, enabling updated environment generation.
papers.selection_reason: Weakness-guided environment generation for embodied navigation agents.
papers.title: From Failures to Learnable Worlds: Policy-Conditioned Environment Generation for Navigation Agents
papers.tldr: WEDGE uses a policy’s observed failures to generate targeted training environments that address its current navigation weaknesses.

papers.abstract: MLLM-based detectors formulate vision-language grounding as autoregressive coordinate generation, yet in dense scenes, they often collapse into a box repetition loop, repeatedly emitting identical boxes until the decoding budget is exhausted. We trace this failure to historical-answer attention takeover: Under full-history autoregression, repeated coordinate tokens in the growing answer history attract disproportionate attention, crowding out the attention sinks needed to attend to new visual evidence. % To break this loop, in this paper, we propose \textbf{Compressed Window Auto-Regression} (WinAR). This new mechanism partitions a long answer sequence into consecutive generation windows and restricts full token-level autoregression to the current window only while compressing each previous window into a fixed set of latent tokens that condition subsequent decoding. This design reduces the repeated exposure to raw historical coordinates that triggers the attention takeover, yet preserves cross-window dependencies essential for coherent multi-object generation. On RSDense, which contains 200-2,000 objects per image, our model WinARDet improves RexOmni F1-score (IoU=0.5) from 32.16 to 39.36 over the baseline, while reducing the redundancy rate from 35.48% to 13.00%. WinARDet also generalizes across decoding strategies and output formats, including parallel box decoding and polygon generation, providing a practical paradigm for long-horizon vision-language grounding across scene densities.
authors: Chenxu Wang, Hangyi Kuang, Bo-Wen Yin, Yuxuan Li, Quan-Sheng Zeng, Yang Zhang, Xu Guo, Xiang Li, Qibin Hou
bullets: Dense-scene autoregressive detectors can repeatedly emit identical boxes until the decoding budget is exhausted.
The proposed Compressed Window Auto-Regression limits token-level attention to the current generation window.
Each previous window is compressed into fixed latent tokens, preserving cross-window dependencies while reducing historical-coordinate interference.
On RSDense, WinARDet raises F1 at IoU 0.5 from 32.16 to 39.36 and lowers redundancy from 35.48% to 13.00%.
The approach also extends to parallel box decoding and polygon generation across varying scene densities.
papers.selection_reason: Novel compressed window autoregression for MLLM-based dense vision-language grounding, relevant to multimodal LLMs and token efficiency.
papers.title: WinARDet: Compressed Window Auto-Regression for Long-Horizon Vision-Language Grounding
papers.tldr: WinARDet prevents repetitive box-generation loops in dense-scene vision-language grounding by compressing past decoding windows into latent tokens.

papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet strengthening their reasoning through reinforcement learning (RL) remains an open challenge. Any-order generation can suffer from entropy degradation, which narrows the reasoning paths available for exploration. Recent work mitigates this issue by applying standard GRPO with left-to-right generation. However, independently generating every rollout from the input prompt can leave alternative continuations from intermediate states underexplored, while trajectory-level advantages assign uniform credit to all tokens without distinguishing the contributions of individual reasoning segments. We propose ForkGRPO, an RL framework that couples efficient exploration with fine-grained segment-level credit assignment. It samples multiple continuations from high-entropy intermediate states along a reference trajectory, prioritizing textual boundaries and reusing shared prefixes. The continuations provide complementary learning signals: within-state group-relative advantages guide which continuations to reinforce, while Monte Carlo state-value differences indicate which reasoning segments improve expected outcomes. Among the evaluated architecture-preserving RL methods, ForkGRPO achieves the best performance on three of four benchmarks, while improving over the directly comparable JustGRPO by up to 1.2 percentage points and using up to 27.8% fewer generated tokens. ForkGRPO-Fast further achieves a $2.49\times$ training wall-clock speedup with negligible accuracy loss.
authors: Zhaoyan Jia, Chengwei Zhou, Gourav Datta, Massoud Pedram
bullets: Addresses entropy degradation and insufficient exploration in any-order diffusion generation.
Samples continuations from high-entropy intermediate states, prioritizing textual boundaries and reusing shared prefixes.
Uses group-relative advantages for continuation selection and Monte Carlo value differences for segment-level credit assignment.
Achieves the best results among evaluated architecture-preserving methods on three of four benchmarks, improving over JustGRPO by up to 1.2 percentage points.
Reduces generated tokens by up to 27.8%; ForkGRPO-Fast provides a 2.49× training speedup with negligible accuracy loss.
papers.selection_reason: Reinforcement learning method for diffusion LLMs, relevant to LLM architecture and training.
papers.title: ForkGRPO: Efficient Exploration and Fine-Grained Credit Assignment for Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: ForkGRPO improves reinforcement learning for diffusion language models by exploring alternative continuations efficiently and assigning credit at the reasoning-segment level.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models must reconcile conflicting text and images. Prior work has characterized the resulting behavior in terms of modality biases--e.g., a "blind faith in text"--but why preferences vary across models, domains, and input conditions remains unclear. We develop a predictive account from a Bayesian perspective, positing that VLMs combine conditionally independent evidence from each modality with prior beliefs, subject to modality-specific biases. The resulting two-parameter cue combination model accurately predicts VLM preferences under unseen combinations of input degradation and transfers to new forms of unreliability without refitting. Separating evidence strength from integration bias explains how VLMs can follow text even while weighting visual evidence more heavily, reconciling reports of text and vision dominance under a single combination rule.
authors: Josh Barua, Kyle Mahowald, William Rudman
bullets: Models combine conditionally independent visual and textual evidence with prior beliefs.
The framework separates evidence strength from integration bias, clarifying seemingly contradictory text- and vision-dominance findings.
It predicts model preferences for unseen combinations of input degradation.
The model transfers to new types of unreliability without refitting.
It offers a unified account of why modality preferences vary across models, domains, and conditions.
papers.selection_reason: Bayesian account of VLM evidence integration relevant to multimodal LLM behavior.
papers.title: Vision-Language Models Integrate Conflicting Evidence Like Biased Bayesian Observers
papers.tldr: A two-parameter Bayesian cue-combination model explains how vision-language models integrate conflicting text and image evidence with modality-specific biases.

papers.abstract: Whole-body control plays a crucial role in enabling humanoid robots to execute expressive motions. Faithful execution requires preserving both the intended action and its expressive characteristics. Existing whole-body trackers typically balance joint and keypoint tracking with physical stability across diverse motions, but these objectives do not necessarily prioritize the expressive characteristics of each action. Our analysis shows that lower average positional tracking error does not guarantee better preservation of dynamic and postural motion characteristics. To address this gap, we propose a residual learning framework with compensation objectives targeting amplitude, energy, body expansion, body lean, and pelvis height. To concentrate compensation while limiting interference with the underlying tracking behavior, motion-aware gating allocates correction capacity according to body-part activity, preserving larger correction ranges in more active parts and restricting them elsewhere. For each frozen tracker, we train motion-specific residual policies and distill them into a unified policy shared across motion categories. Simulation and physical experiments on the Unitree G1 across eight motion categories demonstrate superior preservation of dynamic and postural motion characteristics compared with the corresponding baselines.
authors: Lingfan Bao, Hanshang Zhu, Yan Pan, Jincheng Wang, Jingyang Yu, Tianhu Peng, Yiyang Jia, Dimitrios Kanoulas, Chengxu Zhou
bullets: Lower positional tracking error does not necessarily preserve dynamics or posture.
Residual policies compensate for amplitude, energy, body expansion, body lean, and pelvis height.
Motion-aware gating focuses corrections on active body parts while limiting interference elsewhere.
Motion-specific residuals are distilled into one unified policy across motion categories.
Simulation and physical experiments on a Unitree G1 across eight categories show improved expressive-characteristic preservation over corresponding baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Humanoid whole-body control with residual learning for expressive motion preservation fits robot learning and control.
papers.title: Beyond Kinematic Tracking: Preserving Expressive Characteristics in Humanoid Whole-Body Control
papers.tldr: A residual-learning framework helps humanoid whole-body controllers preserve expressive motion characteristics—not just positional accuracy—across diverse motions.

papers.abstract: User feedback enables LLMs to refine reusable personalized skills, but often mixes persistent preferences with request-specific corrections. Indiscriminately retaining both risks negative transfer, motivating selective retention at the level of individual requirements. We frame this challenge as selective transfer over atomic rules and propose SkillGrain, a framework for learning reusable personalized skills from user feedback. SkillGrain decomposes feedback into independently actionable rules, predicts their transferability, and retains only those suitable for future requests. To learn these decisions, we combine rubric-guided skill rewards with fine-grained credit assignment that separately evaluates rule content and retention decisions. We further jointly optimize skill induction and skill-conditioned generation through reinforcement learning, ensuring that learned skills support downstream personalization. We construct a benchmark spanning five personalized writing tasks to evaluate cross-request generalization. Experiments across three base models in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings show that SkillGrain achieves the best overall average performance among competing methods.
authors: Li Wang, Chen Zhang, Yirong Yang, Xingyu Chen, Jinkun Zhao, Tianhao Peng, Wenjun Wu
bullets: Separates persistent preferences from request-specific corrections to reduce negative transfer.
Decomposes feedback into atomic, independently actionable rules and predicts each rule’s transferability.
Uses rubric-guided rewards and fine-grained credit assignment to evaluate rule content and retention decisions separately.
Jointly optimizes skill induction and skill-conditioned generation with reinforcement learning.
Across five personalized writing tasks and three base models, reports the best overall average performance in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings.
papers.selection_reason: Selective retention of reusable skills from user feedback is a continual/online learning problem for LLMs.
papers.title: Learning What to Keep: Transfer-Aware Personal Skill Learning from User Feedback
papers.tldr: SkillGrain selectively retains feedback rules that are likely to transfer across future requests, improving reusable personalized skill learning.

papers.abstract: Does a language model answer better because its compressed memory contains useful document information? Replacing memory vectors with zeros can lower a trained model's score without showing that it outperforms a model trained without memory. We combine zeroing with separately trained models that cannot access stored text or receive the same constant input for every document. Across nine systems, some models rely on memory yet perform worse than the trained alternative. For example, in experiments that predict states in generated stories, zeroing memory worsens a model's prediction loss, yet a model trained without memory achieves lower loss than the original model with intact memory. On TriviaQA, giving xRAG memory from another question's passage raises F1, which measures word overlap with accepted answers, from 19.38 without a document to 24.78. Its effect on how often outputs contain an accepted answer is statistically uncertain. The question's retrieved passage scores higher still (29.88 F1). Thus a gain over no document alone does not establish that the gain requires the question's passage. Evaluations must therefore specify the comparison model, absolute performance, and generation and scoring conditions.
authors: Minsu Oh, Seunghui Jwa, Chanjun Park, Yeo-Chan Yoon
bullets: Zeroing memory can hurt performance without proving memory improves over a model trained without memory.
Across nine systems, some depend on memory yet perform worse than memory-free trained alternatives.
In story-state prediction, intact memory underperformed a separately trained no-memory model despite zeroing worsening loss.
On TriviaQA, unrelated passage memory increased xRAG F1 from 19.38 to 24.78, while the question’s passage reached 29.88; accepted-answer rates were statistically uncertain.
Evaluations should report comparison models, absolute performance, and generation/scoring conditions.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates compressed memory mechanisms in LLMs, directly relevant to LLM memory research.
papers.title: Evaluating Compressed Memory: Dependence, Utility, and Content Benefit
papers.tldr: Compressed-memory gains do not necessarily show that models use the correct document information, so evaluations need stronger comparison baselines and metrics.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for multi-turn agentic tasks that require interactions with users and environments over extended sequences of actions. A common approach to improving LLM agents is to use more capable expert models to provide training supervision, either by behavior cloning the expert's trajectories or by using the expert to correct the actions in trajectories generated by the weaker student model. However, expert LLMs can provide richer supervision than actions alone: they can directly generate textual critique that explain why specific actions are incorrect. We study whether training on such feedback benefits LLM agents and propose Critique-Augmented Agentic Fine-Tuning (CAFT), a framework that elicits textual expert feedback on student-generated trajectories. For each incorrect action, the expert yields both a corrected action and a textual critique explaining the student's mistake--which we then use as the training target for fine-tuning. Across four student models from the Nemotron 3 and Gemma 4 families on the agentic domains $\tau^2$-Bench Airline+Retail and WebShop, adding critiques to action-level supervision improves performance by 8% on average over action-only distillation. Additionally, CAFT checkpoints can also provide a better warm start for reinforcement learning than expert-trajectory distillation. Our results demonstrate that textual critiques can strengthen supervision for multi-turn LLM agents.
authors: Thomas Zeng, Zelei Cheng, Mingyang Zhou, Sambit Sahu, William Campbell, Genta Indra Winata
bullets: Expert feedback can explain why a student’s actions are incorrect, providing richer supervision than corrected actions alone.
CAFT elicits critiques and corrected actions from an expert on student-generated trajectories, then fine-tunes the agent on both.
Evaluated across four Nemotron 3 and Gemma 4 student models in Airline+Retail, WebShop, and related agentic settings.
Adding critiques improved performance by 8% on average over action-only distillation.
CAFT checkpoints also provided a stronger warm start for reinforcement learning than expert-trajectory distillation.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Critique-Augmented Agentic Fine-Tuning (CAFT) using textual expert feedback to improve multi-turn LLM agent performance, contributing to agent training methodologies.
papers.title: Beyond Corrected Actions: Training LLM Agents on Textual Critiques
papers.tldr: Training LLM agents with expert textual critiques alongside corrected actions improves multi-turn agent performance over action-only supervision.

papers.abstract: Multimodal models and agents have emerged to enable AI systems to learn from and interact with the real world more like humans by integrating information across multiple modalities. However, enabling multimodal agents to continually acquire useful information from complex, heterogeneous multimodal data remains a significant challenge as they move toward long-horizon tasks and lifelong settings. Addressing this challenge requires effective memory mechanisms that can maintain continuity across sessions, adapt to changing users and environments, and refine memory-management policies through accumulated experience. We introduce a two-axis analytical framework for multimodal agent memory structured around two key questions: how multimodal information is formed and represented (Axis I, Formation and Representation), and how its management adapts with accumulated experience (Axis II, Memory Management). Axis I, Formation and Representation, characterizes what information is retained and how it is encoded (e.g., modality-specific embeddings, textual and structured records, latent and parametric representations) to support subsequent reasoning and action. Axis II, Memory Management, distinguishes three tiers: T1 Static Memory reuses fixed memory; T2 Dynamic Memory updates memory through a stable policy; and T3 Self-Evolving Memory updates memory through an evolving policy. Based on this framework, we synthesize recurring design patterns and derive principles for balancing source fidelity with abstraction, maintaining temporal validity and provenance, grounding memory use in recoverable evidence, and evolving memory policies over time. Furthermore, we discuss the challenges and potential future directions for the memory mechanism of multimodal agents.
authors: Minghao Guo, Qingyue Jiao, Xiujin Liu, Jianhong Pang, Ruimeng Yang, Naihao Xu, Liwei Che, Haochen Xue, Ziqi Wang, Xinying Cai, Jiaxuan Luo, Jiaxin Deng, Xuesong Ye, Jintao Qu, Wenyao Gao, Jingwen Gu, Chenyang Zhao, Shichun Liu, Guibin Zhang, Zefang Liu, Siyin Wang, Wujiang Xu, Danrui Li, Zeru Shi, Woongyeong Yeo, Shuang Liu, Wei-Chieh Huang, Weizhi Zhang, Tianyu Yang, Kangsan Kim, Yebowen Hu, Bowen Wen, Bowen Jiang, Haohao Su, Ming Yin, Sheldon Yu, Mian Zhang, Yuyan Chen, Hanrong Zhang, Kai Mei, Zihao Zhang, Mingyu Jin, Xi Zhu, Hengyi Wang, Tianxin Wei, Linyong Nan, Zhenwen Liang, Zhendong Chu, Ziqi Huang, Yongye Su, Sixun Dong, Shujian Liu, Kaiqu Liang, Jiaojiao Han, Zhaoye Fei, Kun Wang, Shihan Dou, Zhichun Guo, Xingjian Diao, Zeqi Gu, Heng Wang, Tao Feng, Cheng Qian, Hamid Palangi, Silei Xu, Xi Yun, Yi Zhu, Shilong Liu, Qingsong Wen, Sung Ju Hwang, Zuxuan Wu, Yu-Gang Jiang, Yiyu Shi, Dimitris N. Metaxas, Jiaxuan You, Julian McAuley, Mengdi Wang, Jiawei Han, Philip S. Yu, Ziyi Ye
bullets: Motivated by the difficulty of continually retaining useful information from complex, heterogeneous multimodal data.
Axis I classifies memory by how information is formed and represented, including embeddings, textual or structured records, and latent or parametric forms.
Axis II categorizes memory management into static, dynamically updated, and self-evolving policies.
The framework synthesizes design patterns and principles for abstraction, temporal validity, provenance, evidence grounding, and policy evolution.
It outlines open challenges and future directions for multimodal agent memory.
papers.selection_reason: Framework for multimodal agent memory, relevant to memory mechanisms for embodied agents and long-horizon adaptation.
papers.title: Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning: The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory
papers.tldr: This paper presents a two-axis framework for understanding how multimodal agents form, represent, manage, and evolve memory for long-horizon, lifelong interaction.

papers.abstract: Embodied visual tracking requires a robot to identify a designated target from visual observations and control its own motion to follow that target through an environment. Following an isolated person is a comparatively simple demonstration of embodied visual tracking, but following the intended person among distractors remains challenging. Existing methods exhibit a substantial drop in success from single-target to distractor tracking, motivating a focus on the shared spaces that person-following robots must navigate. We present \method{}, a vision--language waypoint policy built around the hypothesis that visual and language representations should be aligned before tracking-specific motion is learned. The policy combines complementary frozen visual encoders, multiscale temporal context, a transformer backbone, and a lightweight head for robot-centric waypoint prediction. Its training progresses through vision--language alignment, multimodal reasoning mid-training, and tracking specialization on 19,532 oracle episodes. Compared with 41.54\% distractor-tracking success for our earlier OmTrackVLA model, the complete multi-stage recipe achieves 55.80\%. We then explore on-policy refinement using filtered oracle labels for states visited by the policy. This preliminary study adds 2.42 percentage points of distractor-tracking success, reaching 58.22\%, while reducing collision rate by 1.99 pts. The final policy records the highest distractor- and ambiguous-tracking success rates among the compared methods. These results support staged multimodal learning as a promising direction for tracking among distractors and motivate further study of on-policy refinement for person following in shared spaces.
authors: Kyusong Lee, Heting Ying, Tiancheng Zhao
bullets: Targets the challenge of following the intended person in shared spaces with visual distractors.
Uses frozen visual encoders, multiscale temporal context, a transformer, and waypoint prediction.
Trains in stages: vision-language alignment, multimodal reasoning, and tracking specialization.
On-policy refinement raises distractor-tracking success from 55.80% to 58.22% and reduces collision rate by 1.99 percentage points.
The study is preliminary and motivates further work on on-policy refinement for person following.
papers.selection_reason: Vision-language waypoint policy for embodied tracking, relevant to embodied navigation and VLA.
papers.title: VLX-Go: Robust Embodied Tracking through Multi-Stage Learning and On-Policy Refinement

papers.abstract: Multimodal knowledge graphs (MMKGs) organize information across different modalities to support multimodal Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), which aims to improve the performance of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). The effectiveness of these multimodal Graph RAG methods largely depends on the quality of the constructed MMKGs. However, most existing methods construct MMKGs without explicit guidance on graph quality, while reinforcement learning (RL)-based methods that rely on final-answer correctness may provide only indirect feedback on MMKG quality. To address these limitations, we propose MMKG-R1, a novel MMKG-quality-driven RL framework for training an MLLM as a multimodal knowledge constructor. To be specific, MMKG-R1 introduces multiple quality-aware rewards to directly evaluate both the quality of information extracted from individual knowledge sources and the quality of the assembled MMKG. These rewards are then used to guide the RL training. Experiments across multiple datasets show that MMKG-R1 constructs MMKGs that improve downstream question-answering accuracy.
authors: Zongyu Wu, Yilong Wang, Xiaochen Wang, Minhua Lin, Yuan Zhong, Fenglong Ma, Xiang Zhang, Suhang Wang
bullets: Targets the lack of explicit guidance for MMKG quality in existing construction methods.
Trains an MLLM as a multimodal knowledge constructor with reinforcement learning.
Uses rewards that assess both extracted information from individual sources and the assembled graph.
Experiments on multiple datasets show improved downstream question-answering accuracy.
The abstract does not specify quantitative gains or detailed limitations.
papers.selection_reason: RL-based MLLM training for multimodal knowledge graph construction, relevant to multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: MMKG-R1: Constructing Multimodal Knowledge Graphs via Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: MMKG-R1 uses quality-aware reinforcement learning to train an MLLM to construct better multimodal knowledge graphs for improved multimodal Graph RAG question answering.

papers.abstract: This paper presents LLM-jp-4, a family of Japanese sovereign large language models (LLMs) developed with an emphasis on transparency, reproducibility, and practical usability. LLM-jp-4 comprises an 8B dense model and a 32B-A3B mixture-of-experts model, both trained from scratch on approximately 12 trillion tokens. To support independent verification and reproduction, we establish explicit criteria for selecting training data, external models, and software, and make the development process publicly available. Evaluation results demonstrate substantial improvements over previous LLM-jp models and competitive performance against open-weight models of similar scale. By documenting the development principles, training procedures, and empirical findings of LLM-jp-4, we aim to provide a reference for future sovereign AI development.
authors: LLM-jp, :, Chaoran Liu, Daisuke Kawahara, Hideyuki Tachibana, Hirokazu Kiyomaru, Jun Suzuki, Koshi Eguchi, Kouta Nakayama, Qianying Liu, Rio Yokota, Ryo Takahashi, Sadao Kurohashi, Sosuke Hosokawa, Taishi Nakamura, Takashi Kodama, Yun-Ang Wu, Yusuke Miyao, Yusuke Oda

papers.tldr: LLM-jp-4 is a transparent, reproducible family of Japanese sovereign LLMs that achieves improved and competitive performance through large-scale from-scratch training.

papers.abstract: Reliable recognition of accessibility-critical objects (e.g., audible pedestrian signals, door-activation buttons, and handrails) is essential for assistive navigation technologies that support safe, independent mobility for blind and low-vision (BLV) users. Yet these categories are underrepresented in existing large-scale vision datasets, and the few datasets that include them suffer from limited class coverage, inconsistent annotations, and poor diversity. We introduce NavAble, a large-scale dataset spanning 11 accessibility-critical object classes, combining 41K curated open-source images with 8K newly collected, densely annotated real-world images. To extend scale and diversity, we develop a synthetic data generation pipeline that renders high-fidelity 3D assets across 37 environments under diverse styles and viewpoints, yielding 452K frames with rich ground-truth annotations from 565 assets. The pipeline minimizes manual effort by combining automated web image crawling, VLM-based filtering, SAM 3D-based asset generation, and convenient camera trajectory configuration, enabling large-scale data generation at a diversity unattainable through manual collection. Experiments show that fine-tuning existing segmentation models on the NavAble Dataset achieves reliable accessibility-object segmentation (>80% mIoU on our held-out test set). We also demonstrate the effectiveness of synthetic data augmentation, which yields up to +3.5 mIoU over real-world-only fine-tuning. Beyond benchmark evaluation, validation on egocentric data from two mobility-assistive robots demonstrates improved perception reliability in real-world navigation scenarios. Together, NavAble establishes a scalable foundation for BLV navigation perception, directly addressing the data scarcity and embodiment gaps. The dataset and pipeline are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/NavAble/NeurIPS_2026_BLV.
authors: Hochul Hwang, Jahir Sadik Monon, Soowan Yang, Shiven Umeshbhai Patel, Anh Nhat Hong Nguyen, Kien Nguyen, Keshav Garg, Dylan Gage, Duretti Hordofaa, Anshu Anjna, Eshed Ohn-Bar, Donghyun Kim
bullets: Covers 11 accessibility-critical object classes using 41K curated images, 8K densely annotated real-world images, and 452K synthetic frames.
Generates diverse synthetic data across 37 environments, 565 3D assets, and varied styles and viewpoints.
Combines web crawling, VLM-based filtering, SAM 3D asset generation, and configurable camera trajectories to reduce manual data-collection effort.
Fine-tuned segmentation models exceed 80% mIoU on a held-out test set; synthetic augmentation improves performance by up to 3.5 mIoU over real-only training.
Robot egocentric validation shows improved perception reliability in real-world mobility-assistive navigation scenarios.

papers.title: NavAble: A Large-Scale Dataset and Synthetic Data Generation Pipeline for Blind Navigation
papers.tldr: NavAble provides a large, diverse dataset and synthetic-data pipeline for improving recognition of accessibility-critical objects in blind and low-vision navigation.

papers.abstract: Robotic ultrasound can standardize image acquisition and reduce operator workload and variability, but policy learning remains limited by the lack of realistic, controllable simulation environments. While controllable world models have advanced rapidly in natural-image domains, ultrasound world modeling remains challenging because each frame captures only a cross-section of unobserved 3D anatomy, causing small probe motions to induce large appearance changes. Existing approaches rely on robot-tracked poses and latent-space prediction, but do not directly generate the observations required for interactive control. We propose SonoWorld, a causal ultrasound world model that learns video dynamics from unlabeled clinical videos and grounds them to 6-DoF control using a small set of freehand clinical scans tracked with an EM sensor. SonoWorld is trained in three stages: pretraining a latent-action-conditioned video diffusion model on around 6.9 million unlabeled multi-organ ultrasound frames; grounding the learned video dynamics to metric probe poses with a small EM-tracked thyroid dataset; and applying distribution matching distillation to enable causal, long-horizon autoregressive generation with selectively caching eviction tokens at inference time. We evaluate controllability through pose-following fidelity, round-trip consistency, and axis-specific control under synthetic actions on held-out tracked scans, and further validate it with a user study. In model-based action discrimination, SonoWorld correctly ranks the target-directed probe motion over an equal-magnitude opposite motion in up to 74.8% of trials. To our knowledge, SonoWorld is the first causal, pose-controllable ultrasound world model learned primarily from freehand clinical videos, providing a data-driven interactive environment for robotic ultrasound data acquisition and policy evaluation.
authors: Zefan Yang, Zheyuan Zhang, Boris Maihe, Yikang Liu, Hang Yu, Ankush Mukherjee, Xiao Chen, Pingkun Yan, Terrence Chen, Shanhui Sun
bullets: Addresses the lack of realistic, controllable simulation environments for robotic ultrasound, where small probe motions can cause large image changes.
Learns video dynamics from about 6.9 million unlabeled multi-organ ultrasound frames and grounds them to 6-DoF probe poses using a small EM-tracked thyroid dataset.
Uses staged training with latent-action-conditioned video diffusion, pose grounding, and distribution-matching distillation for causal long-horizon generation.
Evaluated pose-following, round-trip consistency, axis-specific control, and user-study performance on held-out tracked scans.

papers.title: SonoWorld: Towards Interactive Pose-Controllable Ultrasound World Models
papers.tldr: SonoWorld is a causal ultrasound world model that generates pose-controllable video for interactive robotic ultrasound simulation and policy evaluation.

papers.abstract: Jailbreak attacks against large language models (LLMs) are evaluated using attack success rate (ASR), which depends on correctly identifying responses that fulfill prohibited requests. Existing evaluators can mistake refusals or topically related responses for successful attacks. We show that changing only the judge LLM can alter reported ASR by up to $82$ percentage points. We introduce the semantic reconstruction game, a training-free evaluator that decomposes compliance judgments into constrained semantic comparisons. Given only a response, an LLM reconstructs the request answered by its substantive content, excluding information merely repeated or refused. The game compares this reconstruction against similar decoy requests to determine whether it matches the original request, allowing abstention when neither candidate matches. Across three off-the-shelf LLM judges, the game achieves the lowest mean error against human labels among evaluated methods and reduces variation in reported ASR. It prioritizes avoiding false positives, even at the cost of missing some successful jailbreaks.
authors: Liam Davis, Romain Emil-Popescu, Suman Jana
bullets: Existing jailbreak evaluation can misclassify refusals or merely related answers as successful attacks.
Changing only the judging LLM can shift reported attack success rates by up to 82 percentage points.
The method reconstructs the request answered by a response’s substantive content, excluding repeated or refused information.
It compares the reconstruction with the original and decoy requests, while allowing abstention when neither matches.
Across three off-the-shelf judges, it had the lowest mean error against human labels and reduced ASR variation, but may miss some successful jailbreaks.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free semantic reconstruction evaluator for LLM jailbreak compliance; relevant to LLM evaluation and safety.
papers.title: Did the LLM Answer the Question? A Semantic Reconstruction Game for Jailbreak Evaluation
papers.tldr: A training-free semantic reconstruction evaluator makes jailbreak success-rate judgments more reliable by reducing false positives and judge-dependent variation.

papers.abstract: One-step diffusion distillation achieves strong performance on small datasets but remains insufficient for high-resolution or complex text-to-image settings. Extending to multistep distillation often requires training data, suffers from early-step degradation, inconsistent outputs across sampling budgets, and incurs high computational cost. We identify that these limitations stem from simultaneous training, where a single adapted network approximates multiple score functions of different student distributions at once, causing biased distribution matching and unstable optimization. Therefore, we propose Progressive Multistep Data-free Distillation (PMDD), which assigns a dedicated adapted network per student distribution while avoiding the memory overhead of maintaining multiple adapted networks. Combined with a stage-wise unforget loss to preserve earlier-step generations, PMDD reduces optimization bias in the student, provides faster convergence, and a single unified model that supports multiple inference budgets. Extensive experiments show that PMDD matches or outperforms data-free few-step baselines at every multistep budget, reaches FID 1.99 on ImageNet 64x64 in two steps, below its 512-NFE teacher (2.32), and achieves FID 7.76 on zero-shot COCO 512x512, while requiring 4-5x less training compute than data-free DMDv2 to support three inference budgets.
authors: Ngoc Duy Tran, Kien Do, Duc Thanh Nguyen, Truyen Tran
bullets: Multistep distillation is challenging for high-resolution and complex text-to-image generation because it can require data, degrade early steps, produce inconsistent budgets, and be computationally expensive.
PMDD assigns a dedicated adapted network to each student distribution without retaining all networks simultaneously, reducing optimization bias.
A stage-wise unforget loss preserves earlier-step generations during progressive training.
The unified model matches or exceeds data-free few-step baselines across budgets, reaching FID 1.99 on ImageNet 64×64 in two steps and 7.76 on zero-shot COCO 512×512.
It uses 4–5× less training compute than data-free DMDv2 when supporting three inference budgets.
papers.selection_reason: Data-free multistep diffusion distillation reduces training and inference compute, relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: Data-free Multistep Diffusion Distillation
papers.tldr: PMDD enables efficient data-free multistep diffusion distillation by progressively reducing distribution-matching bias while supporting multiple sampling budgets in one model.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense token-level supervision on student rollouts, but this supervision can become unreliable when the student and teacher diverge, either because of a large initial policy gap or compounding errors in long-horizon reasoning and tool use. We introduce Divergence-Triggered Dynamic Distillation (DTDD), an adaptive OPD framework that uses segment-level student-teacher divergence to trigger teacher takeover during training. When divergence triggers an intervention during reasoning, the student prefix continues to receive standard OPD supervision. The teacher then generates a recovery suffix, which the student learns through behavior cloning, using cross-entropy on the teacher-generated tokens. We evaluate DTDD in three regimes: long-horizon reasoning, distillation from a base initialization without offline supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and multi-turn agents. We also compare alternative trigger designs and teacher-intervention rates. DTDD reduces the post-warmup peak gradient norm by $8.6\times$ and, from a base initialization, reaches $21.3\%$ held-out math accuracy in $2.6\times$ fewer optimizer updates than OPD; both methods finish near $22\%$. It improves best-observed performance by $4.8$ and $4.1$ percentage points on ALFWorld with LoRA and agentic code, respectively. Ablations show that segment-averaged triggers outperform token-spike triggers. Behavior cloning is also more effective than the tested OPD surrogate for training teacher-generated recoveries. Across 23 experimental arms, takeover tends to help when the teacher substantially outperforms the OPD-trained student, provided that the teacher can recover from student-visited states, the student can learn those recoveries, and teacher intervention is neither excessive nor insufficient.
authors: Qijia He, Zequn Li, Spencer Luo, Tianle Chen, Pradyumna Narayana, Zixian Ma, Ranjay Krishna, Lan Nie, Sugato Basu
bullets: Problem: OPD supervision can become unreliable after large policy gaps or compounding reasoning and tool-use errors.
Method: Segment-level divergence triggers teacher intervention; the student prefix receives OPD supervision, while a teacher-generated recovery suffix is learned via behavior cloning.
Results: DTDD reduced post-warmup peak gradient norm by 8.6× and reached 21.3% held-out math accuracy in 2.6× fewer updates from a base initialization, with similar final accuracy to OPD.
It improved best-observed ALFWorld and agentic-code performance by 4.8 and 4.1 percentage points, respectively.
Scope: Takeover helps when the teacher is substantially better and can recover from student states, while intervention rates must avoid being too high or too low.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive on-policy distillation for LLM reasoning and agentic training; relevant to LLM training methods.
papers.title: DTDD: Divergence-Triggered Dynamic Distillation for Reliable On-Policy Supervision
papers.tldr: DTDD stabilizes on-policy distillation by having the teacher take over when student–teacher divergence signals likely rollout failure, improving training speed and best observed performance in several long-horizon and agentic settings.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning for code usually rewards passing tests, which a model can do while remaining wrong on the inputs the tests do not cover. A program verifier instead decides whether a program satisfies a formal specification for all inputs. Language models are almost always paired with verifiers at inference time only, and turning a verifier into a reward raises two difficulties. It reports only acceptance or rejection, which gives no gradient when every attempt fails, and a policy can cheat it, most simply by telling it to assume what the proof was supposed to establish. We build an agentic environment and reward that address both. The reward reads the verifier's diagnostics rather than its verdict, scoring a candidate by the weighted fraction of proof obligations it discharges, extended with hidden probes from a reference proof's annotations. An integrity audit outranks the verifier, rejecting any candidate that alters the specification or assumes what it was meant to prove. The model works as an agent against a live verifier over many turns, with a separately trained proof specialist as a frozen collaborator. Across Qwen3 models from 1.7B to 14B and a 35B Qwen3.6 mixture-of-experts model, held-out verification on code generation rises from 66.1% to 93.5% on DafnyBench and from 56.3% to 100% on SWE-Proof. This reward leads every other training signal we compare, including a binary pass-or-fail reward trained under otherwise identical settings, with the widest margin on code generation. When the agent must also deliver the repository patch, graded by each project's withheld tests, the fraction of held-out issues it resolves rises from 59.6% to 72.5%. Evaluated unchanged on three verification suites withheld from training, the checkpoints improve on all of them, including one whose language and verifier are absent from training.
authors: George Ma, Yuhao Zhang, Bing He, Zeren Shui, Ferhat Erata, Murali Krishna Ramanathan, Somayeh Sojoudi, Hao Zhou
bullets: Addresses sparse verifier rewards and policies that exploit or weaken specifications.
Scores partial progress from discharged proof obligations, augmented with hidden reference-proof probes.
Uses an integrity audit to reject specification changes or circular assumptions.
Agents interact with a live verifier over multiple turns alongside a frozen proof specialist.
Verification improves across model sizes and unseen suites, while held-out issue resolution rises from 59.6% to 72.5%.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic RL with verifier-grounded rewards for code generation across Qwen LLMs; directly relevant to LLM training and reasoning.
papers.title: Verifier-Grounded Agentic RL for Provably Correct Code
papers.tldr: Verifier-grounded agentic RL substantially improves formally verified code generation and held-out software fixes by using diagnostic proof feedback and integrity checks.

papers.abstract: We present Keypoint Constraint Learning (KCL), a framework for learning task-relevant motion constraints from visual demonstrations and for planning safely with the extracted constraints. To make constraint learning tractable from RGB-D observations, we represent demonstrations using sparse 3D object-centric keypoints and semantic mask centroids extracted through segmentation, visual feature clustering, and point tracking. In this reduced geometric space, we learn keypoint dynamics and infer distance- and orientation-based constraints that make the expert trajectories feasible and approximately locally optimal by enforcing KKT optimality conditions in the reduced state space. We then plan with the learned constraints under uncertainty, using robustness margins derived from accumulated prediction error, and provide a theoretical analysis of how keypoint perception error and learned dynamics error affect the recovered constraints. We evaluate KCL on visual demonstrations from navigation to rigid/deformable manipulation, showing that it recovers multi-stage geometric constraints and outperforms baselines in downstream safe planning.
authors: Zheng Qiu, Zhouyu Zhang, Ninghan Zhong, Glen Chou
bullets: Represents RGB-D demonstrations with object-centric keypoints and semantic mask centroids extracted from segmentation, feature clustering, and tracking.
Learns keypoint dynamics and infers distance- and orientation-based constraints using KKT optimality conditions.
Plans safely under uncertainty by adding robustness margins based on accumulated prediction error.
Analyzes how perception and learned-dynamics errors affect the recovered constraints.
Evaluations across navigation and rigid/deformable manipulation show recovery of multi-stage constraints and improved downstream safe planning over baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Learns keypoint constraints from visual demonstrations for safe motion planning; relevant to robot learning and navigation.
papers.title: Learning Keypoint Constraints from Visual Demonstrations for Safe Motion Planning
papers.tldr: KCL learns geometric motion constraints from sparse 3D visual keypoints and uses them for uncertainty-aware safe planning across navigation and manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: This work concerns our submission for the Multilingual track of the 2026 BabyLM Challenge. We improve on our baseline using data that has been summarized and translated by an LLM, showing that higher-quality data can come from synthetic sources. We further improve with 2 simple changes: using a larger model, and using a character-level vocabulary. Both of these changes require LoRA-style fine-tuning for realizing their full potential. We dub our final Qwen3-based model Qwenfant, which, at the time of submission, ranks 1st in the Multilingual track.
authors: Lukas Edman, Alexander Fraser
bullets: Uses LLM-generated summaries and translations as higher-quality synthetic training data.
Improves the baseline with a larger model and character-level vocabulary.
Finds that both changes reach their full potential with LoRA-style fine-tuning.
The submitted Qwenfant model ranked first in the 2026 Multilingual track at submission time.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a character-level BabyLM model (Qwenfant) trained on synthetic parallel text, contributing to LLM training methodologies and multilingual language modeling.
papers.title: Qwenfant: Train Big Character-level BabyLMs on Concise Parallel Text
papers.tldr: Qwenfant improves Multilingual BabyLM Challenge performance by training a larger, character-level Qwen3 model on concise LLM-summarized and translated text with LoRA-style fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: In so-called "Industry 4.0," integrated sensors, analytics tools, and other digital technologies supplement industrial workflows, potentiating enhanced visibility and automation. Prognostics and health management (PHM) and natural language processing (NLP) practitioners alike have explored the application of large language models (LLMs) to industrial asset management, but many prior works' focus on exam-like benchmarks has limited their assessment of LLMs' ability to automate practical operations. Herein, we introduce CoffeeBench, a fault diagnostics task for LLM agents, using a simulated appliance. The LLMs we evaluate struggle to consistently identify faults from the sensor information alone, but the best-performing ones can iteratively refine the fault-option space to eventually obtain a successful diagnosis. Our subsequent analyses, therefore, focus on: differentiating models by diagnostic efficiency (RQ1); examining the lagging performance of the three worst models (RQ2); and identifying viable heuristics for selective prediction (RQ3), including that initial diagnostic uncertainty and LLM-judged soundness of reasoning are high-signal predictors of diagnostic success. In addition to our benchmark results (Section 3.1), we provide practical insights for improving the performance of the open-weight models on CoffeeBench, such as by explicitly tracking episode state on their behalf to reduce timeouts (Section 3.2) or applying a deliberation loop to refine diagnostic hypotheses (Section 3.3).
authors: Lucas H. McCabe, Sarah Lukens, H. Howie Huang
bullets: Introduces CoffeeBench, a fault-diagnosis benchmark for LLM agents operating on a simulated appliance.
Evaluates diagnostic efficiency, poor-performing models, and heuristics for selectively trusting predictions.
The strongest models can narrow the fault-option space iteratively to eventually reach successful diagnoses.
Initial diagnostic uncertainty and the model’s judged reasoning soundness predict diagnostic success.
Practical improvements include explicitly tracking episode state to reduce timeouts and using deliberation loops to refine hypotheses.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces CoffeeBench for diagnosing appliance faults using LLM agents, focusing on agent reasoning and efficiency in a simulated industrial context.
papers.title: Can LLM Agents Efficiently Identify Appliance Faults? Insights From Diagnosing a Simulated Appliance
papers.tldr: CoffeeBench shows that LLM agents struggle to reliably diagnose simulated appliance faults from sensor data alone, but iterative hypothesis refinement and uncertainty-based selection can improve practical diagnosis.

papers.abstract: We present Kandinsky S2V 1.0, an open family of speech-to-video models for controllable audio-driven human animation, comprising Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Lite (2B parameters) and Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro (21B parameters). From a single reference image, a speech waveform, and a text prompt, the models generate long-form 25 FPS video in which lip motion, expression, pose, and gesture follow the speech. The architecture draws text and audio conditioning from one Qwen2.5-Omni model and adds a reference-aware three-scale visual memory. Training starts from the Kandinsky 5.0 Video foundation models [1] and combines mixed reference-memory layouts with an area-adaptive face loss. The training corpus contains 1.17M single-speaker clips selected by active-speaker detection, with captions generated directly in English and Russian. A side-by-side human evaluation against the strongest open-source baseline and two proprietary commercial models shows that Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro performs comparably to or better than these models on average and is also preferred for lip synchronization. On common speech to video benchmarks, Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Lite and Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro rank among the top performing models according to mean rank over five reported metrics. Beyond the base models, we provide {\pi}-Flow distilled variants of both Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Lite and Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro. The distilled Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro model generates video in 16 sampling steps without classifier-free guidance, achieving a 5.4 times end-to-end speedup over the base model, while matching or exceeding it on nearly all reported benchmark metrics. To accelerate open research and deployment in speech-to-video generation, we release the code, model checkpoints, and diffusers integration under the MIT license.
authors: Nikolay Semenov, Artem Riabinin, Sergey Bassenko, Anna Averchenkova, Julia Agafonova, Anastasia Aliaskina, Kirill Kozlov, Lev Novitskiy, Nikita Samsonov, Nikolai Gerasimenko, Denis Dimitrov
bullets: Generates long-form 25 FPS avatar video from one image, speech waveform, and text prompt.
Uses unified text/audio conditioning, three-scale reference-aware visual memory, and area-adaptive face loss.
Includes Lite (2B) and Pro (21B) models trained on 1.17M active-speaker clips.
Pro performs comparably to or better than evaluated open and proprietary models, with preferred lip synchronization; both rank highly on common benchmarks.
π-Flow distillation enables the Pro model to generate in 16 steps without classifier-free guidance, delivering a reported 5.4× end-to-end speedup while largely preserving quality.
papers.selection_reason: Audio-driven avatar video generation, relevant to video diffusion and generation.
papers.title: Kandinsky S2V 1.0: Audio-Driven Avatar Video Generation
papers.tldr: Kandinsky S2V 1.0 is an open speech-to-video family that animates a reference image with synchronized speech-driven lip motion, expressions, poses, and gestures, with strong benchmark performance and a faster distilled variant.

papers.abstract: Understanding neural scaling laws is increasingly important for theory and practice, yet first-principles explanations remain limited even in simple settings. In this work, we study capacity-limited scaling in a bottlenecked bigram model with power-law (Zipf) token statistics, viewed as an analytically tractable toy model of a large language model. Fixed random embeddings serve as a proxy for representational capacity and induce an explicit bottleneck of width, allowing us to derive scaling laws for prediction regret as a function of model width, vocabulary size, and the Zipf exponent. Our results complement recent theoretical accounts based on optimization dynamics by isolating scaling due purely to representational constraints. In the appropriate regime, the theory recovers the functional form of classical neural scaling laws and suggests that heavy-tailed language statistics may underlie both optimization- and capacity-driven scaling. Experiments natural language datasets (WikiText2, OpenWebText) closely match the predicted curves.
authors: Julian Enoch, Elvis Dohmatob
bullets: Studies prediction regret under Zipf-distributed token statistics.
